questions.title: Give Jane read access to Pods
questions.scenario: In namespace 'dev', user 'jane' must be able to get and list Pods - nothing more, and only in that namespace.
questions.tip: Role/RoleBinding are namespaced; ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding are cluster-wide. Always finish with 'kubectl auth can-i'.
questions.stakes: Forget -n and the Role lands in 'default': Jane stays locked out of 'dev' and pings you at 2 a.m.
questions.analogy: A Role is a key card for one floor; a RoleBinding hands the card to a person.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the namespaced permission set (a Role) named 'pod-reader'. Type the correct command in full.

options.why: A ClusterRole is cluster-scoped: '-n' is ignored and the object is not limited to 'dev'.
No '-n dev': the Role lands in the current namespace (usually 'default').
The flags are singular: --verb and --resource.

s1.explain: A Role is namespaced, so the permission cannot leak outside 'dev'; -n dev puts it there. 'create role' with --verb/--resource is also far faster than writing YAML.
s1.hint: Namespaced permissions = a Role. The generator takes verbs and resources as singular flags; mind the namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Bind that Role to user 'jane' (binding name: read-pods).

options.why: It references a ClusterRole, but 'pod-reader' is a Role: the binding would grant nothing.
A ClusterRoleBinding has no --role flag; it can only bind ClusterRoles.
--serviceaccount expects 'namespace:name' and targets ServiceAccounts, not users.

s2.explain: A Role alone grants nothing: the RoleBinding is what gives it to someone. It links the Role to a subject (user, group or ServiceAccount) inside that one namespace.
s2.hint: A RoleBinding links the Role to a subject. Which flag names a user? It must live in the Role's namespace.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Verify that jane can list Pods in 'dev'.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=jane -n dev
kubectl auth can-i list pods --user=jane -n dev
options.why: --user picks a credential entry in your kubeconfig; impersonation is done with --as.
'can-i' is a sub-command of 'auth'.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i pods list --as=jane -n dev
options.why: Order matters: verb first, then resource.

s3.explain: 'can-i' asks the API server what it would really answer, so you test the final RBAC result. --as=jane impersonates her; 'yes' proves the Role and the binding work together.
s3.hint: kubectl can ask the authorizer on someone's behalf: impersonate jane, same verb, resource and namespace.

questions.title: Upgrade a worker node
questions.scenario: The control plane already runs v1.37.1. Upgrade worker 'node01' to v1.37.1 (Pods are running on it). The kubeadm package on node01 is already upgraded.
questions.tip: Worker upgrade order: drain -> kubeadm upgrade node -> upgrade kubelet/kubectl packages + restart kubelet -> uncordon.
questions.stakes: Skip the drain and the Pods on that node die mid-request while users watch.
questions.analogy: Like closing a lane before roadworks: drain, fix, reopen (uncordon).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - From the control plane: safely evict the workloads from node01 and make it unschedulable.

options.why: Cordon only marks the node unschedulable; running Pods are NOT evicted.
Refuses to proceed when DaemonSet Pods (CNI, kube-proxy) or emptyDir volumes exist: it needs the two extra flags.
Removes the Node object entirely; the node would have to re-join the cluster.

s1.explain: Drain cordons the node (no new Pods) and evicts the running ones so they restart elsewhere instead of dying with the upgrade. It refuses unless you accept that DaemonSet Pods stay (--ignore-daemonsets) and emptyDir data is lost (--delete-emptydir-data).
s1.hint: Evict and cordon in one command. DaemonSet Pods cannot leave, and emptyDir data is lost on eviction: both need consent.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - On node01 (after ssh): upgrade its local kubelet configuration.

options.why: 'apply' is only for the FIRST control-plane node.
'plan' only reports the available versions; it changes nothing.

s2.explain: A worker has no control plane to upgrade: 'kubeadm upgrade node' only updates its local kubelet configuration ('upgrade apply' is for the first control-plane node). Afterwards upgrade the kubelet package and restart it.
s2.hint: On a worker, kubeadm does not 'apply' a version: it updates the node's own kubelet configuration.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The kubelet is upgraded and restarted. From the control plane, let node01 receive Pods again.

options.why: That is the opposite: it makes the node unschedulable.
There is no such command.

s3.explain: Drain marked the node SchedulingDisabled and nothing removes that by itself: without uncordon the upgraded node stays empty forever. The classic forgotten last step.
s3.hint: drain left the Node marked unschedulable; undo exactly that.

questions.title: Let the auditors read Nodes
questions.scenario: Members of the group 'auditors' (for example user 'kim') must be able to get, list and watch Nodes. Nodes are cluster-scoped, so a namespaced Role will not do.
questions.tip: Cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces, storageclasses) can only be granted by a ClusterRole bound with a ClusterRoleBinding.
questions.stakes: A Role grants nothing on Nodes: auditors hit 'Forbidden' on audit day.
questions.analogy: A namespace is a room; Nodes are the building itself, so you need a building pass (ClusterRole).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create a ClusterRole named 'node-reader' allowing get, list and watch on nodes.

options.why: A Role lives in one namespace (here 'default'): it can never grant access to cluster-scoped Nodes.
'read' is not an RBAC verb: kubectl rejects it. The read verbs are get, list and watch.
nodes/status is only the status subresource: 'kubectl get nodes' would still be forbidden.

s1.explain: Nodes are cluster-scoped, so the permission must be a ClusterRole: a namespaced Role cannot grant access to them. The built-in view/edit/admin roles do not cover Nodes for a read-only auditor, so you create your own.
s1.hint: Nodes are cluster-scoped, so the permission set must be cluster-wide too. Three read verbs.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Bind 'node-reader' to the GROUP 'auditors' cluster-wide (binding name: auditors-node-reader).

options.why: A RoleBinding only grants inside one namespace: cluster-scoped Nodes stay forbidden.
--user binds a USER literally named 'auditors'; kim, a member of the group, gets nothing.
A ClusterRoleBinding has no --role flag: it can only reference a ClusterRole.

s2.explain: A ClusterRoleBinding applies the ClusterRole everywhere, which cluster-scoped Nodes need. --group matches the whole 'auditors' group, so new auditors need no new binding; --user would cover one person only.
s2.hint: Cluster-wide binding, and the subject is a GROUP, not a user.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Verify that user 'kim', member of group 'auditors', can list nodes.

options.why: Impersonating a group requires impersonating a user too (--as): the request is rejected.
That impersonates a USER named 'auditors' with no groups: the answer is 'no'.
can-i takes a verb and a RESOURCE (nodes), not the name of a ClusterRole.

s3.explain: --as-group must go with --as: it simulates 'kim' arriving with the group 'auditors', exactly what the binding matches. 'yes' proves the group binding works, not only a user one.
s3.hint: Impersonate the user AND the group: group membership comes from the credentials, not from the user name.

questions.title: A ServiceAccount for the CI pipeline
questions.scenario: The CI pipeline runs as ServiceAccount 'deployer' in namespace 'ci'. It must be able to manage workloads in 'ci' only: reuse the built-in ClusterRole 'edit'.
questions.tip: A ServiceAccount's username is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name> - that is the string you pass to --as.
questions.stakes: Pass the wrong --as string and 'can-i' says 'no' for the wrong reason: you blame RBAC.
questions.analogy: A robot's badge has a long printed name: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the ServiceAccount 'deployer' in namespace 'ci'.

options.why: No -n ci: the ServiceAccount is created in the current namespace (usually 'default').
'ci:deployer' is not a valid object name (no colons): the namespace is given with -n.
Kubernetes has no User objects: users only exist in certificates or the identity provider.

s1.explain: Give the pipeline its own identity instead of reusing 'default', so you can grant it only what it needs. Since v1.24 no token Secret is created automatically: 'kubectl create token deployer -n ci' issues a short-lived one when needed.
s1.hint: A ServiceAccount is a namespaced identity; one generator creates it.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Grant the ClusterRole 'edit' to that ServiceAccount, in namespace 'ci' only (binding name: deployer-edit).

options.why: --serviceaccount must be <namespace>:<name>; kubectl refuses a bare name.
That binds a USER named 'deployer', not the ServiceAccount: the pipeline still gets 'forbidden'.
A ClusterRoleBinding grants 'edit' in EVERY namespace - far more than asked.

s2.explain: A RoleBinding may point to a ClusterRole: the rules then apply only inside the binding's namespace. That reuses the built-in 'edit' without giving the pipeline anything outside 'ci'; a ClusterRoleBinding would grant it cluster-wide.
s2.hint: A ClusterRole can be granted in ONE namespace through a RoleBinding. ServiceAccounts are named namespace:name.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Verify that the ServiceAccount can create Deployments in 'ci'.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer -n ci
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=deployer -n ci
options.why: That impersonates a user named 'deployer', not the ServiceAccount: the answer is 'no'.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:deployer:ci -n ci
options.why: Namespace and name are swapped: the format is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=serviceaccount:ci:deployer -n ci
options.why: The 'system:' prefix is part of the username: without it you impersonate an unknown user.

s3.explain: A ServiceAccount's username is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>, which is what --as expects. Also test '-n default': it must answer 'no', proof the permission stays inside 'ci'.
s3.hint: To impersonate a ServiceAccount, use its full user name: system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>.

questions.title: Join a new worker node
questions.scenario: A fresh worker 'node02' has containerd, kubelet and kubeadm installed. The bootstrap token printed by 'kubeadm init' expired weeks ago. Join node02 to the cluster whose API server is 172.30.1.2:6443.
questions.tip: Bootstrap tokens expire after 24h by default. 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command' gives you a fresh, complete join command.
questions.stakes: A wrong or expired token (24 h by default) and the node never joins, with the clock ticking.
questions.analogy: The token is a visitor pass with an expiry; the CA hash checks the building's ID before you go in.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - On the control plane: print a complete, valid join command (new token + CA hash).

options.why: Only lists existing tokens (here none valid) - no CA hash, no join command.
Only prints a random token string; it is NOT registered in the cluster, so a join with it fails.
'join' runs on the new node; --print-join-command belongs to 'kubeadm token create'.

s1.explain: A bootstrap token expires after 24 hours by default. '--print-join-command' creates a fresh one and prints the CA certificate hash too, which pins the cluster's identity so the new node cannot be fooled by a fake API server.
s1.hint: Tokens expire after 24 h. kubeadm can create a fresh one and print the whole join line with it.

context: node02$ HASH=5d1f...e07a      # the full 64 hex digits
s2.prompt: Step 2 - On node02: join the cluster, using the TOKEN and HASH shell variables already set.

options.why: 'init' bootstraps a NEW control plane (and has no --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash flag); workers use 'join'.
2379 is etcd's client port. Nodes join through the API server endpoint, port 6443.
Token and hash are swapped: the token has the form abcdef.0123456789abcdef.

s2.explain: The token proves to the cluster that the node may join; --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash proves to the node that it reached the real cluster. Without the hash kubeadm refuses, unless you explicitly skip the verification.
s2.hint: The worker joins through the API server address, proving it with the token and the CA public-key hash (sha256:).

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Back on the control plane: check that node02 is registered and becomes Ready.

options.why: Shows the kubelet's certificate requests - not whether the node is Ready.
Lists bootstrap tokens; it says nothing about nodes.
'node02' is not a resource type: it is 'kubectl get node node02'.

s3.explain: The node registers at once but stays NotReady until the CNI Pod and kube-proxy run on it: give it a minute before suspecting a problem.
s3.hint: From the control plane, list the cluster's machines and their status.

questions.title: Bootstrap a control plane from a config file
questions.scenario: On 'controlplane' (192.168.10.10), bootstrap a new cluster with kubeadm-config.yaml (kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4). The CNI you will install requires the Pod network 10.244.0.0/16.
questions.tip: With a config file, every setting goes IN the file: kubeadm refuses to mix --config with most flags such as --pod-network-cidr.

docs.title: Customizing components with the kubeadm API

questions.stakes: Mix --config with flags and kubeadm refuses: minutes lost on your very first command.
questions.analogy: One blueprint, no sticky notes: every setting goes in the file.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Set the Pod network CIDR: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: the Pod network required by the CNI

checks.msg: Add 'podSubnet: 10.244.0.0/16' under 'networking:' (2 spaces of indentation).
Keep the Service subnet 10.96.0.0/12.

forbid.msg: The ClusterConfiguration field is networking.podSubnet.
podSubnet must be nested under 'networking:', not at the top level.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: the Pod network required by the CNI

options.why: podCIDR is a Node field, not a ClusterConfiguration field: kubeadm warns about an unknown field and allocates no Pod CIDRs.
At column 0 it becomes a top-level key of ClusterConfiguration (unknown field): networking has no podSubnet.
A duplicate serviceSubnet key: the Pod network is still unset and the Services now overlap the CNI range.

s1.recap: Add 'podSubnet: 10.244.0.0/16' under networking in the ClusterConfiguration.
s1.explain: The CNI hands out Pod IPs from a range that must match what the cluster allocates to nodes. podSubnet sets it (it becomes the controller-manager's --cluster-cidr), so each node gets a slice (spec.podCIDR). A mismatch gives overlapping or unroutable Pod IPs.
s1.hint: The Pod CIDR belongs to the networking section of the ClusterConfiguration; the indentation decides the parent.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Bootstrap the control plane with that file.

options.why: kubeadm refuses to mix --config with --pod-network-cidr: the value must stay in the file.
There is no cluster yet, and these kubeadm types are not API objects: kubectl cannot use them.

options.cmd: sudo kubeadm init phase preflight --config kubeadm-config.yaml
options.why: Only runs the preflight checks: nothing is bootstrapped.

s2.explain: --config makes the file the single source of truth, including the podSubnet you just set. Do not add flags such as --pod-network-cidr: kubeadm refuses to mix them with --config. '--dry-run' previews without changing the node.
s2.hint: kubeadm init can read everything from the config file instead of flags (and refuses to mix most of them).

context: To start using your cluster, you need to run the following as a regular user:
s3.prompt: Step 3 - As your regular user, copy the admin kubeconfig to where kubectl looks by default.

options.why: kubelet.conf is the node's identity (system:node:controlplane), limited by the Node authorizer - not an admin.
That creates ~/.kube/admin.conf; kubectl reads ~/.kube/config by default.
ca.crt is just the CA certificate, not a kubeconfig (no server, no user credentials).

s3.explain: init writes the admin credentials to /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf, but kubectl looks in ~/.kube/config, so you copy it. admin.conf belongs to the kubeadm:cluster-admins group; super-admin.conf (system:masters) is a break-glass credential: keep it out of daily use.
s3.hint: kubectl looks in $HOME/.kube/config by default; kubeadm wrote the admin credentials under /etc/kubernetes.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - The copy belongs to root (mode 600). Make it yours so kubectl can read it.

options.why: It works, but makes cluster-admin credentials readable and writable by every user on the machine.
Without sudo a regular user cannot take ownership of a root-owned file: 'Operation not permitted'.
It is already root's: kubectl, running as you, still gets 'permission denied'.

s4.explain: The copy belongs to root with mode 600, so your user cannot read it and kubectl fails with a permission error. chown fixes that without loosening the permissions. 'get nodes' then shows NotReady until a CNI is installed.
s4.hint: The copy is root's. Change its owner to your own user and group ids.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Check through your kubeconfig that the API server answers and that 'controlplane' is registered.

options.why: Lists Pods of the 'default' namespace: 'No resources found' even on a healthy cluster, and the node never appears.
Reads the bootstrap tokens (as root, from the cluster): it says nothing about the node, and as your user it does not even use your kubeconfig.
kubeadm is a command, not a service: 'Unit kubeadm.service could not be found'.

s5.explain: kubectl get nodes goes through the file you just copied and chowned, so an answer proves the API server, its certificates and your kubeconfig all work. 'controlplane' shows NotReady until a CNI is installed: expected right after init, not a failure.
s5.hint: Ask the API server for the cluster's machines, through the kubeconfig you just fixed.

questions.title: Upgrade the control plane
questions.scenario: The cluster runs v1.36.5. On 'controlplane', the kubeadm package has already been upgraded to 1.37.1. Upgrade the control plane to v1.37.1.
questions.tip: Control-plane order: upgrade kubeadm -> 'kubeadm upgrade plan' -> 'kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z' -> drain -> kubelet/kubectl packages + restart kubelet -> uncordon. One minor version at a time.
questions.stakes: Upgrade a kubelet past the API server and you break the version-skew rule; nodes go NotReady.
questions.analogy: Like a convoy: the leader (control plane) first, followers (nodes) after, never the reverse.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Check which versions you can upgrade to and that the cluster is upgradable.

options.why: 'upgrade node' is for workers and ADDITIONAL control-plane nodes, after the first one was upgraded.
kubectl version has no --upgrade flag; it only prints client and server versions.
There is no 'check' sub-command: the dry run with a report is 'kubeadm upgrade plan'.

s1.explain: 'plan' is the safe first move: it checks the cluster is healthy, lists the versions you can reach (kubeadm upgrades one minor version at a time) and warns if a component config needs manual work, before anything changes.
s1.hint: Before changing anything, kubeadm can show the target versions and check the cluster: a dry look.

context: You can now apply the upgrade by executing the following command:
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Upgrade the control-plane components.

options.why: 'upgrade node' takes no version and only works once the first control plane has been upgraded with 'apply'.
Too early: the kubelet must never be newer than the API server. Upgrade the control plane first.
Static Pods are managed by the kubelet, not the API; besides, the manifests still reference v1.36.5 images.

s2.explain: 'apply' is the step that changes the control plane: it rewrites the static Pod manifests (apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, etcd), renews the certificates and upgrades CoreDNS and kube-proxy. Wait for '[upgrade] SUCCESS!'.
s2.hint: On the first control plane, kubeadm 'applies' an explicit target version.

s4.prompt: Step 3 - Before the kubelet package changes, mark 'controlplane' unschedulable and evict its workloads.

options.why: Refused: 'cannot delete DaemonSet-managed Pods' (kube-proxy, the CNI). The node stays cordoned but nothing is evicted.
Only marks the node unschedulable: the Pods already there keep running while their kubelet restarts under them.
Removes the Node object: its Pods are orphaned and the node must register again. Never part of an upgrade.

s4.explain: drain = cordon + evict through the Eviction API, so PodDisruptionBudgets are respected. --ignore-daemonsets is required because DaemonSet Pods would be recreated at once on the same node; static control-plane Pods are skipped anyway.
s4.hint: Cordon and evict in one command; DaemonSet Pods cannot leave the node.

s3.prompt: Step 4 - The kubelet and kubectl packages are now 1.37.1. Make the kubelet run the new binary.

options.cmd: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
aliases: sudo systemctl daemon-reload; sudo systemctl restart kubelet

options.why: The kubelet unit does not support 'reload': the old binary keeps running.
That restarts the container runtime, not the kubelet: the node still reports v1.36.5.
'upgrade apply' expects a version, and the kubelet is upgraded by the package manager, not by kubeadm.

s3.explain: kubeadm upgrades the control-plane Pods, not the kubelet: it is a systemd service. daemon-reload picks up changed unit files and restart runs the new binary. Then uncordon and check VERSION in 'kubectl get nodes'.
s3.hint: New package files: systemd must re-read its units first, then the kubelet must be restarted.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - The kubelet runs 1.37.1. Let the scheduler use 'controlplane' again.

options.why: 'unknown flag: --uncordon': drain only goes one way.
The unschedulable mark lives in the Node object (spec.unschedulable), not in the kubelet: the node stays SchedulingDisabled.
The node controller re-adds that taint as long as spec.unschedulable is true: it comes straight back.

s5.explain: uncordon sets spec.unschedulable back to false, so new Pods may land there again. Forgetting it is a classic upgrade leftover: STATUS keeps 'SchedulingDisabled' and capacity silently shrinks.
s5.hint: Undo what drain did to the Node object.

questions.title: Back up etcd
questions.scenario: Take a snapshot of the cluster's etcd (kubeadm stacked etcd, v3.6) to /opt/etcd-backup.db. You are root on 'controlplane', working in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd.
questions.tip: The certificate paths are in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml: --trusted-ca-file -> --cacert, --cert-file -> --cert, --key-file -> --key.
questions.stakes: No snapshot means one bad delete and the whole cluster state is gone: etcd holds the only copy.
questions.analogy: etcd is the cluster's memory; a snapshot is a photo taken before the surgery.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Save the snapshot through the local client URL https://127.0.0.1:2379.

options.why: No certificates: etcd requires client-certificate authentication, the TLS handshake fails.
'restore' rebuilds a data directory FROM a snapshot - the opposite of a backup.

options.cmd: kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-controlplane -- etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db
options.why: No certificates, and the file would be written inside the container, not on the node's /opt.

s1.explain: etcd only answers clients with a certificate it trusts, so give the https:// endpoint and the three files from etcd.yaml: --cacert, --cert, --key. Without them the call is rejected or times out. ETCDCTL_API=3 is already the default since etcd 3.4.
s1.hint: etcd's network client takes the endpoint plus CA, client cert and key; the subcommand writes a snapshot to a file.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Check the snapshot file itself: hash, revision and total keys, as a table.

options.why: That reports the LIVE member, not the snapshot file you just wrote.
/var/lib/etcd is the live data directory, not a snapshot file.
There is no 'verify' sub-command: it is 'snapshot status'.

s2.explain: A snapshot you never checked may be useless. 'snapshot status' reads the file (hash, revision, total keys) to prove it is valid. It is an offline file operation, so it belongs to etcdutl: 'etcdctl snapshot status' was deprecated in 3.5 and removed in 3.6.
s2.hint: Inspecting a snapshot FILE is an offline job for etcd's utility tool, not the network client; ask for a table.

questions.title: Restore etcd from a snapshot
questions.scenario: Someone deleted critical objects. Restore the cluster state from /opt/etcd-backup.db on 'controlplane' (kubeadm stacked etcd). You are root.
questions.tip: Restore into a NEW directory, then point the etcd static Pod's hostPath volume to it: the kubelet re-creates etcd by itself.
questions.stakes: Restore, then forget to point etcd at the new directory: the old state keeps running and you think you fixed it.
questions.analogy: Restoring is loading a save file: the game must then be told to read that save.

s0.prompt: Step 1 - Before touching etcd, check that the backup file is a readable snapshot (hash, revision, keys) as a table.

options.why: Since etcd 3.6, etcdctl only saves snapshots: 'status' is no longer one of its subcommands, so it just prints the help of 'snapshot' (save only) and checks nothing. Use etcdutl.
/var/lib/etcd is the live data directory, not a snapshot file: etcdutl cannot read it as one and fails.
Proves the file exists and has a size, not that it is a valid, uncorrupted snapshot. A truncated copy would pass.

s0.explain: etcdutl snapshot status reads the file offline and prints its hash, revision and key count: a corrupt or empty backup fails here, before you have stopped anything. A restore from a bad file would leave the cluster without its state.
s0.hint: etcd's offline tool reads a snapshot file without any running etcd.

s1.prompt: Step 2 - Restore the snapshot into a new data directory /var/lib/etcd-restored.

options.why: The live data directory is not empty: etcdutl refuses to restore into an existing data dir.
Without --data-dir the data lands in ./default.etcd of the current directory.
'save' takes a NEW snapshot from the live etcd - the opposite direction.

s1.explain: etcdutl rebuilds the data from the file, offline, so etcd must not be using the target. It refuses a directory that already exists, so you restore into a NEW one (new member directory, new cluster ID).
s1.hint: Restoring is offline work on a file: etcd's utility tool writes a brand-new data directory.

s2.prompt: Step 3 - Point the 'etcd-data' hostPath volume to the restored directory: type the right snippet over the etcd-data volume (last 4 lines before 'status'). Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: The 'etcd-data' volume needs hostPath.path: /var/lib/etcd-restored (keep the name etcd-data).
Keep the volumeMount as it is: etcd still sees /var/lib/etcd inside the container.

forbid.msg: The volume still points to the old /var/lib/etcd.
Point to the data dir itself, not to its 'member' sub-directory.

options.why: etcd's --data-dir must contain 'member/': mounting member itself gives etcd an empty-looking dir, it starts a brand-new empty cluster.
The volumeMount still references 'etcd-data': renaming the volume makes the Pod invalid and etcd never starts.
A hostPath volume has 'path', not 'mountPath': the field is unknown and the volume has no path at all.

s2.recap: Change the etcd-data hostPath.path to /var/lib/etcd-restored; the mount and --data-dir stay /var/lib/etcd.
s2.explain: Restoring alone changes nothing: the etcd Pod still mounts the old directory. Only the host side of the hostPath changes; inside the container the path stays /var/lib/etcd, so --data-dir needs no edit. Saving the file is enough: the kubelet watches the manifests.
s2.hint: etcd reads its data from a hostPath volume: change the path to the restored directory, keep name and type.

s3.prompt: Step 4 - After a minute or two, check that the etcd Pod is running again.

options.why: Static Pods are not applied through the API: the kubelet already picked up the change.
kubeadm's etcd is a static Pod, not a systemd service: there is no etcd unit.
No namespace: etcd lives in kube-system, so this returns NotFound.

s3.explain: etcd restarts through the kubelet, so the API server may refuse connections for a while: that is normal, use 'crictl ps' on the node. If the API server stays unhealthy, restart it too (move its manifest out and back).
s3.hint: The kubelet recreates etcd from the manifest; its Pod lives in kube-system, named after the node.

s4.prompt: Step 5 - etcd runs on the restored data. Check that the deleted Deployment 'payments' in namespace 'shop' is back.

options.why: Describes the backup file again, not what the API server now serves: the restore could still point at the old directory.

options.cmd: kubectl rollout undo deployment payments -n shop
options.why: Rollout undo needs the Deployment to exist and only goes back one ReplicaSet revision: it cannot bring a deleted object back.
Shows that an etcd container runs, not which data it serves.

s4.explain: Only the API server reading the restored etcd can prove the restore worked: the Deployment is back with the spec it had at backup time. Anything created after the backup is gone, which is why restores need a recent snapshot.
s4.hint: Ask the API server for the object that was deleted.

questions.title: Switch clusters and namespaces
questions.scenario: Your kubeconfig holds several clusters. The task must be done on cluster 'prod', in namespace 'payments', and every following command should default to that namespace.
questions.tip: Exam tasks start with a 'kubectl config use-context ...' line: always run it, or you work on the wrong cluster.
questions.stakes: Run 'delete' while your context still says prod: the classic career-limiting typo.
questions.analogy: A context is the TV's input button: check which device you control before pressing delete.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List all contexts of your kubeconfig (the current one is marked with '*').

options.why: Contexts are not API resources: they live in your local kubeconfig, under 'kubectl config'.
Prints only the current context, not the list.
Lists clusters only; a context = cluster + user + namespace.

s1.explain: A context bundles cluster, user and namespace. The NAME column is exactly what use-context expects and '*' marks where you are now. Look before you act: the wrong context is the classic way to run a command on prod by mistake.
s1.hint: Contexts live in your kubeconfig; kubectl config has a subcommand to list them all.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Switch to the context that targets cluster 'prod'.

options.why: 'prod' is the CLUSTER name; use-context needs the context NAME: 'no context exists with the name'.
set-context creates/modifies a context entry; it does not switch to it.
There is no switch-context sub-command.

s2.explain: use-context rewrites 'current-context' in the kubeconfig, so it applies to every following command. Give it the context NAME (prod-admin@prod), not the cluster name.
s2.hint: Switching context changes the 'current-context' line of your kubeconfig: use the context NAME, not the cluster's.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Make 'payments' the default namespace of the current context.

options.why: -n only scopes that single command; it does not store a namespace in the context.
There is no set-namespace sub-command (that is the kubens plugin).
The flag is --namespace; --ns does not exist.

s3.explain: --current edits the active context, so later commands default to 'payments' without -n. Check with 'kubectl config view --minify'. In the exam an explicit -n is safer when tasks jump between namespaces.
s3.hint: A default namespace is a property of the current context; modify it in place.

questions.title: Certificates about to expire
questions.scenario: The API server certificates of 'controlplane' expire in a few days. Check them, renew them and make the control plane use the new ones. You are root on controlplane.
questions.tip: kubeadm certs renew writes new files only: the running components keep the old certificates in memory until their static Pods restart.
questions.stakes: Control-plane certificates expire a year after install: kubectl dies on a random Tuesday.
questions.analogy: Certificates are milk cartons: check the date, renew before they turn.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the expiration date of every kubeadm-managed certificate in one table.

options.why: The 'alpha certs' commands graduated years ago: it is 'kubeadm certs' now.
Valid for ONE certificate; the task asks for all of them (and the kubeconfig ones).
'certificates' is a cert-manager CRD, not kubeadm's PKI on disk.

s1.explain: Check before you act: the table lists every certificate with its expiry, including those embedded in admin.conf, controller-manager.conf, scheduler.conf and super-admin.conf, which are easy to forget.
s1.hint: kubeadm has a 'certs' command family; one subcommand prints every certificate's expiry in a table.

context: CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Renew all the leaf certificates at once (the CAs are valid for 9 more years).

options.why: renew needs a target ('all' or one certificate name): alone it only prints the help.
kubeadm cannot renew a CA: there is no 'ca' target, and the CA is not what expires here.
That phase only creates MISSING certificates: existing valid ones are left untouched.

s2.explain: 'renew all' renews every leaf certificate at once (the CAs last 10 years). It only writes new files: running components keep the old certificates until restarted, and admin.conf must be re-copied to ~/.kube/config.
s2.hint: Renew every leaf certificate at once; the CAs are not touched.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Restart the control-plane static Pods: move their manifests to the existing directory /root/manifests-bak (you will move them back after ~20 s).

options.why: Restarting the kubelet does not restart running containers: the components keep the old certificates.

options.cmd: kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment kube-apiserver
options.why: The API server is a static Pod, not a Deployment: there is nothing to roll out.
The kubelet compares the manifest CONTENT: an unchanged file does not restart the Pod.

s3.explain: Static Pods read their certificates only when they start. Moving a manifest away makes the kubelet stop that Pod; moving it back starts it with the new certificates. Wait about 20 s between the two so the stop is noticed.
s3.hint: Static Pods restart when their manifest leaves and comes back: move the files out of the watched directory.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - About 20 s later the static Pods are gone. Put the manifests back so the kubelet restarts them with the new certificates.

options.why: Moves the whole directory INSIDE manifests/: the kubelet does not read subdirectories, so no control-plane Pod comes back.
The API server is one of those Pods and is not running: 'connection refused'. Static Pods are files for the kubelet, not API objects.
The manifests are still in /root/manifests-bak: the restarted kubelet finds nothing to run and the control plane stays down.

s4.explain: The kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests: a file appearing there is a Pod to start. Moving the manifests out and back forces a real restart, so each component loads the renewed certificates (they read them only at startup).
s4.hint: The kubelet starts whatever static Pod manifests appear in its watched directory.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - 'renew all' also renewed admin.conf, but kubectl still reads the old copy in your home. Refresh it.

options.why: Renews /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf again; kubectl keeps reading /root/.kube/config, whose client certificate still expires in a few days.
A certificate is not a kubeconfig: kubectl fails to parse the file and every command breaks at once.
The kubelet has its own kubeconfig (kubelet.conf, rotated automatically): your kubectl file does not change.

s5.explain: Your ~/.kube/config is a copy, embedding the OLD admin client certificate: it works until that one expires, then kubectl gets 'certificate has expired'. Copying the renewed admin.conf again avoids the surprise.
s5.hint: Your personal kubeconfig is a copy of a file kubeadm just regenerated.

questions.title: Prepare a node for kubeadm
questions.scenario: 'kubeadm init' preflight fails on a new node. You are root on it. The kubelet keeps its default failSwapOn: true.
questions.tip: Classic node prerequisites: swap off (unless the kubelet is configured for swap), overlay + br_netfilter modules, net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1, a container runtime with the systemd cgroup driver.
questions.stakes: Swap left on and the kubelet refuses to start; a skipped sysctl breaks Pod networking in odd ways.
questions.analogy: A pre-flight checklist: skip one item and it fails at altitude, not on the ground.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Turn off every active swap device now.

options.why: Only lists the active swap devices: nothing is turned off.
Makes the kernel avoid swapping but swap stays enabled: the kubelet still refuses to start.
Only shows memory and swap usage.

s1.explain: With swap on, the kubelet refuses to start (failSwapOn: true), so preflight fails. swapoff lasts only until reboot: also comment out the swap line in /etc/fstab.
s1.hint: Swap must be off for the kubelet by default; one command disables every active swap device.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Load the 'overlay' and 'br_netfilter' kernel modules with ONE command.

options.why: Without -a, the words after the first module are taken as module PARAMETERS: br_netfilter is not loaded.
insmod expects a path to a .ko file and resolves no names or dependencies.
Only shows whether they are loaded.

s2.explain: overlay is needed by containerd's overlay snapshotter; br_netfilter makes bridged Pod traffic visible to iptables, so Services and NetworkPolicies work. 'modprobe -a' loads both at once; persist them in /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf.
s2.hint: modprobe can load several modules in one call with the right flag.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Enable IPv4 forwarding persistently: type the right line in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: let the node route Pod traffic (IPv4 forwarding)

checks.msg: Add 'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' (key = value).
Keep net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the line in its place.

target: # TODO: let the node route Pod traffic (IPv4 forwarding)

options.why: That is IPv6 forwarding: IPv4 Pod traffic is still not routed and kubeadm preflight still fails.
sysctl keys are full dotted paths (net.ipv4.ip_forward): 'ip_forward' alone is an unknown key.
sysctl.d files use 'key = value', not YAML 'key: value': the line is rejected.

s3.recap: Add 'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' to /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf.
s3.explain: Without IP forwarding the node cannot route packets between Pods and the outside. A file in /etc/sysctl.d/ is applied at every boot, unlike 'sysctl -w', which is lost on reboot.
s3.hint: sysctl keys use dots, not slashes; 1 turns the feature on.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Apply the sysctl settings now, without rebooting.

options.why: -p without a file only reads /etc/sysctl.conf: /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf is ignored.
Only READS the current value.
The kubelet does not apply kernel parameters.

s4.explain: 'sysctl --system' reloads every sysctl.d file now, so preflight passes without a reboot. Check with 'sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward': it must print 1.
s4.hint: Reload every sysctl configuration file now, including those under /etc/sysctl.d.

questions.title: containerd with the systemd cgroup driver
questions.scenario: On node 'node03' (containerd 2.x, config version 4), the kubelet uses cgroupDriver: systemd (the kubeadm default) but containerd still uses cgroupfs, so Pods keep restarting. You are root on node03.
questions.tip: The kubelet and the container runtime MUST use the same cgroup driver. On systemd hosts (cgroup v2), use systemd for both.
questions.stakes: Mismatched cgroup drivers make Pods restart for no visible reason, for hours.
questions.analogy: Two managers giving orders to one team: pick one (systemd) and make both obey.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - /etc/containerd/config.toml is missing. Write containerd's full default configuration to it.

options.why: '>>' appends: if the file exists you get duplicate TOML tables and containerd refuses to start.
ctr is the low-level client: it has no 'config' command.
That writes crictl's OWN config (/etc/crictl.yaml), not containerd's.

s1.explain: Starting from the generated default gives every section with its exact name; typing TOML tables by hand invites a typo that is silently ignored.
s1.hint: containerd can print its own default configuration: redirect it into the file.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Switch runc to the systemd cgroup driver: type the right line over 'SystemdCgroup = false'. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Set 'SystemdCgroup = true' (a boolean, no quotes) in the runc options table.

forbid.msg: 'SystemdCgroup = false' is still there.
The runc option is called SystemdCgroup.

options.why: In TOML "true" is a STRING: containerd expects a boolean and fails to load the option.
systemd_cgroup was the old containerd 1.x CRI-level option (for the removed runtime v1): containerd 2.x rejects or ignores it.
That is the KUBELET's setting name (cgroupDriver: systemd); runc's option is SystemdCgroup.

s2.recap: In [plugins.'io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime'.containerd.runtimes.runc.options], set SystemdCgroup = true.
s2.explain: The kubelet and the runtime must agree on the cgroup driver. On a systemd node both should use systemd, otherwise two managers fight over the same cgroups and Pods restart. In containerd 1.x (config version 2) the same option sits in the cri 'runc.options' table.
s2.hint: The cgroup driver of runc is a boolean option under the runc runtime's options.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Make containerd load the new configuration.

options.why: The kubelet does not read containerd's config: containerd keeps running with cgroupfs.
Only makes containerd start at boot; the running daemon keeps its old config.
migrate converts an OLD config version to the current one; it does not restart anything.

s3.explain: containerd reads config.toml only at start-up, so the edit does nothing until a restart. Running containers keep going during the restart.
s3.hint: containerd reads its configuration only at start.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Verify the setting containerd is ACTUALLY using (through the CRI).

options.why: Prints the built-in DEFAULT (false), not the running configuration.
Shows that the service runs, not which cgroup driver runc uses.
Lists containers: nothing about the runtime's cgroup driver.

s4.explain: Check what containerd really uses, through the CRI the kubelet talks to, not just the file you edited. Expect '"SystemdCgroup": true'. 'containerd config dump' shows the merged configuration.
s4.hint: Ask the runtime through the CRI what it really loaded, and filter for the cgroup option (case-insensitive).

questions.title: Enable an admission plugin
questions.scenario: Security requires that every Pod always pulls its images (no reuse of cached private images). Enable the AlwaysPullImages admission plugin on the API server of 'controlplane'. You are root.
questions.tip: Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml directly (backup OUTSIDE that directory). The kubelet restarts the API server; 'kubectl edit' on the mirror Pod changes nothing.
questions.stakes: One typo in the API server manifest and kube-apiserver vanishes, taking kubectl with it.
questions.analogy: Admission is airport security after the ID check: you are known, but your bag can still be refused.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Back up the API server manifest before editing it.

options.why: The kubelet loads EVERY file in the manifests directory: the backup becomes a second, conflicting API server Pod.

options.cmd: kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-controlplane -o yaml > /root/apiserver.yaml
options.why: That is the mirror Pod with status and generated fields - not the manifest file the kubelet uses.
Not a backup, and edits to a mirror Pod are never applied to the static Pod.

s1.explain: A typo in this static Pod manifest takes the API server down, and kubectl with it. A copy kept outside /etc/kubernetes/manifests (the kubelet runs any YAML left there) lets you restore in seconds.
s1.hint: Copy the manifest OUT of /etc/kubernetes/manifests: a backup left there would be started as a second Pod.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Add AlwaysPullImages to the enabled admission plugins, keeping NodeRestriction: type the right line over the --enable-admission-plugins line. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Keep NodeRestriction in the comma-separated --enable-admission-plugins list.
Add AlwaysPullImages to the comma-separated --enable-admission-plugins list.

forbid.msg: Use ONE --enable-admission-plugins flag: when repeated, only the last value counts.

options.why: The list is REPLACED, not extended: NodeRestriction is lost and kubelets may modify other nodes' objects.
A repeated flag does not merge: the last value wins, so NodeRestriction is silently disabled.
The list is comma-separated: 'NodeRestriction AlwaysPullImages' is one unknown plugin name and the API server exits.

s2.recap: --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,AlwaysPullImages (one flag, comma-separated).
s2.explain: --enable-admission-plugins ADDS to the plugins on by default, so list only what you add and keep NodeRestriction. Order does not matter. AlwaysPullImages forces a registry check, so a Pod cannot reuse a private image another Pod cached on the node.
s2.hint: One flag lists every enabled plugin, comma-separated: keep the existing one and append the new one.

context: The connection to the server 192.168.10.10:6443 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?
s3.prompt: Step 3 - kubectl is down while the API server restarts. On the node, check whether the kube-apiserver container is running or exiting.

options.why: kubectl needs the API server - the very thing that is down.
With kubeadm the API server is a static Pod, not a systemd service.
kubeadm nodes run containerd, not Docker: use crictl, which talks to the CRI.

s3.explain: kubectl is down while the API server restarts, so go around it: crictl -a also lists Exited containers. If it keeps exiting, read 'crictl logs <id>'; if no container appears at all, the YAML is broken: 'journalctl -u kubelet'.
s3.hint: kubectl is down: ask the container runtime on the node, including containers that already exited.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - The API server is back. Create a test Pod 'pull-test' from nginx that asks for IfNotPresent.

options.why: 'unknown flag: --pull-policy': the flag is --image-pull-policy.
There is no 'kubectl create pod' subcommand: 'kubectl run' creates a single Pod.
Creates a Pod, but without asking for IfNotPresent you cannot see the plugin override anything: 'nginx' (latest) defaults to Always anyway.

s4.explain: To see an admission plugin act, ask for what it must change: a Pod created with IfNotPresent. Without the explicit policy the test proves nothing, since an untagged image already defaults to Always.
s4.hint: Create a single Pod and explicitly request the pull policy the plugin should override.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Show the pull policy the API server actually stored for its container.

aliases: kubectl get pod pull-test -o yaml | grep imagePullPolicy
kubectl get pod pull-test -o yaml | grep -i pullpolicy

options.cmd: kubectl describe pod pull-test | grep -i policy
options.why: describe does not print the image pull policy: nothing matches, which proves nothing.
imagePullPolicy belongs to each container, not to the Pod spec: the expression prints an empty line.
Inspects the cached IMAGE on a node, not the Pod's stored spec: the policy is not there.

s5.explain: AlwaysPullImages is a mutating admission plugin: it rewrites every container's imagePullPolicy to Always before the Pod is stored. Reading the stored spec shows 'Always' although you asked for IfNotPresent: the plugin is on.
s5.hint: The policy is a per-container field of the object as stored after admission.

questions.title: Find a chart in a new Helm repository
questions.scenario: The team wants to deploy kube-state-metrics with Helm. Register the repository 'prometheus-community' (https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts), refresh the local index and list every available version of the chart.
questions.tip: Helm repo workflow: 'helm repo add NAME URL' -> 'helm repo update' -> 'helm search repo REPO/CHART --versions'. 'search hub' is Artifact Hub, not your repos.
questions.stakes: Search without 'helm repo update' and you install last month's chart, CVE included.
questions.analogy: A Helm repo is an app store: add the store, refresh the catalogue, then search.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Register the repository under the name 'prometheus-community'.

options.why: The order is NAME then URL: here 'prometheus-community' would be taken as the URL and rejected.
There is no 'helm add' command: the sub-command is 'helm repo add'.
'install' deploys a chart as a release; it does not register a repository (and a repo URL is not a chart).

s1.explain: Helm can only search repositories it knows. 'repo add NAME URL' saves the repository in your Helm config and downloads its index. Check with 'helm repo list'.
s1.hint: Helm needs a local name plus the repository URL.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Refresh the local cache of chart indexes so you see the latest chart versions.

options.why: There is no top-level 'helm update': it is 'helm repo update'.
'refresh' is not a 'helm repo' sub-command (add, list, remove, update, index).
'helm upgrade' upgrades a release; it needs a release name and a chart, and has no --all flag.

s2.explain: Helm searches a LOCAL copy of each repo's index.yaml. 'helm repo update' downloads fresh copies - do it before searching or installing.
s2.hint: Repositories are cached locally: refresh every index.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - List ALL available versions of the chart 'kube-state-metrics' from that repository.

options.why: 'search hub' queries Artifact Hub on the Internet, not the repos you added (and it has no --versions flag).
'helm list' shows installed releases, not the charts available in a repository.
'show chart' prints the Chart.yaml of one version; it has no --versions flag.

s3.explain: Without --versions, 'helm search repo' shows only the latest version of each chart. The CHART VERSION column is what you pass to '--version' at install time.
s3.hint: Search the added repositories (not Artifact Hub) for repo/chart, and ask for every version, not just the latest.

questions.title: Install a chart into a new namespace
questions.scenario: The repo 'podinfo' is already added and updated. Install the chart 'podinfo/podinfo' as release 'web' in namespace 'frontend' (it does not exist yet) with 2 replicas (chart value 'replicaCount').
questions.tip: Helm releases are namespaced: always pass the same '-n NS' to install, list, status, upgrade, rollback and uninstall.
questions.stakes: No --create-namespace and the install fails at the finish line; no -n and it lands in 'default'.
questions.analogy: A chart is flat-pack furniture; a release is one assembled copy, and one box builds many.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Install the release, creating the namespace and setting replicaCount to 2.

options.cmd: helm install web podinfo/podinfo -n frontend --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2
aliases: helm install web podinfo/podinfo --namespace frontend --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2

options.cmd: helm install podinfo/podinfo web -n frontend --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2
options.why: Helm 3 expects RELEASE_NAME then CHART: 'podinfo/podinfo' is not a valid release name.

options.cmd: helm install web podinfo/podinfo -n frontend --set replicaCount=2
options.why: Without --create-namespace the install fails: namespace 'frontend' does not exist.

options.cmd: helm install web podinfo/podinfo -n frontend --create-namespace --set replicas=2
options.why: The chart reads 'replicaCount': an unknown key like 'replicas' is silently ignored and you get the default (1).

s1.explain: --create-namespace is needed because 'frontend' does not exist yet: the install would fail without it. --set replicaCount=2 overrides one chart value (dots for nesting: --set service.type=NodePort); -n keeps the release out of 'default'.
s1.hint: helm install RELEASE CHART: the namespace must also be created, and one value is overridden on the command line.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Verify that the release is deployed (STATUS column).

options.why: Without -n it lists only the releases of the current namespace (usually 'default'): 'web' is not shown.
There is no 'release' resource type: Helm 3 stores release data in Secrets (type helm.sh/release.v1).
Without -n frontend Helm looks in the default namespace: 'release: not found'.

s2.explain: STATUS 'deployed' means Helm applied the manifests, not that the Pods are healthy. Follow with 'kubectl get pods -n frontend': you expect 2 Pods. 'helm list -A' shows every namespace.
s2.hint: Releases are namespaced: list them where you installed.

questions.title: Upgrade a release, then roll it back
questions.scenario: Release 'api' (chart podinfo/podinfo) runs in namespace 'prod'. Revision 1 is the original install; revision 2 was an upgrade that FAILED. Apply the new settings from prod-values.yaml; if the Pods break, go back to the last good revision.
questions.tip: 'helm rollback RELEASE REVISION -n NS'. Without a revision Helm goes to the previous one - which may itself be broken: read 'helm history' first.
questions.stakes: A bad upgrade hits production: 'helm rollback' is your undo, but only if you know the revision.
questions.analogy: Release history is git log: rollback checks out an older revision.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Upgrade release 'api' with the values file prod-values.yaml.

options.cmd: helm upgrade api podinfo/podinfo -n prod -f prod-values.yaml
aliases: helm upgrade api podinfo/podinfo -n prod --values prod-values.yaml
helm upgrade api podinfo/podinfo --namespace prod -f prod-values.yaml

options.why: 'helm upgrade' needs two arguments: the RELEASE and the CHART.

options.cmd: helm install api podinfo/podinfo -n prod -f prod-values.yaml
options.why: 'install' fails: 'cannot re-use a name that is still in use'. Existing releases are changed with 'upgrade'.

options.cmd: helm upgrade podinfo/podinfo api -n prod -f prod-values.yaml
options.why: Wrong order: RELEASE first, then CHART.

s1.explain: 'helm upgrade' renders the chart with your file and creates a NEW revision (3) instead of editing in place: that is what makes a rollback possible. Values you pass replace the previous ones unless you add --reuse-values.
s1.hint: Same release, same chart, new values from a file; releases live in a namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The new Pods crash. List the revisions of release 'api' to choose where to go back.

options.why: Without -n prod Helm searches the default namespace: 'release: not found'.

options.cmd: kubectl rollout history deployment api -n prod
options.why: Shows the Deployment's ReplicaSet revisions, not Helm revisions (which cover every object of the chart).
'helm list' shows only the current revision of each release and has no --revisions flag.

s2.explain: A rollback needs a target. 'history' lists each revision with its STATUS (deployed, superseded, failed): revision 2 failed, so the last good one is 1, not simply 'the previous number'.
s2.hint: Helm keeps every revision of a release: show its history with each STATUS.

context: REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS      CHART          APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
1         Mon Oct 26 09:12:03 2026  superseded  podinfo-6.9.0  6.9.0        Install complete
2         Wed Oct 28 14:40:51 2026  failed      podinfo-6.9.1  6.9.1        Upgrade "api" failed: timed out
3         Sat Oct 31 10:05:17 2026  deployed    podinfo-6.9.1  6.9.1        Upgrade complete
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Roll the release back to the last revision that worked.

options.why: Without a revision Helm rolls back to the previous one (2) - the upgrade that FAILED.

options.cmd: kubectl rollout undo deployment api -n prod
options.why: Only reverts the Deployment: Helm still records revision 3 as deployed and the next upgrade re-applies it.
--version selects a CHART version (e.g. 6.9.0), not a release revision.

s3.explain: A rollback creates a NEW revision (4) that copies revision 1, so the history is never rewritten and shows 'Rollback to 1'. Rolling back to 2 would bring the failed settings back.
s3.hint: Go back to a numbered revision of the release; the history tells you which one was deployed before.

questions.title: Customise chart values before installing
questions.scenario: Install chart 'podinfo/podinfo' as release 'shop' in the existing namespace 'shop', exposed as a NodePort Service on port 30080. Work with a values file instead of a long list of --set flags.
questions.tip: 'helm show values CHART > values.yaml', edit, 'helm install -f values.yaml'. 'helm template' renders locally - handy to check the result, but it installs nothing.
questions.stakes: Edit the chart's own values.yaml and your changes vanish with the next chart version.
questions.analogy: Defaults are the recipe; your values file is your 'less salt' note.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Save the chart's default values into values.yaml.

options.why: 'helm get values' reads an INSTALLED release (and only its user-supplied values), not a chart.
'show chart' prints Chart.yaml metadata (name, version, appVersion), not the values.
'template' renders the Kubernetes manifests, not the configurable values.

s1.explain: Start from the chart's own values.yaml, comments included: it is the only reference for which keys the templates actually read.
s1.hint: helm can print a chart's default values without installing it: redirect them to the file.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Make the Service a NodePort on 30080: type the right snippet in place of the 'type' and 'nodePort' lines of the service block. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: nodePort is ignored for a ClusterIP Service: the type must be NodePort.
8080 is outside the NodePort range (30000-32767 by default): the API server rejects the Service.
The chart reads service.nodePort; an unknown 'port' key is ignored and Kubernetes picks a random node port.

checks.msg: service.type must be NodePort (2 spaces under 'service:').
service.nodePort must be 30080 (2 spaces under 'service:').

forbid.msg: The type is still ClusterIP.
The old nodePort 31198 is still there.

s2.recap: In values.yaml set service.type: NodePort and service.nodePort: 30080.
s2.explain: Chart values are not Kubernetes API fields: the key names are whatever the chart's templates read, so take them from 'helm show values', not from the Service API. NodePorts must be in 30000-32767.
s2.hint: Two keys of the service block, at its indentation: the Service type and the fixed port.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Install release 'shop' in namespace 'shop' using values.yaml.

options.cmd: helm install shop podinfo/podinfo -n shop -f values.yaml
aliases: helm install shop podinfo/podinfo -n shop --values values.yaml
helm install shop podinfo/podinfo --namespace shop -f values.yaml

options.cmd: helm template shop podinfo/podinfo -n shop -f values.yaml
options.why: 'template' only renders the manifests to stdout: nothing is installed and no release is recorded.
values.yaml is chart input, not a Kubernetes manifest: it has no apiVersion/kind.
The second argument must be the CHART; values.yaml is not a chart (pass it with -f).

s3.explain: A values file keeps the settings reviewable and repeatable, unlike a long list of --set flags. Several -f files are merged left to right and --set wins over -f. Check with 'kubectl get svc -n shop'.
s3.hint: Install the release with your values file, in its own namespace.

questions.title: Render and apply a Kustomize overlay
questions.scenario: The 'shop' application is managed with Kustomize: a base in /opt/shop/base and an overlay in /opt/shop/overlays/prod (it contains kustomization.yaml and a replica patch). Preview what the overlay produces, apply it, and later remove it.
questions.tip: kubectl has Kustomize built in: 'kubectl kustomize DIR' renders, 'kubectl apply -k DIR' applies, 'kubectl delete -k DIR' removes. -k takes a DIRECTORY.
questions.stakes: Apply the base by mistake and staging runs with production settings.
questions.analogy: Kustomize is tracing paper over a drawing: the base is untouched, the overlay changes what you see.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Print the fully rendered manifests of the prod overlay WITHOUT touching the cluster.

options.why: 'build' belongs to the standalone 'kustomize build DIR' syntax; 'kubectl kustomize' takes the directory directly.
This applies the objects to the cluster - the task is only to preview them.
Shows the recipe (resources, patches), not the merged result of base + overlay.

s1.explain: Look before you apply: 'kubectl kustomize' (= kustomize build) renders base + patches + transformers to YAML and touches nothing, so you can catch a wrong namespace or replica count first.
s1.hint: kubectl has Kustomize built in: one subcommand only RENDERS a directory to standard output.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The output looks right. Apply the prod overlay to the cluster.

options.why: -f (even with -R) reads each YAML file as a plain manifest: kustomization.yaml is not an API object, and the base is never merged in.
-k expects the DIRECTORY that contains kustomization.yaml, not the file itself.
Applies the base alone: the prod patches of the overlay are not included.

s2.explain: -k runs the Kustomize build first and then applies the result like -f would. Without -k the overlay is not used: only -k performs the build.
s2.hint: apply has a flag that takes a kustomization directory instead of files.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Later: delete every object created by this overlay, and only those.

options.why: Builds the base alone: without the overlay's namespace and patches it targets other objects (e.g. in 'default').
Deletes every workload in the namespace (not only this app) and misses ConfigMaps, Secrets, etc. ('all' is only a subset).
'kubectl kustomize' only renders; it has no --delete flag.

s3.explain: 'delete -k' removes exactly the objects this overlay renders, no more and no less. Deleting the namespace or selecting by label could also remove things you did not create.
s3.hint: delete takes the same kustomization flag: exactly what the overlay renders goes away.

questions.title: Write a staging overlay
questions.scenario: Overlay /opt/shop/overlays/staging must put every object in namespace 'staging', add the local file service.yaml to the base resources, and run the 'nginx' image with tag 1.27. Then apply it and check the image.
questions.tip: Common kustomization.yaml fields: resources (files/dirs), namespace, namePrefix, labels, images (name + newName/newTag), patches, configMapGenerator.
questions.stakes: A file missing from 'resources' is silently left out: the overlay renders, but not what you meant.
questions.analogy: kustomization.yaml is the table of contents: not listed, not in the book.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment and the resources list (namespace, resources, images). Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: namespace staging, add service.yaml, nginx tag 1.27
target: # TODO: namespace staging, add service.yaml, nginx tag 1.27

options.why: newName replaces the image NAME: the container would run an image called '1.27'. The tag goes in newTag.
The base is no longer listed: only the Service would be generated, the Deployment disappears.
newTag is at the top level instead of inside the images entry: Kustomize rejects the unknown field.

checks.msg: Set 'namespace: staging' at the top level.
Keep '- ../../base' in the resources list.
Add '- service.yaml' to the resources list.
Add an images entry: '- name: nginx' with '  newTag: "1.27"'.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - replace it.
newName changes the image name, not the tag.
newTag must be inside the images entry (2 spaces).

s1.recap: kustomization.yaml: namespace: staging, resources + service.yaml, images: - name: nginx / newTag: "1.27".
s1.explain: Overlay settings are transformers: 'namespace' sets metadata.namespace on every object, 'resources' pulls in the base and service.yaml, 'images' retargets a container by image name (newTag). Quote the tag: a bare 1.27 is a number, not a string.
s1.hint: Three top-level kustomization fields: target namespace, the list of resources (base + local file), image tag override.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Apply the staging overlay to the cluster.

options.why: kustomization.yaml is a build recipe, not an API object: -f fails and nothing is built.
Only renders the YAML to stdout; nothing is applied.
The base has no namespace or image change: you must apply the overlay directory.

s2.explain: 'kubectl diff -k DIR' shows what would change before you apply. 'apply -k' then applies the rendered result, namespace and image included.
s2.hint: apply with the kustomization directory flag, on the staging overlay.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Check that the Deployments in 'staging' run nginx:1.27 (IMAGES column).

options.why: No -n staging: it lists the current namespace (usually 'default').
Adds the labels column, not the container images.
Shows what the overlay WOULD produce, not what actually runs in the cluster.

s3.explain: '-o wide' adds an IMAGES column, so you check that the image really is nginx:1.27 instead of trusting your edit.
s3.hint: The wide output of Deployments adds CONTAINERS and IMAGES columns; mind the namespace.

questions.title: Create a custom resource from its CRD
questions.scenario: A CRD for databases was installed by the platform team. Create a 'Database' named 'orders' in namespace 'shop' (engine postgres) with a nightly backup at 02:00 that keeps 7 backups.
questions.tip: CRD name = <plural>.<group>. 'kubectl explain <plural>.spec.<field>' documents custom resources too (types, -required- fields).
questions.stakes: Create the resource before its CRD exists and you get 'no matches for kind' at the worst moment.
questions.analogy: A CRD adds a word to the dictionary; a custom resource is a sentence using it.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the CustomResourceDefinitions installed in the cluster.

options.why: There is no 'customresources' type: definitions are 'customresourcedefinitions' (short name crd).
A CRD is named <plural>.<group> (databases.db.example.com): 'databases' alone is NotFound.
APIServices register aggregated API groups; they do not list the CRDs by name.

s1.explain: A custom resource can only exist if its CRD does, and CRDs are cluster-scoped: 'get crd' shows which kinds you may create. 'api-resources --api-group=db.example.com' adds short names and whether the kind is namespaced.
s1.hint: CRDs are cluster-scoped objects with a short resource name.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Show the documentation of the 'spec.backup' field of a Database (field names, types, required).

options.why: explain needs the resource first: RESOURCE.field.subfield.
Shows the values of existing instances (maybe none), not the schema with types and required fields.
This documents the CustomResourceDefinition object itself, which has no 'spec.backup' field.

s2.explain: A CRD publishes a schema, so you do not guess field names: 'explain' reads it like for built-in types. A wrong field name is rejected when you apply.
s2.hint: explain walks a type's schema with dots: plural resource name, then spec, then the field.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment: backup schedule "0 2 * * *", retention 7. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: The schema says retention is an <integer>: "7" is a string and the API server rejects the object.
The field is 'schedule' (required), not 'cron': strict field validation rejects the unknown field.
backup is at the top level, beside spec: it is not a field of the object, and spec.backup stays empty.

checks.msg: 'backup:' must be under spec (2 spaces).
spec.backup.schedule must be "0 2 * * *" (4 spaces).
spec.backup.retention must be the integer 7 (no quotes).

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - replace it.
The field is called 'schedule'.

s3.recap: spec.backup: schedule "0 2 * * *" (string) + retention 7 (integer).
s3.explain: The API server validates a custom resource against the CRD's schema: a wrong type or a missing required field is rejected, and strict field validation rejects unknown fields too. That is why you copy the names from 'explain'.
s3.hint: Two fields under spec.backup: a cron string (quoted) and an integer.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Create the Database object from db.yaml.

options.why: The file says namespace 'shop': kubectl refuses when -n does not match the object's namespace.
'kubectl create <kind>' generators exist only for some built-in types, not for custom resources.
Dry run: nothing is created in the cluster.

s4.explain: A custom resource is applied like any object: the CRD only tells the API server what the kind means. Check with 'kubectl get databases -n shop'.
s4.hint: Create the object from the file; the CRD makes the API server accept its kind.

questions.title: Install an operator and create its resource
questions.scenario: The Redis operator ships as /opt/operator/crds.yaml (CRD RedisCluster, group cache.acme.io) and /opt/operator/operator.yaml (Deployment 'redis-operator' in namespace 'redis-system'). Install it and ask it for a 3-node Redis 7.2 cluster 'sessions' in namespace 'web'.
questions.tip: Operator = CRDs (new API types) + a controller Deployment that watches them. Install CRDs first, check the controller logs, then create custom resources.
questions.stakes: Create the custom resource before the controller runs and nothing reacts: no error, just silence.
questions.analogy: An operator is a robot admin that has read the runbook for one application.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - First install the API types the operator will watch.

options.why: The controller would start before its CRDs exist: its watches fail ('no matches for kind RedisCluster').
A server dry run only validates: no CRD is stored.
Helm installs charts (a directory or .tgz), not a plain manifest file.

s1.explain: Install the types before what uses them: the operator and any custom resource need the CRD to be Established first. Very large CRDs can exceed the annotation size limit of 'apply': use 'kubectl create' or '--server-side'.
s1.hint: The operator watches a custom type: its CRDs must exist before anything uses them. The file is in /opt/operator.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The operator is running. Read its logs through its Deployment to check that the controller started.

options.why: Without 'deploy/' the argument is a Pod name; no Pod is called exactly 'redis-operator'.
No -n redis-system: kubectl looks in the current namespace and finds no such Deployment.
Logs are not an API resource you can 'get': use 'kubectl logs'.

s2.explain: A running Pod is not a working controller. The logs show that it started ('Starting workers controller=rediscluster') and reveal RBAC 'forbidden' errors, the usual silent failure. 'logs deploy/NAME' picks one Pod of the Deployment.
s2.hint: kubectl logs can target a Deployment (it picks one of its Pods); mind the operator's namespace.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment: 3 replicas, Redis version 7.2. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: Unquoted, 7.2 is a YAML number; the schema wants a <string>, so the object is rejected.
The schema field is 'replicas' (required); 'size' is unknown and rejected.
Not indented: the fields become top-level keys beside spec, and spec stays empty.

checks.msg: spec.replicas must be the integer 3 (2 spaces under spec).
spec.version must be the STRING "7.2" (quoted, 2 spaces under spec).

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - replace it.
The field is 'replicas', not 'size'.

s3.recap: RedisCluster spec: replicas: 3 and version: "7.2" (quoted string).
s3.explain: You declare the desired state (3 replicas, Redis 7.2) and the operator makes it true: after 'kubectl apply -f sessions.yaml' it creates the StatefulSet and Services and reports in .status. You never create those yourself.
s3.hint: Two spec fields: an integer, and a version written as a string (quote it, or 7.2 becomes a number).

s4.prompt: Step 4 - sessions.yaml is applied. Check the RedisCluster 'sessions' (its status columns).

aliases: kubectl get rediscluster sessions -n web -o wide

options.why: No -n web: the object is searched in the current namespace and is NotFound.
The CRD is the TYPE (redisclusters.cache.acme.io); 'sessions' is an instance of it.
The operator creates Pods such as sessions-0, sessions-1...; there is no Pod named exactly 'sessions'.

s4.explain: 'get' on a custom resource works like on a built-in; the status columns come from the CRD's additionalPrinterColumns. Use 'describe' for Events when it does not become ready.
s4.hint: A custom resource is listed like any type, by its kind's name; printer columns show its status.

questions.title: Nodes NotReady after kubeadm init
questions.scenario: A fresh kubeadm cluster: all nodes are NotReady. kubeadm-config shows podSubnet 10.50.0.0/16 and serviceSubnet 10.96.0.0/12. Install Calico with its operator: operator-crds.yaml, tigera-operator.yaml and custom-resources.yaml are in the current directory.
questions.tip: NotReady + 'cni plugin not initialized' = no config in /etc/cni/net.d. The CNI IP pool must match (or sit inside) the kubeadm --pod-network-cidr.
questions.stakes: Control plane Ready, nodes NotReady, CoreDNS Pending: no CNI, and your demo is blocked.
questions.analogy: Without a CNI, nodes are houses with no roads.

context: $ kubectl describe node node01 | grep -i network
Ready  False  ...  container runtime network not ready: NetworkReady=false
reason:NetworkPluginNotReady message:Network plugin returns error: cni plugin not initialized
s1.prompt: Step 1 - On node01, look in the directory where the container runtime expects the CNI network configuration.

options.why: /opt/cni/bin holds the CNI plugin BINARIES (bridge, host-local...); the network configuration lives in /etc/cni/net.d.
That is the kubelet's static Pod directory (control-plane components), not CNI config.
Kubelet certificates; nothing to do with the network plugin.

s1.explain: The kubelet reports NotReady while no CNI configuration exists: containerd/CRI-O read the first *.conf/*.conflist in /etc/cni/net.d. An empty directory confirms the diagnosis before you install anything.
s1.hint: The runtime reads CNI config files from a fixed directory under /etc/cni: is it empty?

s2.prompt: Step 2 - First the API types: install Calico's (very large) CRDs from operator-crds.yaml.

options.why: Client-side apply stores each object in an annotation limited to 256 KiB: the Installation CRD is rejected ('metadata.annotations: Too long'). Calico's docs use create.
Wrong order: the Installation CRD does not exist yet ('no matches for kind Installation') - and its CIDR is not fixed yet.
A client dry run only prints what would be sent: no CRD exists afterwards.

s2.explain: Since Calico 3.30 the CRDs ship apart from the operator, in operator-crds.yaml (32 CRDs, about 3.4 MB). 'create' (or server-side apply) is needed: client-side apply would copy each CRD into an annotation, and the Installation CRD exceeds its 256 KiB limit.
s2.hint: These CRDs are too large for client-side apply's annotation: create them (or apply server-side).

s6.prompt: Step 3 - Now install the Tigera operator itself from tigera-operator.yaml.

options.why: The manifest's namespaced objects declare 'tigera-operator': kubectl refuses the mismatching -n.
The CRDs are already there ('AlreadyExists'), and the operator that acts on them is still not installed.
A client dry run creates nothing, and the operator would still be missing.

s6.explain: tigera-operator.yaml is small (a namespace, RBAC and the operator Deployment), so plain apply works too. The operator then waits for an Installation resource before it deploys anything.
s6.hint: The second file holds the operator's Deployment and RBAC, not the CRDs.

context: $ kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml | grep -i subnet
s3.prompt: Step 4 - Make the Calico IP pool match the cluster's pod subnet: type the right line in place of the 'cidr' line. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: 10.96.0.0/12 is the SERVICE subnet (ClusterIPs). Pod IPs must come from the pod subnet.
/26 is the per-node block size (blockSize: 26), not the pool: 64 addresses for the whole cluster.
Indented like 'ipPools': cidr leaves the pool entry and becomes an unknown calicoNetwork field.

checks.msg: The pool entry needs 'cidr: 10.50.0.0/16' (6 spaces, inside the ipPools item).

forbid.msg: The default 192.168.0.0/16 is still there.
cidr must be indented inside the ipPools list item (6 spaces).

s3.recap: custom-resources.yaml: ipPools[0].cidr = podSubnet 10.50.0.0/16 (not the service CIDR, not the /26 block size).
s3.explain: The CNI pool must agree with the cluster's podSubnet (10.50.0.0/16): the controller-manager hands each node a podCIDR from it, so a different pool gives overlapping Pod IPs or broken routes. Calico's default 192.168.0.0/16 is the usual trap.
s3.hint: The pool's cidr must equal kubeadm's podSubnet from the scenario.

s4.prompt: Step 5 - Create the Installation (and APIServer) resources from the edited file.

options.why: 'replace' only updates existing objects: these do not exist yet (NotFound).
The operator is already installed (AlreadyExists), and the edited file is never used.
Dry run: nothing is sent to the cluster, Calico is never deployed.

s4.explain: The Installation resource is what makes the operator deploy calico-node on every node; it writes 10-calico.conflist into /etc/cni/net.d and the nodes turn Ready ('kubectl get nodes -w').
s4.hint: Create the operator's custom resources from the edited file.

s5.prompt: Step 6 - The operator now deploys Calico. Check its Pods (calico-node on every node) in the namespace the operator creates for them.

options.why: With the operator, calico-node and calico-kube-controllers run in calico-system: kube-system only shows the control plane and CoreDNS.
Shows the operator Pod only, not the Calico components it creates.
No such namespace: 'No resources found in calico namespace.' tells you nothing.

s5.explain: The Tigera operator reconciles the Installation into Pods in calico-system. Once calico-node is Running on a node, it writes the CNI config into /etc/cni/net.d and that node turns Ready; CoreDNS leaves Pending at the same moment.
s5.hint: The operator installs Calico into a namespace of its own, not where the operator itself runs.

questions.title: Debug a container with crictl
questions.scenario: On node01 (containerd runtime), the 'billing' container of Pod billing-7c9d8-x2kqp (namespace finance) keeps exiting. Investigate directly on the node with crictl.
