questions.tip: crictl talks to the CRI runtime: 'ps -a' (containers, incl. exited), 'pods' (sandboxes), 'logs ID', 'inspect ID', 'images'. It takes IDs, not Pod names.
questions.stakes: When the API server is down, kubectl is useless: crictl is the only flashlight left.
questions.analogy: kubectl talks to the front desk; crictl walks into the kitchen (the runtime).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - On node01, list ALL containers, including the ones that have exited.

options.why: Without -a only RUNNING containers are listed: the exited billing container is hidden.
Lists Pod sandboxes, not the application containers and their state.
The node runs containerd: Docker is not the Kubernetes runtime (dockershim is gone since v1.24).

s1.explain: Without -a crictl shows only running containers, so a crashing one can be invisible. Exited plus a growing ATTEMPT count means the kubelet keeps restarting it: CrashLoopBackOff seen from the node.
s1.hint: crictl talks to the CRI; by default it lists running containers only: add the flag for all.

context: CONTAINER       IMAGE           CREATED          STATE    NAME     ATTEMPT  POD ID          POD                 NAMESPACE
3f9c1a2b7e44d   6a2e1f0c9d8b1   20 seconds ago   Exited   billing  5        b81c2d3e4f5a6   billing-7c9d8-x2kqp  finance
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Print the output of that exited container.

options.why: crictl logs takes a CONTAINER ID (or unique prefix), not a container name.
That is the POD sandbox ID: logs belong to containers.
Containers are not systemd units: their output is in /var/log/pods, read by 'crictl logs'.

s2.explain: A crash leaves its reason in the container's last output. crictl logs reads it by container ID with no API server needed (the files live under /var/log/pods/). Add --tail 20 to limit the output.
s2.hint: crictl prints a container's output by container ID, even after it exited.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Show the container's full status (exit code, reason, image, mounts) as JSON.

options.why: inspectp inspects the POD sandbox (network namespace, IP), not the container's exit status.
stats shows CPU/memory usage of running containers; no exit code or reason.
crictl has no 'describe' command (that is kubectl): it is 'inspect'.

s3.explain: Logs show what the app printed; inspect shows why the runtime stopped it: status.exitCode (137 = killed, often out of memory), reason and message. It is the node-side 'Last State' of kubectl describe.
s3.hint: crictl's 'inspect' command family: the container one gives JSON with state, exit code, mounts.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Check which billing images are present in the node's CRI image store.

options.cmd: sudo ctr images ls | grep billing
options.why: Plain ctr uses containerd's 'default' namespace; Kubernetes images live in the 'k8s.io' namespace, so nothing shows.
Docker is not the runtime here: its image store is separate (and probably not installed).

options.cmd: kubectl get images -n finance | grep billing
options.why: Images are not Kubernetes API objects.

s4.explain: A container that cannot start may simply lack its image: 'crictl images' lists what the node really has, and 'crictl pull IMAGE' tests registry access from the node itself, not from your laptop.
s4.hint: List the images in the runtime's store and filter for the name.

questions.title: Find the plugins behind CSI and CRI
questions.scenario: You inherit a cluster and must identify its plugins: which CSI drivers are registered, which CRI socket the kubelet uses on node01, and then create a StorageClass 'nfs-fast' backed by the NFS CSI driver.
questions.tip: CSI driver name = StorageClass 'provisioner' (kubectl get csidrivers). CRI = kubelet's containerRuntimeEndpoint socket. CNI config = /etc/cni/net.d, binaries = /opt/cni/bin.
questions.stakes: Blame the wrong plugin layer and you debug networking for an hour when storage was the problem.
questions.analogy: CRI, CNI and CSI are USB ports for runtime, network and storage: one socket, many vendors.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the CSI drivers registered in the cluster.

options.why: There is no 'drivers' resource: the type is CSIDriver (storage.k8s.io).
Lists StorageClasses: a class can name a provisioner that is not installed, so it proves nothing about registered drivers.
Shows volumes attached to nodes, not the installed drivers.

s1.explain: CSI drivers register themselves with a cluster-scoped CSIDriver object, so the list tells you what storage the cluster can provide. 'kubectl get csinodes' shows on which nodes a driver's node plugin is registered.
s1.hint: Registered CSI drivers are cluster-scoped API objects with their own resource type.

context: NAME             ATTACHREQUIRED   PODINFOONMOUNT   STORAGECAPACITY   MODES        AGE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - On node01, list the running containers with crictl, explicitly using the same CRI socket as the kubelet.

options.why: dockershim was removed in Kubernetes v1.24; the kubelet uses the containerd socket.
/etc/cni/net.d is the CNI configuration directory, not the CRI socket.
crictl never talks to the API server: it has no --kubeconfig flag, it needs the CRI socket.

s2.explain: crictl must talk to the kubelet's own CRI socket (containerd: /run/containerd/containerd.sock, CRI-O: /var/run/crio/crio.sock): that is also how you learn which runtime the node uses. Make it permanent in /etc/crictl.yaml (runtime-endpoint).
s2.hint: crictl has a global flag for the runtime socket; the kubelet uses containerd's unix socket under /run.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Type the right provisioner line in place of 'provisioner: TODO' so that PVCs of this class are provisioned by the NFS CSI driver. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: There is no in-tree NFS provisioner: PVCs of this class would stay Pending forever.
That is the name of the driver's controller Deployment, not the CSI driver name registered in CSIDriver.
no-provisioner means static provisioning only (pre-created PVs): nothing is created for new PVCs.

checks.msg: provisioner must be the CSI driver name: nfs.csi.k8s.io.

forbid.msg: 'provisioner: TODO' is still there - replace it.

s3.recap: StorageClass provisioner = the CSIDriver name (nfs.csi.k8s.io).
s3.explain: A StorageClass names the driver that provisions its volumes: the provisioner must equal the CSI driver's name (nfs.csi.k8s.io), or nobody handles the claim and it stays Pending. 'parameters' are passed to that driver (server, share).
s3.hint: A StorageClass names its provisioner by the CSI driver's name, as registered in the cluster.

questions.topic: High availability (kubeadm init with a load balancer)
questions.title: Bootstrap an HA control plane
questions.scenario: Build an HA cluster: cp1 (192.168.10.11), cp2 and cp3 sit behind the load balancer lb.k8s.lab:6443 (192.168.10.100). On cp1, finish kubeadm-config.yaml (kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4) and bootstrap the first control plane so cp2 and cp3 can join later as control planes.
questions.tip: HA starts at 'kubeadm init': controlPlaneEndpoint (or --control-plane-endpoint) = the LOAD BALANCER, plus --upload-certs. kubeadm cannot turn a cluster made without an endpoint into an HA one.

docs.title: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

questions.stakes: Point the endpoint at cp1 and every kubeconfig and node follows cp1: when it dies, so does the cluster.
questions.analogy: The endpoint is the switchboard number on business cards: staff can change, the number printed everywhere stays.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Set the shared endpoint of all control planes: type the right line in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: the address every node and client uses for the API
target: # TODO: the address every node and client uses for the API

options.why: That is cp1's own address: every kubeconfig and kubelet would talk to cp1 only. When cp1 fails the cluster is unreachable, and kubeadm cannot change it into HA later.
2379 is etcd's client port, not the API server's: kubeconfigs and join commands would point at a port where no API answers.
Indented, it becomes networking.controlPlaneEndpoint, an unknown field: kubeadm only warns and the endpoint stays empty (cp1's own address).

checks.msg: Add 'controlPlaneEndpoint: "lb.k8s.lab:6443"' at the top level of the ClusterConfiguration.
Keep networking.podSubnet 10.244.0.0/16.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the line in its place.

s1.recap: controlPlaneEndpoint: "lb.k8s.lab:6443" (the load balancer) in the ClusterConfiguration.
s1.explain: The endpoint is written into every kubeconfig, join command and the API certificate. Set to the load balancer, any control plane can fail while clients keep one stable address. Set to cp1, the cluster is tied to cp1 for good: kubeadm cannot convert it to HA later.
s1.hint: A top-level ClusterConfiguration field: the load balancer's name and API port, quoted.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Bootstrap cp1 from that file, and store the shared certificates in the cluster so cp2 and cp3 can fetch them when they join.

options.why: The cluster starts, but the CA, service-account and front-proxy keys stay on cp1: each new control plane would need them copied by hand (scp).
kubeadm refuses: it can not mix '--config' with arguments [control-plane-endpoint]. The endpoint is already in the file.

options.cmd: sudo kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs --config kubeadm-config.yaml
options.why: Only the upload phase: there is no cluster yet (no API server to store the Secret in), so nothing is bootstrapped.

s2.explain: --upload-certs encrypts the certificates every control plane must share (CAs, sa.key, front-proxy, etcd CA) into the kubeadm-certs Secret and prints the key that decrypts them. It is one of the few flags allowed next to --config; the endpoint is not, it lives in the file.
s2.hint: Init from the config file, plus the flag that uploads the shared certificates encrypted into a Secret.

context: [upload-certs] Storing the certificates in Secret "kubeadm-certs" in the "kube-system" Namespace
You can now join any number of control-plane node by running ...
As a safeguard, uploaded-certs will be deleted in two hours; ...
s3.prompt: Step 3 - The admin kubeconfig is in place. Check that the encrypted shared certificates really are stored in the cluster.

options.why: That looks in the 'default' namespace: 'NotFound', although the Secret exists in kube-system.
The certificates are stored in a Secret, not a ConfigMap: 'NotFound'. (The kubeadm-config ConfigMap holds the ClusterConfiguration.)
Those are cp1's local files, which always exist after init: it proves nothing about the copy cp2 and cp3 will download.

s3.explain: kubeadm join --control-plane downloads kubeadm-certs from kube-system and decrypts it with the key. The Secret is deleted after two hours: if it is gone, the join fails, so check it before you rely on the printed control-plane join command.
s3.hint: kubeadm stores those certificates in a Secret in kube-system; its name starts with kubeadm.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Clients will reach the API as lb.k8s.lab. Show the DNS names and IPs the API server certificate is valid for.

options.why: ca.crt is the cluster CA: it signs the server certificates but does not list the API server's names.
That is the client certificate the API server presents to kubelets: it carries no server names (no SAN extension).
It lists expiry dates and CAs of each certificate, not the names (SANs) they are valid for.

s4.explain: kubeadm adds the controlPlaneEndpoint host (lb.k8s.lab) to the API server certificate, next to the node name, IP and 'kubernetes' names. Without it, TLS through the load balancer fails with 'x509: certificate is valid for ..., not lb.k8s.lab'.
s4.hint: openssl x509 can print just one extension of the API server certificate: the alternative names.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Show the API server address your kubeconfig uses: with an HA endpoint it must be the load balancer, not cp1.

options.why: Lists the real API server addresses behind the 'kubernetes' Service (192.168.10.11:6443): the members, not the shared endpoint clients use.
Dumps every object and log of the cluster: thousands of lines, and the kubeconfig's server is not among them.
Prints cp1's own name: it says nothing about where kubectl connects.

s5.explain: kubeadm writes controlPlaneEndpoint into admin.conf, the kubelets' kubeconfigs and the join commands. Seeing https://lb.k8s.lab:6443 here proves clients will survive the loss of cp1; seeing cp1's address would make the whole HA setup useless for them.
s5.hint: The address lives in the 'clusters' part of the kubeconfig.

questions.title: Join a second control plane
questions.scenario: cp1 was bootstrapped YESTERDAY with 'kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint lb.k8s.lab:6443 --upload-certs'. The saved join commands are useless now: the token (24 h) and the certificate key (2 h) have expired. Add cp2 as a second control plane. You are root on cp1 and cp2.
questions.tip: Certificate key expired? 'kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs' on a control plane, then 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command --certificate-key KEY' prints the full control-plane join.

docs.title: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

questions.stakes: Join without --control-plane and 'cp2' is just a worker: you believe you have HA, but one dead cp1 still stops everything.
questions.analogy: The certificate key is the code of a safe-deposit box that self-destructs after two hours: refill the box, get a new code.

context: root@cp1# kubectl -n kube-system get secret kubeadm-certs
Error from server (NotFound): secrets "kubeadm-certs" not found
s1.prompt: Step 1 - On cp1: store the shared certificates in the cluster again, encrypted with a NEW certificate key.

options.why: It only prints a random key: nothing is uploaded, and the kubeadm-certs Secret is still missing.
It extends the expiry of cp1's own certificates; it uploads nothing, so cp2 still cannot download them.
A fresh token, but the kubeadm-certs Secret is still gone: a control-plane join cannot fetch the CA and keys.

s1.explain: The uploaded certificates are a Secret that kubeadm deletes after two hours, together with the validity of its key. The 'upload-certs' phase re-encrypts cp1's shared certificates with a brand-new key, stores them in kube-system and prints that key.
s1.hint: kubeadm init can run a single phase: the one that uploads the certificates, with its upload flag.

context: [upload-certs] Storing the certificates in Secret "kubeadm-certs" in the "kube-system" Namespace
root@cp1# KEY=7d3b0f5c9e1a...c42f      # the full 64 hex digits
s2.prompt: Step 2 - On cp1: print a complete CONTROL-PLANE join command, with a new token and that key.

options.why: 'token create' has no --control-plane flag ('unknown flag'): it is the --certificate-key that turns the printed command into a control-plane join.
That prints a WORKER join: no --control-plane, no --certificate-key.
The upload phase has no --print-join-command flag: join commands come from 'kubeadm token create'.

s2.explain: Yesterday's token expired too (24 h). 'token create --print-join-command' makes a new one and adds the CA hash; with --certificate-key it also appends '--control-plane --certificate-key KEY', ready to paste on cp2.
s2.hint: A fresh token with the full join line; for a control plane it must also carry the certificate key.

context: root@cp2# HASH=sha256:9f4c...b81d      # with its sha256: prefix
s3.prompt: Step 3 - On cp2: join the cluster as a control plane, using TOKEN, HASH and KEY.

options.why: cp2 joins as a WORKER: no API server, no etcd member. The cluster still has a single control plane.
No key: kubeadm cannot download the shared certificates and stops, because /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt is missing on cp2.
That bootstraps a SECOND, separate cluster on cp2 (new CA, new etcd): the load balancer would then mix two clusters.

s3.explain: --control-plane makes kubeadm create an API server, scheduler, controller-manager and a new etcd member on cp2; --certificate-key decrypts the shared CA and keys from kubeadm-certs, so cp2 serves certificates signed by the same CA. Join control planes one at a time.
s3.hint: Join through the load balancer with token and CA hash, plus the two control-plane flags (role, certificate key).

s5.prompt: Step 4 - The join succeeded. On cp2, make kubectl in this shell use the admin kubeconfig that join wrote.

options.why: That is the node's own identity (system:node:cp2): it may read Pods and Nodes but is forbidden Deployments, Secrets of other nodes and most admin work.
A CA certificate is not a kubeconfig: every kubectl command fails to load the configuration.
There is no kubeconfig in $HOME/.kube on cp2 yet: 'no context exists with the name'.

s5.explain: A control-plane join writes /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf on the new node too, pointing at the shared endpoint. As root, KUBECONFIG is the quickest way to use it; a regular user copies it to $HOME/.kube/config, as after init.
s5.hint: join prints the same kubeconfig advice as init, for the same file.

s4.prompt: Step 5 - Check that cp2 runs its own control-plane Pods (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager).

options.cmd: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=cp2
aliases: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=cp2

options.why: That searches the 'default' namespace: the static control-plane Pods live in kube-system, so 'No resources found'.
kubernetes.io/hostname is a NODE label: no Pod carries it, so 'No resources found'.

s4.explain: The ROLES column only reflects a label; the proof is the static Pods kube-apiserver-cp2, etcd-cp2, kube-scheduler-cp2 and kube-controller-manager-cp2 Running. Then rebalance CoreDNS ('kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment coredns').
s4.hint: Filter kube-system's Pods by the node they run on: a field selector on spec.nodeName.

questions.title: Inspect an HA control plane
questions.scenario: Cluster 'ha-lab' has three stacked control planes (cp1, cp2, cp3: one etcd member each) behind lb.k8s.lab:6443. cp3 is rebooting for maintenance. You are root on cp1, in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd.
questions.tip: etcd needs a quorum of (n/2)+1 members (rounded down): 3 members tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2, 4 still only 1. Hence an ODD number of control planes.
questions.stakes: Reboot a second control plane while one is down and etcd loses quorum: the API refuses every write, cluster-wide.
questions.analogy: A committee that needs a majority to vote: with 3 members, one can be absent; with 2 absent, nothing can be decided.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List only the control-plane nodes, by their role label.

options.why: kubeadm no longer sets the old 'master' label: 'No resources found', although there are three control planes.
kubectl get has no --role flag ('unknown flag'): roles are only labels, selected with -l.
No node carries a 'role' label: 'No resources found'. The key is node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.

s1.explain: The ROLES column is derived from node-role.kubernetes.io/<role> labels, so a label selector on that key returns exactly the control planes (the label has an empty value: the key alone matches).
s1.hint: Control-plane nodes carry a role label (node-role.kubernetes.io/...); select nodes by it.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Ask etcd itself (local member, default endpoint) which members form the cluster.

options.why: No certificates: etcd requires client-certificate authentication, so the TLS handshake fails.
That shows the etcd static Pods the kubelets report, not etcd's own membership (members added or removed by etcdctl do not show).
It reports only the endpoints you query (here the local one): no list of the other members.

s2.explain: Membership is etcd's own data, so ask etcd. In the stacked topology kubeadm adds one member per control plane ('join --control-plane'): three control planes, three members, each with its peer (2380) and client (2379) URL.
s2.hint: etcdctl with CA, client cert and key; the subcommand lists the members of the cluster.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Check the health of EVERY member of that list, in one command.

options.why: Without --cluster only the default endpoint (cp1's local member) is checked: 'healthy', and nothing about cp2 or cp3.
That REMOVES cp3 from etcd: after its reboot it cannot rejoin, and the cluster is down to 2 members (no failure tolerated).
cp3 is rebooting: its kubelet cannot serve logs, and one member's logs say nothing about the others.

s3.explain: --cluster reads the member list and checks every client URL. cp3 shows 'unhealthy', yet etcd still works: 3 members need a quorum of (3/2)+1 = 2, and cp1 + cp2 are 2. Lose one more and etcd stops accepting writes: wait for cp3 before touching another node.
s3.hint: Endpoint health, but for every member: a flag makes etcdctl discover them all.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - A colleague's kubeconfig talks straight to cp3 and fails. Point it at the load balancer instead: replace the server line. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: Works today, but pins cp1: the next reboot of cp1 breaks this kubeconfig again. Only the load balancer survives any one node.
The API server speaks only HTTPS on 6443: kubectl gets 'Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server'.
2379 is etcd's client port, and the load balancer does not even listen there: 'connection refused'.

checks.msg: The cluster's server must be https://lb.k8s.lab:6443 (4 spaces of indentation).
Keep the cluster name ha-lab.

forbid.msg: Do not pin one control plane: use the load balancer.

s4.recap: server: https://lb.k8s.lab:6443 - kubeconfigs of an HA cluster target the load balancer.
s4.explain: In an HA cluster every client (kubectl, kubelets, controllers) must use the controlPlaneEndpoint, so the load balancer can route around a dead API server. The existing CA data still fits: lb.k8s.lab is in the API server certificate because it is the controlPlaneEndpoint.
s4.hint: The server line takes the load balancer's https URL and API port.

questions.title: Upgrade an HA control plane
questions.scenario: The HA cluster (cp1, cp2, cp3 behind lb.k8s.lab:6443) runs v1.36.5. On every control plane the kubeadm package is already 1.37.1. Upgrade the control planes to v1.37.1, one node at a time. You are root on each node.
questions.tip: 'kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z' on ONE control plane only; 'kubeadm upgrade node' on each other one. Node by node: drain, kubelet + kubectl packages, restart kubelet, uncordon.
questions.stakes: Drain and upgrade two control planes at once and etcd may lose quorum mid-upgrade: the whole API goes read-only.
questions.analogy: Changing the tyres of a moving convoy: one truck pulls over at a time, and only rejoins before the next one stops.

context: You can now apply the upgrade by executing the following command:
s1.prompt: Step 1 - On cp1, the FIRST control plane you upgrade: upgrade its control-plane components.

options.why: 'upgrade node' brings a node to the version the cluster already records (kubeadm-config), still v1.36.5 until 'apply' has run: cp1 stays on v1.36.5.
kubeadm 1.37.1 cannot install a version newer than itself, and minor versions cannot be skipped: the upgrade is refused.
Too early: a kubelet must never be newer than the API servers it talks to. Control-plane components first, kubelet after.

s1.explain: 'apply' runs once, on the first control plane: it checks the cluster, records v1.37.1 in the kubeadm-config ConfigMap and upgrades cp1's static Pods (including its etcd member). The other control planes then follow that recorded version.
s1.hint: Only the first control plane 'applies' the target version; it is given explicitly.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - cp1 is fully done (kubelet included, uncordoned). On cp2: upgrade its control-plane components.

options.why: 'upgrade node' takes no version: it reads the one 'apply' recorded in the cluster. kubeadm rejects the extra argument.
Read-only: it changes nothing, and is not needed on the other control planes.
A mirror Pod: the kubelet recreates it from the unchanged manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests, still v1.36.5.

s2.explain: On every other control plane, 'upgrade node' fetches the ClusterConfiguration that 'apply' wrote and rewrites this node's static Pod manifests and kubelet config. Since v1.28 kubeadm upgrades CoreDNS and kube-proxy only once the last control plane is upgraded.
s2.hint: Other control planes take the version already recorded in the cluster: no version argument.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Before upgrading cp2's kubelet package, mark it unschedulable and evict its workloads.

options.why: Refused: cp2 runs DaemonSet Pods (kube-proxy, the CNI) that drain cannot evict without --ignore-daemonsets.
Only blocks NEW Pods: those already on cp2 (CoreDNS, for example) are cut off when the kubelet restarts.
Removes the Node object: its Pods are garbage-collected at once, with no graceful eviction and no PodDisruptionBudget check.

s3.explain: drain = cordon + evict through the Eviction API, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets, so the cluster's workloads move away gracefully. DaemonSet Pods are skipped (they belong on every node). Static control-plane Pods are not evicted either.
s3.hint: Cordon + evict in one command; DaemonSet Pods cannot leave the node.

context: root@cp2# systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
s4.prompt: Step 4 - cp2 runs kubelet 1.37.1. Put it back into service BEFORE you move on to cp3.

options.why: Too soon: cp2 is still cordoned, so evicted Pods have one schedulable control plane left, and cp2 stays out of service.
There is no 'undrain' command: the reverse of drain/cordon is 'kubectl uncordon'.
unschedulable: true IS the cordon: the node stays SchedulingDisabled.

s4.explain: uncordon clears spec.unschedulable so cp2 takes Pods again. Only then repeat 'upgrade node', drain, kubelet and uncordon on cp3: one node at a time keeps 2 of 3 etcd members and API servers up all along.
s4.hint: Undo the unschedulable mark drain left on the Node.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Before upgrading cp3: check that cp1 and cp2 both report kubelet v1.37.1 and are schedulable.

options.why: Shows your client and the ONE API server the load balancer picked: not the kubelets, and not every node.
Prints the kubeadm binary installed on this node: it was already 1.37.1 before you started.
Only the kubelet binary of the node you are logged on, not the version each node really runs, nor whether it is cordoned.

s5.explain: The VERSION column is what each node's kubelet reports, and STATUS shows 'SchedulingDisabled' if an uncordon was forgotten. One look confirms cp1 and cp2 are done before cp3 is taken out of service.
s5.hint: One listing shows each node's kubelet version and whether it is still cordoned.

questions.title: Prepare the network for an HA control plane
questions.scenario: Three control planes: cp1 (192.168.10.11, already bootstrapped), cp2 (192.168.10.12) and cp3 (192.168.10.13), behind HAProxy on lb.k8s.lab (192.168.10.100). The nodes run Ubuntu with ufw enabled. Make the network ready for cp2 and cp3 to join.
questions.tip: Control-plane ports: 6443 (API), 2379-2380 (etcd), 10250 (kubelet), 10259 (scheduler), 10257 (controller-manager). Use an odd number of control planes (3, 5).

docs.title: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

questions.stakes: Forget the health check and the load balancer keeps sending a third of the requests to a dead API server.
questions.analogy: The load balancer is a receptionist who checks which desks are staffed before sending each visitor over.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - From cp2: test whether cp1's etcd PEER port can be reached over TCP (2-second timeout).

options.why: ICMP only proves the host is up: a firewall can still drop TCP 2380.
6443 is the API server port; etcd's members talk to each other on 2380 (peer) and 2379 (client).
ss lists the LOCAL listening sockets of cp2 (where etcd does not run yet): it says nothing about reaching cp1.

s1.explain: nc -z opens a TCP connection and closes it at once; -v prints the result. 'succeeded' means open; 'refused' means nothing listens; a timeout means a firewall drops the packets. A new stacked member needs cp1's 2380 and 2379.
s1.hint: netcat in zero-I/O scan mode, verbose, with a timeout; etcd peers talk on 2380.

context: nc: connect to 192.168.10.11 port 2380 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress
s2.prompt: Step 2 - etcd listens, but the firewall drops the traffic. On cp1: allow etcd's client AND peer ports.

aliases: ufw allow proto tcp from any to any port 2379:2380

options.why: Only the peer port: a joining control plane also calls cp1's client port 2379 to register itself as a new etcd member.
etcd speaks TCP: opening UDP changes nothing, the TCP connections still time out.
6443 is already allowed (see ufw status): it is the API port, etcd stays blocked.

s2.explain: Stacked etcd uses 2380 between members (replication, elections) and 2379 for clients; a joining control plane uses both. ufw writes port ranges with a colon and needs the protocol. Kubernetes only uses TCP on the control-plane ports.
s2.hint: ufw allows a port RANGE with a colon, and the protocol after a slash: client and peer ports are consecutive.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Add cp2 and cp3 to the backend, with a health check like cp1: type the right lines in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: No 'check': HAProxy never marks a dead API server down and keeps routing its share of requests there (kubectl timeouts during a reboot).
2379 is etcd's client port: API clients sent there hit etcd, which rejects them (wrong protocol, wrong certificate).
10250 is the kubelet API, not the Kubernetes API: kubectl requests would reach kubelets and fail.

checks.msg: Add 'server cp2 192.168.10.12:6443 check' under the backend.
Add 'server cp3 192.168.10.13:6443 check' under the backend.
Keep the cp1 line.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the lines in its place.
Every backend server is an API server on port 6443.

s3.recap: server cpN 192.168.10.1N:6443 check - every API server in the backend, each health-checked.
s3.explain: HAProxy is a plain TCP forwarder here (mode tcp: TLS goes end to end). 'check' is the TCP health check on 6443 the kubeadm HA guide asks for: a stopped API server leaves the rotation within seconds. One that still listens while its etcd is down stays in; an HTTPS check on /readyz would catch that.
s3.hint: One server line per backend: name, IP:API port, and the health-check keyword, like cp1.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Through the load balancer, check that an API server really answers (health endpoints allow anonymous requests).

options.why: HAProxy itself accepts the TCP connection: 'succeeded' even when every API server behind it is down.
Plain HTTP to a TLS port: the API server answers 'Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server'.
The load balancer only listens on 6443 ('connection refused'), and etcd is not the API anyway.

s4.explain: Only an API server can answer /livez with 'ok', so the reply proves the whole path: frontend, backend, a live kube-apiserver. -k skips the CA check for this test (or pass --cacert). A plain TCP test stops at HAProxy.
s4.hint: Health endpoints answer anonymous HTTPS; the LB's certificate name may not match: tell curl to skip verification.

questions.title: Deployment with resource limits
questions.scenario: Create a Deployment 'web' (image nginx:1.26, 3 replicas) whose container is limited to cpu 500m and memory 128Mi.
questions.tip: For anything the imperative command cannot express: generate with '--dry-run=client -o yaml', edit, then apply.

docs.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

questions.stakes: No limits: one leaking Pod eats the node and its neighbours get OOM-killed.
questions.analogy: Requests are a restaurant booking; limits are the cap on how much one table can eat.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Generate the manifest into deploy.yaml WITHOUT creating anything in the cluster.

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26 --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

options.why: 'kubectl run' creates a Pod, not a Deployment.

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26 --replicas=3 -o yaml > deploy.yaml
options.why: Without --dry-run=client the Deployment is created immediately in the cluster.

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment web --image nginx:1.26 --replicas 3 --dry-run -o yaml > deploy.yaml
options.why: A bare --dry-run is not valid any more: it needs a value (client, server or none).

s1.explain: --dry-run=client -o yaml prints the object without sending it to the cluster, so you get a correct skeleton to edit instead of typing YAML from memory. Tip: export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml" saves typing during the exam.
s1.hint: The deployment generator, plus a client-side dry run printed as YAML and redirected into the file.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Limit the container to cpu 500m and memory 128Mi: type the right snippet in place of 'resources: {}'. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'limits:' must be a child of 'resources:' (indented 2 more spaces).
'cpu: 500m' must be under limits (2 more spaces).
'memory: 128Mi' must be under limits (2 more spaces).

forbid.msg: 'resources: {}' is still there - replace it.

options.why: 'limits' is at the same level as 'resources': it becomes an unknown container field and nothing is limited.
requests = what the scheduler reserves. The task asks for limits = the maximum the container may use.
128M is SI (128,000,000 bytes); the task says 128Mi (134,217,728 bytes). Watch the suffix.

s2.recap: Replace 'resources: {}' with a resources/limits block (cpu 500m, memory 128Mi).
s2.explain: A limit is a cap the container cannot exceed: more memory than 128Mi gets it OOM-killed, more CPU than 500m gets it throttled. It lives under spec.template.spec.containers[].resources; indentation is 2 spaces, never tabs.
s2.hint: Limits sit under resources, one level per key: resources > limits > cpu / memory.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Create the Deployment from the file.

options.why: -k expects a directory containing a kustomization.yaml, not a manifest file.
The file must be passed with -f.
'replace' fails when the object does not exist yet.

s3.explain: Nothing exists in the cluster until you apply the file. 'apply -f' works for creation and for later updates of the same file.
s3.hint: Create the object from the file you edited.

questions.title: Reserve a node for GPU workloads
questions.scenario: Node 'node01' is reserved for GPU workloads. Only Pods that tolerate dedicated=gpu may be scheduled there.
questions.tip: Taint = repel. Toleration = permission to ignore a taint (it does NOT attract the Pod; use nodeSelector/affinity for that).
questions.stakes: GPU nodes cost a lot per hour: without a taint, any cheap Pod squats on them.
questions.analogy: A taint is a VIP rope; a toleration is the wristband: it allows entry but does not force it.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Taint node01 with key 'dedicated', value 'gpu' and effect NoSchedule.

options.why: The format is key=value:effect - the effect follows a colon.
Labels attract (via selectors/affinity), they never repel. 'gpu:NoSchedule' is not even a valid label value.
The resource type 'nodes' is missing before the node name.

s1.explain: A taint repels every Pod that does not tolerate it, which reserves the node. Format key=value:effect. NoSchedule blocks new Pods only; NoExecute also evicts running ones; PreferNoSchedule is a soft hint.
s1.hint: A taint is key=value:effect on the node.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Make this Pod tolerate dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: let this Pod run on the tainted node

checks.msg: Add 'tolerations:' directly under 'spec:' (2 spaces of indentation).
tolerations is a LIST: each toleration starts with '- '.
The toleration needs 'key: dedicated'.
The toleration needs 'value: gpu'.
The toleration needs 'effect: NoSchedule'.

forbid.msg: 'Exists' must not have a value; with 'value: gpu' you need operator Equal (or omit the operator).
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: let this Pod run on the tainted node

options.why: operator Exists must NOT have a value (the API rejects it). Use Equal + value, or Exists without value.
nodeSelector ATTRACTS the Pod to nodes labelled dedicated=gpu; it does not tolerate the taint: the Pod stays Pending.
tolerations is a list: without '- ' this is a map and the API rejects the Pod.

s2.recap: Add a 'tolerations' list under spec with key/operator/value/effect.
s2.explain: A toleration lets the Pod be scheduled on the tainted node, it does not make it go there: to force it, add a nodeSelector or node affinity too. 'tolerations' is a sibling of 'containers' in the Pod spec.
s2.hint: The toleration repeats the taint's key, value and effect; Equal compares the value.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The reservation is over. Remove the taint from node01.

options.why: There is no --remove flag: a trailing '-' removes a taint.
There is no 'untaint' command.
That removes a LABEL called 'dedicated', not a taint.

s3.explain: The trailing dash removes the taint, for taints and labels alike. Pods already running there are not affected by removing a NoSchedule taint.
s3.hint: The same taint as before, with a trailing minus, removes it.

questions.title: Roll out a new image, then roll back
questions.scenario: In namespace 'shop', Deployment 'api' runs nginx:1.26. Update it to nginx:1.27, follow the rollout, then bring it back to the last validated release.
questions.tip: 'kubectl rollout undo' alone goes back ONE revision. To reach a specific one, read 'rollout history' and use --to-revision.
questions.stakes: A bad image reaches every user within minutes; rollback is your 30-second escape.
questions.analogy: Rollout history is the browser's back button.

context: $ kubectl get deployment api -n shop -o wide
NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE   CONTAINERS   IMAGES       SELECTOR
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Update the container of Deployment 'api' to image nginx:1.27.

options.cmd: kubectl set image deployment/api server=nginx:1.27 -n shop
aliases: kubectl set image deploy/api server=nginx:1.27 -n shop
kubectl set image deployment api server=nginx:1.27 -n shop
kubectl -n shop set image deployment/api server=nginx:1.27

options.cmd: kubectl set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.27 -n shop
options.why: The key is the CONTAINER name ('server', see the CONTAINERS column), not the Deployment name: 'unable to find container named api'.
'set image' has no --image flag: it takes container=image pairs.
'rollout restart' only re-creates the Pods with the same template; it cannot change the image.

s1.explain: 'set image' changes the Pod template, and any template change starts a rollout: a new ReplicaSet, hence a new revision. The old ReplicaSet is kept, which is what makes the rollback possible.
s1.hint: set image takes CONTAINER=IMAGE on a deployment; the container's name is not the Deployment's.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Follow the rollout until it has finished (the command must block until then).

options.why: 'rollout history' lists the revisions and returns at once; it does not follow the rollout.
There is no 'rollout watch' sub-command: the one that waits is 'rollout status'.
'rollout' is a kubectl command, not an API resource: 'get rollout' fails.

s2.explain: 'rollout status' prints 'Waiting for deployment "api" rollout to finish: 2 of 4 updated replicas are available...' and returns 'successfully rolled out' (exit code 0) when done.
s2.hint: The rollout command family has a subcommand that blocks until the rollout ends.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The team reports a regression. List the revisions of Deployment 'api'.

options.why: 'kubectl get' has no --revisions flag. ReplicaSets hold the revisions, but 'rollout history' is the command that lists them.
There is no top-level 'history' command: it is 'kubectl rollout history'.
'describe' has no such flag and only shows the current template (plus old/new ReplicaSets).

s3.explain: Each revision is an old ReplicaSet kept by the Deployment (spec.revisionHistoryLimit, default 10). CHANGE-CAUSE comes from the 'kubernetes.io/change-cause' annotation. Add --revision=N to see one revision's Pod template.
s3.hint: Revisions of a Deployment are listed by the rollout command family.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Roll 'api' back to the last validated release.

options.why: Without --to-revision, undo goes back ONE revision: to revision 3 (nginx:1.26), not to the validated revision 2.
'rollout undo' has no --revision flag (that one belongs to 'rollout history'): use --to-revision.
There is no 'rollout rollback' sub-command: it is 'rollout undo'.

s4.explain: A rollback re-uses the old ReplicaSet: the chosen revision disappears from the history and comes back as the newest one. --to-revision picks the validated release; plain 'undo' only goes back one step, which may be another bad one.
s4.hint: undo can target a specific revision number instead of just the previous one.

questions.title: Zero-downtime rolling update strategy
questions.scenario: Deployment 'checkout' (namespace 'shop', 4 replicas) must never have fewer than 4 available Pods during an update, and never more than 5 Pods in total.
questions.tip: maxSurge = extra Pods allowed above 'replicas'; maxUnavailable = Pods allowed below it. They cannot both be 0.
questions.stakes: Too high a maxUnavailable and users hit errors during every single deploy.
questions.analogy: A relay race: the next runner is already running before the last one drops the baton.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Save the live Deployment 'checkout' as YAML into checkout.yaml.

options.cmd: kubectl get deployment checkout -n shop -o yaml > checkout.yaml
aliases: kubectl get deploy checkout -n shop -o yaml > checkout.yaml
kubectl -n shop get deployment checkout -o yaml > checkout.yaml

options.cmd: kubectl describe deployment checkout -n shop > checkout.yaml
options.why: 'describe' prints a human-readable report, not a manifest that can be applied.

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment checkout -n shop --dry-run=client -o yaml > checkout.yaml
options.why: 'create deployment' requires --image and would generate a NEW default manifest, not the live object.

options.cmd: kubectl get deployment checkout -n shop --export > checkout.yaml
options.why: --export was removed from kubectl long ago, and without -o yaml you only get a table.

s1.explain: 'get -o yaml' dumps the live object, so you edit what is really running (you may delete status, uid and resourceVersion). 'kubectl edit' is the other way to change it in place.
s1.hint: Read the live object as YAML and redirect it into the file.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Allow 1 extra Pod and 0 unavailable Pods during updates: type the right block in place of the rollingUpdate block (3 lines). Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'rollingUpdate:' must stay directly under 'strategy:' (4 spaces).
'maxSurge: 1' must be a child of rollingUpdate (6 spaces).
'maxUnavailable: 0' must be a child of rollingUpdate (6 spaces).

forbid.msg: The default 25% values are still there - replace them.

options.why: Swapped: maxUnavailable 1 lets the Deployment drop to 3 available Pods, and maxSurge 0 forbids the extra Pod.
Both at 0 is rejected by the API: the rollout could never make progress (maxUnavailable may not be 0 when maxSurge is 0).
The values are at the same level as 'rollingUpdate:', so they land in 'strategy' where they are unknown fields: kubectl rejects them (strict field validation).

s2.recap: Set strategy.rollingUpdate to maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0.
s2.explain: maxUnavailable 0 means capacity never drops below 4 Ready Pods; maxSurge 1 means 5 in total at most. So kubernetes starts 1 new Pod, waits until it is Ready, then removes 1 old one, and so on. Values may be numbers or percentages.
s2.hint: Two settings of the rolling update strategy: how many extra Pods may exist, how many may be missing.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Push the change to the cluster.

options.why: 'create' fails with AlreadyExists: the Deployment is already there.
With --dry-run=client nothing is sent to the cluster.
'rollout restart' re-creates the Pods of the live Deployment; it does not read your changes from the file.

s3.explain: Changing only the strategy does not start a rollout: it applies to the NEXT change of the Pod template (image, env, ...).
s3.hint: Send the edited file back to the cluster.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - A colleague now updates the image. Watch the 'checkout' Pods (label app=checkout) live.

options.why: 'kubectl get' has no --follow flag (that is 'kubectl logs -f'); watching is -w / --watch.
That streams the logs of ONE Pod of the Deployment; it does not show Pods being replaced.
'-l checkout' means 'has a label KEY named checkout': no Pod matches. The selector is app=checkout.

s4.explain: This is the proof: you should see at most 5 Pods and never fewer than 4 Ready, because each new Pod becomes Ready before an old one is terminated. -w streams the changes.
s4.hint: List Pods by label in the namespace, and keep watching instead of printing once.

questions.title: Configure a Pod from a ConfigMap
questions.scenario: In namespace 'dev', create ConfigMap 'app-config' with APP_MODE=production and APP_PORT=8080, then expose every key as an environment variable of Pod 'web'.
questions.tip: envFrom imports ALL keys of a ConfigMap; env[].valueFrom.configMapKeyRef picks ONE key. Env vars are read at container start: a changed ConfigMap needs a Pod restart.

docs.title: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap

questions.stakes: Baked-in config means a rebuild and a redeploy for every typo.
questions.analogy: A ConfigMap is the settings file you change without reinstalling the app.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the ConfigMap 'app-config' with the two keys.

options.why: One --from-literal per key: this creates a single key APP_MODE with value 'production,APP_PORT=8080'.
--from-file=KEY=PATH reads a file: it looks for files named 'production' and '8080' and fails.
There is no --literal flag: it is --from-literal.

s1.explain: Sources: --from-literal=K=V (repeat it), --from-file=[KEY=]PATH (key = file name by default), --from-env-file=FILE (one K=V per line).
s1.hint: The configmap generator takes one literal flag per key=value pair; mind the namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Load every key of app-config as an environment variable: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'envFrom:' belongs to the container (4 spaces, like 'image:').
envFrom is a LIST: its item starts with '- configMapRef:'.
'name: app-config' must be a child of configMapRef (2 more spaces than 'configMapRef').

forbid.msg: configMapKeyRef selects ONE key and only exists under env[].valueFrom.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: configMapKeyRef only exists under env[].valueFrom (one key at a time); envFrom takes configMapRef.
'env' items need a 'name' (the variable) and a value/valueFrom; configMapRef is an envFrom field.
envFrom is a list: without '- ' it is a map and the API rejects the Pod.

s2.recap: Add envFrom: - configMapRef: name: app-config to the container.
s2.explain: envFrom loads every key of the ConfigMap as a variable, with no need to list them: a key added later appears after the next Pod restart. One key only would use env + valueFrom.configMapKeyRef.
s2.hint: One container field imports ALL keys of a ConfigMap as variables: a list of references.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Pod 'web' is Running. Check the value of APP_MODE inside the container.

options.cmd: kubectl exec web -n dev -- printenv APP_MODE
aliases: kubectl exec -n dev web -- printenv APP_MODE
kubectl -n dev exec web -- printenv APP_MODE

options.why: $APP_MODE is expanded by YOUR shell before kubectl runs: you print your local value (empty).
That shows the ConfigMap data, not what the container actually received.

options.cmd: kubectl logs web -n dev -- printenv APP_MODE
options.why: 'kubectl logs' does not run commands in the container; that is 'kubectl exec'.

s3.explain: Do not trust the manifest, ask the container: everything after '--' runs inside it. To use container variables in a shell expression: kubectl exec web -- sh -c 'echo $APP_MODE'. Environment variables are fixed when the container starts.
s3.hint: Run a command inside the container that prints one environment variable.

questions.title: Mount a Secret into a Pod
questions.scenario: In namespace 'prod', store the database credentials (username=admin, password=s3cret) in Secret 'db-cred' and mount it read-only at /etc/db in Pod 'db-client'.
questions.tip: Secret data is only base64-ENCODED, not encrypted. Encryption at rest needs an EncryptionConfiguration (kube-apiserver --encryption-provider-config); access must be limited with RBAC.
questions.stakes: A secret in an environment variable leaks into logs and crash dumps; base64 is not encryption.
questions.analogy: A Secret is a safe-deposit box; base64 is a sticker on it, not the lock.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the Secret 'db-cred' with keys username and password.

options.cmd: kubectl create secret generic db-cred --from-literal=username=admin --from-literal=password=s3cret -n prod
aliases: kubectl -n prod create secret generic db-cred --from-literal=username=admin --from-literal=password=s3cret

options.why: 'create secret' needs a type sub-command: generic, tls or docker-registry.

options.cmd: kubectl create secret generic db-cred --from-literal=username:admin --from-literal=password:s3cret -n prod
options.why: Literals are KEY=VALUE: 'username:admin' is rejected (no '=').
A ConfigMap is for non-confidential data; the task asks for a Secret.

s1.explain: A Secret keeps credentials out of the image and the Pod spec. kubectl base64-encodes the values for you; in YAML 'data' needs base64 while 'stringData' accepts plain text.
s1.hint: A generic Secret from literals, one flag per key, in the right namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The container already mounts volume 'creds' read-only at /etc/db. Declare that volume, backed by Secret db-cred: type the snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'volumes:' belongs to the Pod spec (2 spaces, like 'containers:').
The volume must be a list item named 'creds' (the name used by volumeMounts).
Use 'secret:' with 'secretName: db-cred' as its child.

forbid.msg: This is a Secret, not a ConfigMap.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: A secret volume uses 'secretName', not 'name' ('name' is the configMap volume field): the API rejects the unknown field.
The volume must be named 'creds' like in volumeMounts: the Pod is rejected (volumeMounts[0].name: Not found: "creds").
There is no ConfigMap 'db-cred': the Pod stays in ContainerCreating (FailedMount).

s2.recap: Add volumes: - name: creds / secret: / secretName: db-cred under the Pod spec.
s2.explain: Each key becomes a file: /etc/db/username and /etc/db/password. Mounted Secrets are refreshed automatically (not with subPath); env vars from Secrets are not.
s2.hint: A Pod-level volume whose source is a Secret, named exactly like the volumeMount.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - An auditor claims the password is 'encrypted' in the Secret. Show it in clear text.

options.cmd: kubectl get secret db-cred -n prod -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
aliases: kubectl get secret db-cred -n prod -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode
kubectl get secret db-cred -n prod -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d

options.cmd: kubectl get secret db-cred -n prod -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64
options.why: Without -d, base64 ENCODES the value a second time.
'describe' only shows the size of each key (password: 6 bytes), never the value.

options.cmd: kubectl get secret db-cred -n prod -o jsonpath='{.stringData.password}' | base64 -d
options.why: stringData is write-only: the API server merges it into 'data' and never returns it.

s3.explain: base64 is an encoding, not encryption: anyone allowed to 'get' Secrets can read them in clear text. Protect them with RBAC and with encryption at rest.
s3.hint: Secret data is only base64: extract the field with jsonpath and decode it.

questions.title: Autoscale a Deployment on CPU
questions.scenario: Deployment 'frontend' in namespace 'web' must scale between 2 and 8 replicas, targeting 60% average CPU utilisation.
questions.tip: CPU % is computed against the container REQUESTS: no cpu request = no CPU target. And no metrics-server = no metrics at all ('kubectl top' fails too).
questions.stakes: Without CPU requests the HPA shows <unknown> and never scales while traffic spikes.
questions.analogy: An HPA is a thermostat for replicas: it needs a thermometer (metrics) and a reference (requests).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the HorizontalPodAutoscaler for Deployment 'frontend'.

options.why: Those are the YAML field names (minReplicas/maxReplicas); the flags are --min and --max.
'kubectl scale' sets a fixed replica count (--replicas); it does not autoscale.
There is no 'kubectl create hpa' generator: the imperative command is 'kubectl autoscale'.

s1.explain: 'kubectl autoscale' creates an autoscaling/v2 HPA named after the Deployment. Recent kubectl also offers --cpu=60% (and --memory) and marks --cpu-percent as deprecated; both forms are accepted here. Custom or external metrics need a YAML manifest.
s1.hint: The imperative HPA generator takes min, max and a target CPU percentage.

context: NAME       REFERENCE             TARGETS              MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS   AGE
$ kubectl describe hpa frontend -n web | grep Warning
Warning  FailedGetResourceMetric  failed to get cpu utilization: missing request for cpu in container "frontend"
s2.prompt: Step 2 - The HPA cannot compute CPU utilisation. Give the 'frontend' containers a cpu request of 200m.

options.cmd: kubectl set resources deployment frontend --requests=cpu=200m -n web
aliases: kubectl set resources deploy frontend --requests=cpu=200m -n web
kubectl -n web set resources deployment frontend --requests=cpu=200m

options.cmd: kubectl set requests deployment frontend --cpu=200m -n web
options.why: There is no 'set requests' command: it is 'kubectl set resources ... --requests=cpu=200m'.

options.cmd: kubectl set resources hpa frontend --requests=cpu=200m -n web
options.why: Requests belong to the Pod template of the Deployment; an HPA has no containers.
'kubectl scale' only changes the replica count; it has no --requests flag.

s2.explain: Utilisation = actual usage / request, so with no request there is nothing to divide by and the HPA shows <unknown>. 120m used out of 200m requested = 60%. Changing the Pod template triggers a rollout.
s2.hint: kubectl can set resource requests on a workload's containers without editing YAML.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Still <unknown>. Check whether metrics-server is installed in the cluster.

options.why: metrics-server is a cluster add-on that lives in kube-system, not in the application namespace.
There is no such flag; 'kubectl top' simply fails when the Metrics API is missing - it does not tell you why.

options.cmd: kubectl get hpa frontend -n web -o wide
options.why: The HPA only consumes metrics: its output will not tell you whether metrics-server exists.

s3.explain: The HPA reads CPU from the metrics.k8s.io API, which metrics-server serves (check 'kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics'). Once it runs, TARGETS shows e.g. 'cpu: 12%/60%' within a minute.
s3.hint: metrics-server is usually a Deployment in kube-system: look for it by name.

questions.title: Stop sending traffic to cold Pods
questions.scenario: Pods of Deployment 'api' (namespace 'shop') receive traffic before the application has warmed up. Add a readiness probe: HTTP GET /healthz on port 8080, first check after 5 s, then every 10 s.
questions.tip: Readiness failing = Pod removed from the Service endpoints (no restart). Liveness failing = container restarted. Startup probe = protects slow starters from the liveness probe.
questions.stakes: No readiness probe: users hit a still-warming Pod and see 502s at every deploy.
questions.analogy: Readiness is the 'open' sign on the shop door; liveness checks the cashier still breathes.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Display the documentation of the httpGet field of a readiness probe, without leaving the terminal.

options.why: Probes are defined per CONTAINER: the path goes through spec.containers.
'describe' shows live objects; the schema documentation is 'kubectl explain'.
'explain' takes a dotted field path starting with the resource; there is no --resource flag.

s1.explain: 'kubectl explain' reads the API server's own schema, so it is the fastest documentation in the exam and always matches your cluster's version. Add --recursive to see every nested field at once.
s1.hint: explain follows the field path from pod.spec down to the probe's HTTP section.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Type the readiness probe in place of the TODO comment (HTTP GET /healthz:8080, initial delay 5 s, period 10 s). Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'readinessProbe:' belongs to the container (8 spaces, like 'ports:').
'httpGet:' must be a child of readinessProbe (2 more spaces).
'path: /healthz' must be a child of httpGet (2 more spaces).
'port: 8080' must be a child of httpGet (2 more spaces).
'initialDelaySeconds: 5' must be at the probe level (same indentation as httpGet).
'periodSeconds: 10' must be at the probe level (same indentation as httpGet).

forbid.msg: A liveness probe restarts the container; the task asks for readiness.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: A liveness probe RESTARTS the container when it fails; it does not keep traffic away from a Pod that is not ready yet.
tcpSocket has no 'path': it only checks that the port accepts connections (the API rejects the unknown field).
path and port are at the probe level: httpGet is empty and 'path' is an unknown probe field.

s2.recap: Add readinessProbe with httpGet (path, port) plus initialDelaySeconds and periodSeconds.
s2.explain: A readiness probe keeps the Pod out of the Service endpoints until it passes, so a cold Pod gets no traffic (a failing liveness probe would restart it instead). The timing fields sit next to the handler (httpGet), not inside it.
s2.hint: readinessProbe > httpGet (path, port), then the delay and period at the probe's level.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - After the apply, the new Pods stay 0/1 READY. Find out why (look at the probe events).

options.why: --previous shows the logs of a crashed earlier instance; a failing READINESS probe never restarts the container (RESTARTS is 0).
The Deployment shows the probe configuration but not the probe failures: those are events of the Pod.
CPU/memory usage says nothing about the probe result.

s3.explain: READY 0/1 means the probe fails, and describe shows why in the events: 'Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404' means a wrong path, a refused connection means the app is not listening yet.
s3.hint: Probe failures are events of the Pod: describe the Pod that stays not ready.

questions.title: Run a cache on SSD nodes only
questions.scenario: Pod 'cache' must only run on nodes with an SSD. Today that is node02 (label it disktype=ssd); tomorrow more SSD nodes will join, so do not pin the Pod to node02 by name.
questions.tip: nodeSelector = the simplest node constraint (exact label match). nodeName bypasses the scheduler entirely.
questions.stakes: A typo in the label and the Pod stays Pending: the cache never starts, and nothing says why.
questions.analogy: A nodeSelector is a postal address: exact match, or no delivery.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Label node02 with disktype=ssd.

options.why: Annotations are not used by selectors: nodeSelector matches LABELS.
A taint REPELS Pods from node02 - the opposite of what we want.
That labels the Pod; nodeSelector matches labels of the NODES.

s1.explain: The scheduler matches labels, so the node must carry the label first. This also scales: tomorrow's SSD nodes only need the same label and the Pod can use them, with no edit. Check with 'kubectl get nodes -l disktype=ssd'.
s1.hint: Add a key=value label to the node.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Restrict the Pod to nodes labelled disktype=ssd: type the snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: only nodes with an SSD

checks.msg: 'nodeSelector:' belongs to the Pod spec (2 spaces).
nodeSelector is a MAP: 'disktype: ssd' as its child (4 spaces), no '- '.

forbid.msg: nodeName pins the Pod to one node and bypasses the scheduler.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: only nodes with an SSD

options.why: nodeName pins the Pod to node02 by name (no scheduler at all): future SSD nodes are ignored.
nodeSelector is a map of label: value, not a list: the API rejects '- disktype: ssd'.
'disktype' is at the same level as nodeSelector: the selector is empty and 'disktype' is an unknown Pod field.

s2.recap: Add nodeSelector: disktype: ssd under the Pod spec.
s2.explain: nodeSelector restricts the Pod to nodes carrying ALL the listed labels (AND). Use the label, not the node name, so new SSD nodes qualify too. For OR / NotIn / Exists you need node affinity.
s2.hint: The simplest placement rule: a map of node labels in the Pod spec.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The Pod is created. Verify on which node it is running.

options.why: That shows the Pod's own labels, not the node it runs on.
That lists the SSD nodes, not where the Pod was placed.

options.cmd: kubectl get pod cache -o yaml | grep nodeSelector
options.why: That shows what you asked for, not where the scheduler actually put the Pod.

s3.explain: -o wide adds the NODE column, so you check where it really landed. If no node matches, the Pod stays Pending with '0/3 nodes are available: ... didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector'.
s3.hint: The wide output adds the NODE column.

questions.title: Pin analytics to two zones
questions.scenario: Pod 'analytics' (namespace 'data') must run only in zone eu-west-1a or eu-west-1b (node label topology.kubernetes.io/zone). This is a hard requirement.
questions.tip: required... = hard rule (Pending if nothing matches); preferred... = soft (weight). 'IgnoredDuringExecution': removing the label later does not evict running Pods.
questions.stakes: Pin analytics to the wrong zone and cross-zone traffic bills you every month.
questions.analogy: Affinity is a seating plan: 'required' is a rule, 'preferred' is a wish.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the nodes with their zone label shown as an extra column.

options.why: --selector (-l) FILTERS the nodes that have the label; it does not show the label's value.
--show-labels is a boolean that prints ALL labels; it does not take a key.
'describe' has no -L (label columns) flag.

s1.explain: -L KEY (--label-columns) adds one column per label key; repeat it or separate keys with commas.
s1.hint: get has a flag that adds a column per label KEY.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Type the hard node-affinity rule in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: hard rule on the zone label

checks.msg: Under nodeAffinity: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution, then its child nodeSelectorTerms.
nodeSelectorTerms is a LIST: '- matchExpressions:'.
The expression needs 'key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone' and 'operator: In'.
values must contain eu-west-1a.
values must contain eu-west-1b.

forbid.msg: 'preferred' is a soft rule; the task requires a hard one.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: hard rule on the zone label

options.why: 'preferred...' is only a soft preference, and its items need 'weight' + 'preference', not nodeSelectorTerms.
requiredDuringSchedulingRequiredDuringExecution does not exist in the API (it was only planned): unknown field.
The nodeSelectorTerms level is missing: matchExpressions is not a direct field of requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.

s2.recap: nodeAffinity > requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution > nodeSelectorTerms > matchExpressions (key, In, values).
s2.explain: 'required...' is a hard rule: the Pod stays Pending if no node matches ('preferred...' is only a wish). Several nodeSelectorTerms are ORed, expressions inside one term are ANDed, and 'In' with two zones is what expresses 'zone A or B'.
s2.hint: The hard rule is the 'required...' variant; terms contain matchExpressions; In takes a list of zones.

s4.prompt: Step 3 - You applied the manifest, but the Pod stays Pending. Show the scheduler's reason.

options.why: A Pending Pod has no container yet: kubectl logs prints nothing at all, so you never see the scheduling reason.
Without '-n data' you read the events of the current namespace: the FailedScheduling event of 'analytics' is not among them.
The node's view: its labels and capacity, but no event about a Pod that was never placed on it.

s4.explain: The FailedScheduling event counts the nodes and why each one was rejected: here '2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector'. It tells you whether to fix the rule or the nodes before you touch anything.
s4.hint: A Pending Pod's reason is an event attached to the Pod.

context: NAME           STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION   ZONE
Events:  Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available: 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s).
s3.prompt: Step 4 - The Pod is Pending. Ops confirm node02 was moved to eu-west-1b but its label was not updated. Fix the label.

options.why: The label already exists: without --overwrite kubectl refuses ('already has a value (eu-west-1c), and --overwrite is false').
Node affinity matches LABELS; an annotation is ignored by the scheduler.

options.cmd: kubectl label pods analytics topology.kubernetes.io/zone=eu-west-1b -n data
options.why: That labels the Pod; node affinity looks at the labels of the NODES.

s3.explain: The scheduler retries Pending Pods: once node02 carries the right zone, 'analytics' is scheduled there. The affinity was right; the node data was wrong, so fix the label, not the Pod.
s3.hint: The label exists with an old value: relabel the NODE and allow replacing the value.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Check that 'analytics' is now Running and on which node it landed.

options.cmd: kubectl get pod analytics -n data -o wide
aliases: kubectl -n data get pod analytics -o wide
kubectl get po analytics -n data -o wide

options.why: Shows Running but not the NODE column: you cannot tell where it landed.
Shows the zone of each node, not which node runs the Pod.
Adds the Pod's own labels, still no node.

s5.explain: -o wide adds the NODE column: node02, now labelled eu-west-1b, is the only worker that matches. The scheduler retried by itself once the label changed; nothing had to be recreated.
s5.hint: The default table hides the node; one output option adds it.

questions.title: Give payments a higher priority
questions.scenario: When the cluster is full, the Pods of Deployment 'payments' (namespace 'shop') must win over batch Pods. Create PriorityClass 'high-priority' with value 1000000 and use it for 'payments'.
questions.tip: A higher-priority Pod that cannot be scheduled may PREEMPT (evict) lower-priority Pods. preemptionPolicy: Never gives queue priority without evicting anyone.
questions.stakes: No priority and the payments Pod waits behind batch jobs while customers cannot pay.
questions.analogy: Priority is an ambulance: the other cars pull over (get preempted).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the PriorityClass 'high-priority' with value 1000000.

options.why: The flag is --value (the class's 'value' field); there is no --priority flag.
--global-default makes it the default for EVERY Pod without a class: all Pods would be equal again and batch would not lose.
There is no 'priority' resource: the object is a PriorityClass.

s1.explain: When the cluster is full, the scheduler may evict (preempt) Pods with a LOWER priority to place a higher one. PriorityClass is cluster-scoped; user values go up to 1,000,000,000, higher ones are reserved for the system classes.
s1.hint: PriorityClass is cluster-scoped; the generator takes the class name and its value.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Make the 'payments' Pods use this class: type the line in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'priorityClassName: high-priority' belongs to the Pod template spec (6 spaces, like 'containers:').

forbid.msg: Do not set 'priority' yourself: the admission controller fills it from the class.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: spec.priority is filled by the Priority admission plugin from the class name; setting it by hand without the class is rejected.
The field is priorityClassName: 'priorityClass' is an unknown field.
priorityClassName takes the NAME of the class, not its value.

s2.recap: Add priorityClassName: high-priority to the Pod template spec.
s2.explain: The class only matters once Pods name it: priorityClassName goes in the Pod template, so changing it rolls out new Pods. 'kubectl get pc' lists the classes, including the built-in system ones.
s2.hint: One Pod spec field names the class.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Show each Pod's name and the priority value it was admitted with, in namespace 'shop'.

options.why: The priority is in .spec.priority (set at admission); .status.priority does not exist (column shows <none>).
That lists the classes (cluster-scoped, -n is ignored), not the priority of each Pod.
Describes the class itself; it does not list the Pods using it.

s3.explain: payments Pods show 1000000, Pods without a class show 0 (unless a globalDefault class exists). Preempted Pods get the event 'Preempted by pod ...'.
s3.hint: custom-columns maps headers to JSON paths: the name in metadata, the admitted priority in spec.

questions.title: Wait for the database before starting
questions.scenario: Pod 'web' (namespace 'shop') must not start nginx before the Service 'db' resolves in DNS. Add an init container 'wait-db' (busybox:1.36) that loops until 'nslookup db.shop.svc.cluster.local' succeeds.
questions.tip: Init containers run one after the other, each to completion, BEFORE the app containers. With restartPolicy: Always an init container becomes a sidecar and does not block anything.
questions.stakes: The app starts before its database, crash-loops, and pages you before the DB is even up.
questions.analogy: Init containers are stagehands: the show starts only when they are done.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Type the init container in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: wait for the db Service first

checks.msg: 'initContainers:' belongs to the Pod spec (2 spaces, like 'containers:').
initContainers is a LIST: its first item is '- name: wait-db'.

checks.regex: ^    command:\s*\[\s*"sh",\s*"-c",\s*"until nslookup db\.shop\.svc\.cluster\.local; do sleep 2; done"\s*\]\s*$
checks.msg: The loop is shell syntax: run it with ["sh", "-c", "..."].

forbid.msg: restartPolicy: Always turns it into a sidecar that does not block 'web'.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: wait for the db Service first

snippet: command: ["sh", "-c", "until nslookup db.shop.svc.cluster.local; do sleep 2; done"]

options.why: Without 'initContainers:' this item is appended to 'containers': it runs IN PARALLEL with nginx and is restarted forever once it exits.
snippet: command: ["sh", "-c", "until nslookup db.shop.svc.cluster.local; do sleep 2; done"]

options.why: restartPolicy: Always makes it a native SIDECAR: 'web' starts as soon as it has started, without waiting for the loop to end.
snippet: command: ["sh", "-c", "until nslookup db.shop.svc.cluster.local; do sleep 2; done"]

options.why: Without a shell, the whole string is taken as the executable name: 'exec: "until nslookup db.shop.svc.cluster.local; ...": executable file not found'.
snippet: command: ["until nslookup db.shop.svc.cluster.local; do sleep 2; done"]

s1.recap: Add initContainers: - name: wait-db / image / command ["sh", "-c", "until ...; done"].
s1.explain: Init containers run to completion, in order, before the main containers, so nginx cannot start until the lookup succeeds. Use the full name: busybox's nslookup tries every search domain for a bare 'db' and exits 1 if one attempt fails, so the loop would never end. A failed init container is retried.
s1.hint: initContainers run before the app; this one loops until the database's DNS name resolves.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The Pod is stuck. Show the output of the init container.

options.why: Without -c you get the default container 'web', which has not started: 'is waiting to start: PodInitializing'.
'wait-db' is a container of Pod 'web', not a Pod: 'pods "wait-db" not found'.
There is no --init-container flag: init containers are selected with -c like any container.

s2.explain: While an init container runs, the Pod shows Init:0/1 and the main container has no logs: ask the init container with -c. The log would say "server can't find db.shop.svc.cluster.local: NXDOMAIN": the Service 'db' does not exist yet.
s2.hint: logs of a Pod can target one container by name, including an init container.

questions.title: Quota on a team namespace
questions.scenario: Namespace 'team-a' gets a quota: at most 10 Pods, 2 CPU and 4Gi of memory requested in total. Containers that do not declare requests must still be accepted.
questions.tip: Once a quota covers requests.cpu/memory, every new Pod MUST declare those requests - or get them from a LimitRange default. Quotas are checked at admission: existing Pods are not evicted.
questions.stakes: One team with no quota fills the cluster and everyone else's deploys go Pending.
questions.analogy: A ResourceQuota is the household budget; a LimitRange caps each purchase.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the ResourceQuota 'team-a-quota' imperatively.

options.why: Each resource is not a flag: everything goes in ONE --hard=name=value,... list.
The --hard format is name=value pairs separated by commas; ':' is rejected.
There is no 'create limitrange' generator, and a LimitRange constrains each Pod/container, not the namespace total.

s1.explain: A ResourceQuota caps the TOTALS of a namespace; a LimitRange sets min / max / defaults per container. Once a quota covers requests, the API server rejects Pods that declare none, which is the next step's problem.
s1.hint: The quota generator takes every limit in a single comma-separated --hard list of name=value.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Give containers without requests a default of cpu 100m / memory 128Mi: type the snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'defaultRequest:' belongs to the limits item (4 spaces, like 'type:').
'cpu: 100m' must be a child of defaultRequest (6 spaces).
'memory: 128Mi' must be a child of defaultRequest (6 spaces).

forbid.msg: Use defaultRequest: 'min' only validates and 'requests' is not a LimitRange field.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: 'min' only VALIDATES: a container without requests is still rejected by the quota (must specify requests.cpu).
A LimitRange has no 'requests' field: the defaults for requests are 'defaultRequest' ('default' sets default LIMITS).
cpu and memory are at the same level as defaultRequest: they are unknown fields of the limits item and defaultRequest is empty.

s2.recap: Add defaultRequest: cpu 100m / memory 128Mi to the Container item of the LimitRange.
s2.explain: With a quota on requests, a Pod without requests is rejected. The LimitRange default fixes that: the LimitRanger admission plugin injects it when the Pod is created, BEFORE the quota check. Existing Pods are not modified.
s2.hint: LimitRange defaults for REQUESTS have their own key under the limit item (not 'default', which is for limits).

s4.prompt: Step 3 - Create the LimitRange from the edited limits.yaml (its metadata already names namespace team-a).

options.why: The file says team-a, the flag says default: kubectl refuses, 'the namespace from the provided object "team-a" does not match the namespace "default"'.
replace only updates an existing object: 'limitranges "defaults" not found'.
There is no 'create limitrange' generator: kubectl rejects the extra arguments.

s4.explain: The namespace in metadata decides where the object goes; -n only has to agree with it. From now on the LimitRanger admission plugin injects defaultRequest into every container created in team-a without requests.
s4.hint: Create an object from a file; its metadata already says where it goes.

s3.prompt: Step 4 - Scaling Deployment 'web' to 12 replicas stops at 10 Pods. Show the quota's Used vs Hard values.

options.why: That is the LimitRange (per-container defaults), not the namespace consumption.
'top' shows ACTUAL usage from metrics-server; quotas count declared requests and objects.
The 'exceeded quota' errors are events of the ReplicaSet, and it shows no quota figures.

s3.explain: Used shows pods 10/10: the quota is doing its job, it is not a bug. The ReplicaSet events say 'exceeded quota: team-a-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=10, limited: pods=10'.
s3.hint: describe the quota: it shows Used next to Hard for each resource.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - The team agrees: 10 Pods is the limit. Set Deployment 'web' to 10 replicas so it stops retrying.

options.why: The Deployment owns that ReplicaSet and sets it back to 12 at once: the quota errors go on.
The ReplicaSet recreates them: same count, same 'exceeded quota' events for the two missing Pods.
Raising the quota is exactly what the team did NOT agree to: the limit stays 10.

s5.explain: Desired 12 against a hard limit of 10 leaves the ReplicaSet failing forever, with an event at each retry and a rollout that never completes. Scaling the Deployment itself (not its ReplicaSet) makes desired = allowed.
s5.hint: Change the desired count on the object that owns the ReplicaSet.

questions.title: A static Pod on node01
questions.scenario: Run Pod 'static-web' (nginx:1.26) as a static Pod on node01: it must be managed by the kubelet, not by the API server. A ready manifest was copied to node01:/tmp/static-web.yaml. You are on node01 (ssh node01; sudo -i).
questions.tip: Static Pod = a file in the kubelet's staticPodPath. Its API object is a read-only MIRROR named <pod>-<node>. Delete the file to delete the Pod.
questions.stakes: Delete a static Pod with kubectl and it comes back: the kubelet owns it, not the API.
questions.analogy: A static Pod is a plant in the kubelet's own pot; the API only sees its photo.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Find the static Pod directory configured for this kubelet.

options.why: kubelet.conf is the kubelet's KUBECONFIG (credentials to reach the API server), not its configuration.
That is a static Pod manifest itself; the path is a kubelet setting.
kubectl has no --static flag, and the directory is only known to the kubelet.

s1.explain: The kubelet only runs manifests from its own staticPodPath, so look it up instead of assuming. kubeadm sets /etc/kubernetes/manifests in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (see 'systemctl cat kubelet' for the --config flag).
s1.hint: The kubelet's config file under /var/lib/kubelet names the static Pod directory.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Turn the prepared manifest into a static Pod.

options.why: That creates a regular Pod through the API server (scheduled anywhere), not a static Pod.
/var/lib/kubelet/pods holds the kubelet's runtime data (volumes per Pod UID), it is not watched for manifests.
This is not the configured staticPodPath (see step 1): the kubelet never reads that directory.
