s2.explain: The kubelet watches that directory and starts the Pod within seconds, with no restart and no API server involved. It then creates a read-only mirror Pod so 'kubectl get pods' can see it.
s2.hint: A static Pod is just a manifest file in that directory.

context: $ kubectl get pods -o wide | grep static-web
s3.prompt: Step 3 - The test is over. Remove the static Pod for good (you are still root on node01).

options.why: That deletes only the MIRROR Pod: the kubelet still has the manifest and recreates it at once.
The API object is the mirror Pod named static-web-node01: 'pods "static-web" not found'.
After a restart the kubelet reads the manifest directory again and restarts the Pod.

s3.explain: 'kubectl delete' would only remove the mirror Pod and the kubelet would recreate it at once: the file is the source of truth. The control plane itself (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) works the same way.
s3.hint: Deleting the mirror Pod with kubectl does nothing lasting: remove the file itself.

questions.title: Nightly backup CronJob
questions.scenario: In namespace 'ops', create CronJob 'backup' (image busybox:1.36) running every day at 02:00. Keep only the last 3 successful Jobs, retry a failing Job at most 2 times, then test it right away.
questions.tip: Cron format: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Always quote the schedule in the shell. 'kubectl create job NAME --from=cronjob/CJ' = run it now.
questions.stakes: Get the schedule fields in the wrong order and the nightly backup runs every minute, or never.
questions.analogy: A CronJob is an alarm clock that spawns Jobs: minute, hour, day, month, weekday.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Generate the CronJob manifest into cj.yaml without creating it.

options.cmd: kubectl create cronjob backup --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule="0 2 * * *" --dry-run=client -o yaml > cj.yaml
aliases: kubectl create cronjob backup --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule='0 2 * * *' --dry-run=client -o yaml > cj.yaml
kubectl create cj backup --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule="0 2 * * *" --dry-run=client -o yaml > cj.yaml

options.cmd: kubectl create cronjob backup --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule=0 2 * * * --dry-run=client -o yaml > cj.yaml
options.why: Unquoted, the shell splits the schedule into separate arguments and expands '*' into file names: kubectl fails.

options.cmd: kubectl create job backup --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule="0 2 * * *" --dry-run=client -o yaml > cj.yaml
options.why: A Job runs once: 'create job' has no --schedule flag. The scheduled object is a CronJob.

options.cmd: kubectl create cronjob backup --image=busybox:1.36 --cron="0 2 * * *" --dry-run=client -o yaml > cj.yaml
options.why: There is no --cron flag: it is --schedule.

s1.explain: --dry-run=client -o yaml generates a valid CronJob you can edit. '0 2 * * *' = minute 0, hour 2, every day. Without a command after '--', busybox just runs its default command.
s1.hint: The cronjob generator needs an image and a quoted schedule; dry run on the client, YAML into the file.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Keep 3 successful Jobs and allow at most 2 retries: type the snippet in place of the TODO comment and the 2 lines below it (cleaned-up file). Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: history limit (here) and retries (in the Job spec)

checks.msg: 'successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3' belongs to the CronJob spec (2 spaces, like 'schedule:').
'backoffLimit: 2' belongs to the Job spec: jobTemplate > spec (6 spaces).

forbid.msg: backoffLimit is a Job field, not a CronJob field.
successfulJobsHistoryLimit is a CronJob field, not a Job field.
completions is the number of successful Pods required, not a retry limit.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: history limit (here) and retries (in the Job spec)

options.why: backoffLimit belongs to the Job (jobTemplate.spec): in the CronJob spec it is an unknown field.
successfulJobsHistoryLimit is a CronJob field: inside the Job spec it is unknown.
completions = how many Pods must SUCCEED for the Job to be complete; retries are capped by backoffLimit.

s2.recap: successfulJobsHistoryLimit in the CronJob spec; backoffLimit in jobTemplate.spec.
s2.explain: Three levels: CronJob spec (schedule, history limits, concurrencyPolicy) > Job spec (backoffLimit, completions) > Pod spec (containers, restartPolicy OnFailure or Never). Put each setting at its own level or the API server rejects it.
s2.hint: History limits are CronJob spec fields; retries belong to the Job template's spec.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Create the CronJob in namespace 'ops' from cj.yaml.

options.why: The manifest has no namespace: without -n ops it lands in the current namespace (usually default).
The file must be passed with -f.
--dry-run=server validates the object on the API server but persists nothing.

s3.explain: '-n ops' makes the CronJob land in the right namespace. Check it with 'kubectl get cronjob -n ops': SCHEDULE, SUSPEND, ACTIVE, LAST SCHEDULE.
s3.hint: Create it from the file in namespace ops.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Do not wait for 02:00: start a Job named 'backup-manual' from the CronJob now.

options.why: That is a brand-new Job: it ignores the CronJob's template (backoffLimit, command, ...).
'kubectl run' creates a Pod and has no --from flag.
'rollout' only supports Deployments, DaemonSets and StatefulSets.

s4.explain: 'create job --from=cronjob/NAME' starts a Job from the CronJob's template right now, without waiting for 02:00 and without changing the schedule. Follow it with 'kubectl get jobs' and 'kubectl logs job/backup-manual'.
s4.hint: create job can copy a CronJob's template with --from.

questions.title: Keep two api Pods through a drain
questions.scenario: Deployment 'api' in namespace 'shop' runs 3 replicas labelled app=api. Node maintenance starts tonight: at least 2 api Pods must stay available during voluntary disruptions such as drains.
questions.tip: A PDB only limits EVICTIONS (drain, Eviction API). 'kubectl delete pod', node crashes and drain --disable-eviction bypass it. minAvailable = replicas blocks every drain.

docs.title: Specifying a Disruption Budget for your Application

questions.stakes: Without a budget a drain may evict every api replica at once: checkout is down while the new Pods pull their image.
questions.analogy: A PDB is the rule 'two tills stay open': a manager may send one cashier on break, never the last two.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create PodDisruptionBudget 'api-pdb' in 'shop' that keeps at least 2 Pods labelled app=api available.

options.why: There is no --deployment flag (kubectl stops: unknown flag). A PDB never points at a Deployment: it selects Pods by label with --selector.
kubectl refuses: min-available and max-unavailable cannot be both specified. A PDB holds exactly one of the two.
Created in the current namespace (default): a PDB only selects Pods of its own namespace, so it protects nothing in 'shop' and the drain ignores it.

s1.explain: A PDB selects Pods by label in its own namespace and holds minAvailable OR maxUnavailable. minAvailable=2 with 3 healthy Pods leaves 1 allowed disruption. --min-available=3 would leave 0: every drain would hang on these Pods.
s1.hint: The pdb generator takes a label selector and the minimum number of Pods that must stay available.

context: $ kubectl get pods -n shop -l app=api -o wide
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP           NODE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Two api Pods run on node01. Before draining it, check how many api Pods the budget lets you evict right now.

options.why: -l filters PDBs by THEIR OWN labels, not by the Pods they select: a PDB made by 'kubectl create pdb' has no labels, so 'No resources found'.
A Deployment knows nothing about the PDBs that cover its Pods: no budget and no allowed disruptions in its output.
Without -n shop kubectl looks in the current namespace (default): NotFound, although the budget exists.

s2.explain: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS = healthy Pods - minAvailable = 3 - 2 = 1, kept up to date by the disruption controller. 0 means every eviction is refused right now (a Pod not Ready, or a budget as strict as the replica count). The status holds the same: currentHealthy, desiredHealthy, disruptionsAllowed.
s2.hint: The budget's table shows how many Pods may be evicted right now.

context: NAME      MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Drain node01 (it also runs DaemonSet Pods and a Pod with throwaway emptyDir data) while honouring the budget.

options.why: --disable-eviction makes drain DELETE the Pods instead of evicting them: the PDB is bypassed and both api Pods of node01 can go at once.

options.cmd: kubectl cordon node01 && kubectl delete pods -n shop -l app=api
options.why: 'kubectl delete' does not go through the Eviction API: the PDB is not consulted and all 3 api Pods are deleted, on every node.
drain refuses to start: it cannot delete DaemonSet-managed Pods (kube-proxy, CNI) without --ignore-daemonsets.

s3.explain: drain cordons the node, then evicts each Pod through the Eviction API, which checks the PDB. The first api Pod goes (1 allowed); the next eviction gets HTTP 429 and drain retries until the replacement is Ready elsewhere. Pods deleted directly never ask the budget.
s3.hint: drain uses evictions, which honour budgets; DaemonSet Pods and emptyDir data each need an explicit flag.

questions.title: A log agent on every node
questions.scenario: Every node, control plane included, must run one 'log-agent' Pod (image fluent/fluent-bit:3.2) in namespace 'logging'. kubectl has no generator for DaemonSets: start from a Deployment manifest.
questions.tip: No 'kubectl create daemonset': generate a Deployment with --dry-run=client -o yaml, change kind, delete replicas and strategy. Tainted control-plane nodes need a toleration.
questions.stakes: Forget the toleration and the nodes running etcd and the API server ship no logs: the outage you debug is invisible.
questions.analogy: A DaemonSet posts one guard per building; a new building gets its guard. The VIP building needs a pass: a toleration.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Generate a starting manifest ds.yaml without creating anything in the cluster.

options.cmd: kubectl create deploy log-agent --image=fluent/fluent-bit:3.2 -n logging --dry-run=client -o yaml > ds.yaml
aliases: kubectl create deployment log-agent --image=fluent/fluent-bit:3.2 -n logging --dry-run=client -o yaml > ds.yaml
kubectl -n logging create deployment log-agent --image=fluent/fluent-bit:3.2 --dry-run=client -o yaml > ds.yaml
kubectl create deployment log-agent --image=fluent/fluent-bit:3.2 --dry-run=client -o yaml -n logging > ds.yaml

options.cmd: kubectl create daemonset log-agent --image=fluent/fluent-bit:3.2 -n logging --dry-run=client -o yaml > ds.yaml
options.why: There is no 'create daemonset' subcommand: kubectl fails and ds.yaml is left EMPTY (the shell creates the file before kubectl runs).

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment log-agent --image=fluent/fluent-bit:3.2 -n logging -o yaml > ds.yaml
options.why: Without --dry-run=client the Deployment is really created: a stray log-agent Pod runs in 'logging' next to your future DaemonSet.

options.cmd: kubectl run log-agent --image=fluent/fluent-bit:3.2 -n logging --dry-run=client -o yaml > ds.yaml
options.why: 'kubectl run' generates a bare Pod: no selector and no template, so the whole spec must be rebuilt by hand.

s1.explain: A Deployment and a DaemonSet share the selector + Pod template shape, so the generated Deployment is the fastest skeleton. --dry-run=client builds the object locally and -o yaml prints it: nothing reaches the API server.
s1.hint: Start from the deployment generator: dry run on the client, YAML into the file.

context: $ sed -i 's/^kind: Deployment/kind: DaemonSet/' ds.yaml && kubectl apply -f ds.yaml

Error from server (BadRequest): error when creating "ds.yaml": DaemonSet in version "v1" cannot be handled as a DaemonSet: strict decoding error: unknown field "spec.replicas", unknown field "spec.strategy"
s2.prompt: Step 2 - kind is now DaemonSet, but apply fails. Type the right 'spec:' block over the lines from 'spec:' to 'strategy'. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: A DaemonSet has no replicas: it runs one Pod per eligible node. The API rejects the manifest: unknown field "spec.replicas".
strategy is a Deployment field (DaemonSets use updateStrategy): unknown field "spec.strategy", the manifest is rejected.
apps/v1 requires the selector, and it must match the template labels: the API answers 'spec.selector: Required value'.

checks.msg: kind must be DaemonSet.
spec must keep the selector (matchLabels app: log-agent).

forbid.msg: A DaemonSet has no replicas field.
strategy is a Deployment field (DaemonSets use updateStrategy).

s2.recap: DaemonSet spec = selector + template (+ updateStrategy): no replicas, no strategy.
s2.explain: The DaemonSet controller places one Pod per eligible node, so replicas means nothing, and its rollout field is updateStrategy (RollingUpdate or OnDelete), not strategy. Strict field validation rejects both leftovers instead of ignoring them. The selector stays and must match the template labels.
s2.hint: A DaemonSet has no replicas and no Deployment strategy; it still needs its selector.

context: $ kubectl describe node controlplane | grep Taints
s3.prompt: Step 3 - The DaemonSet must also run on the tainted control-plane node. Replace the TODO line. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: also run on control-plane nodes
target: # TODO: also run on control-plane nodes

options.why: The effect must match the taint's (or be empty): NoExecute does not tolerate a NoSchedule taint, so the control plane gets no Pod and DESIRED stays at the worker count.
kubeadm stopped applying the node-role.kubernetes.io/master taint in v1.25: this toleration matches nothing and the control plane gets no agent.
A nodeSelector ATTRACTS, it does not tolerate: the taint still repels the Pod, and the workers are now excluded too, so DESIRED drops to 0.

checks.msg: In the Pod template: tolerations with key node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, operator Exists, effect NoSchedule.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.
A nodeSelector does not tolerate a taint.

s3.recap: tolerations: key node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, operator Exists, effect NoSchedule (Pod template).
s3.explain: A taint repels every Pod that does not tolerate it, DaemonSet Pods included: the controller only adds tolerations for node conditions (not-ready, unschedulable...), not for the control-plane role. Exists matches whatever the value (empty here); key and effect must match.
s3.hint: Tolerate the control-plane taint by key only (any value) for the NoSchedule effect.

context: NAME        DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR   AGE
s4.prompt: Step 4 - DESIRED is 3 for a 3-node cluster. Show the node each log-agent Pod runs on.

options.cmd: kubectl get pods -n logging -l app=log-agent -o wide
aliases: kubectl get pods -l app=log-agent -n logging -o wide
kubectl -n logging get pods -l app=log-agent -o wide
kubectl get po -n logging -l app=log-agent -o wide

options.why: -o wide adds the CONTAINERS, IMAGES and SELECTOR columns to the DaemonSet: still counts, no node names.
app=log-agent is a POD label: no node carries it, so 'No resources found'.
describe has no --show-nodes flag (unknown flag). Its output gives Pod counts and events, not one line per node.

s4.explain: DESIRED counts the nodes the DaemonSet must cover after taints and nodeSelector: 3 proves the toleration works. The NODE column of 'get pods -o wide' then shows exactly one Pod per node, control plane included. A node joining later gets its Pod automatically.
s4.hint: List the Pods by label in their namespace, with the node column.

questions.title: Scale on memory, shrink slowly
questions.scenario: Deployment 'worker' (namespace 'jobs', memory request 256Mi) needs an HPA: 2 to 10 replicas at 70% average memory utilisation. Scale-down: wait 10 minutes of calm, then remove at most 1 Pod every 2 minutes.
questions.tip: behavior sits under spec (scaleUp / scaleDown): stabilizationWindowSeconds + policies (type Pods or Percent, value, periodSeconds). Lost? 'kubectl explain hpa.spec.behavior --recursive'.
questions.stakes: With the default scale-down, warm workers vanish minutes after a burst; the next burst waits on cold Pods and the queue explodes.
questions.analogy: A shop closing tills: wait for 10 quiet minutes, then close one till every 2 minutes, never all at once.

s0.prompt: Step 1 - An HPA on memory needs live metrics. Check that the cluster serves them for the Pods of namespace 'jobs'.

options.why: kubectl top only knows nodes and pods: 'deployment' is rejected.
Shows the memory REQUEST (256Mi), not the current usage: it proves nothing about metrics.
Lists the Pods and their nodes: no CPU or memory figures at all.

s0.explain: kubectl top reads the Metrics API that metrics-server serves, the same one the HPA controller uses. If it fails here ('Metrics API not available'), the HPA would show <unknown> targets and never scale.
s0.hint: The HPA reads the same API as kubectl's resource usage command.

s1.prompt: Step 2 - You do not remember the fields for a slow scale-down. Show their documentation from the cluster itself.

options.why: behavior sits under spec: kubectl answers that the field "behavior" does not exist.
autoscaling/v1 only knows a CPU target: it has no behavior field, so kubectl reports that it does not exist.
describe shows live objects, not schemas: it takes a resource type and a name, so this errors out.

s1.explain: kubectl explain reads the OpenAPI schema served by YOUR cluster, so it matches v1.37 exactly and needs no browser. It lists stabilizationWindowSeconds, selectPolicy and policies (type, value, periodSeconds); --recursive prints the whole tree at once.
s1.hint: explain reads the schema from the cluster: follow hpa > spec > behavior > the shrinking side.

s2.prompt: Step 3 - Type the memory metric (70% average utilisation) over the first TODO. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: targetAverageUtilization was the autoscaling/v2beta1 field, gone with that API: in v2 it is an unknown field and the HPA is rejected.
type and averageUtilization belong under 'target:': here they are unknown fields of resource and the HPA is rejected.
averageUtilization is an integer: "70%" is a string, so the manifest cannot be decoded. The % sign only belongs to kubectl flags.

checks.regex:
^  metrics:\s*
  - type: Resource\s*
    resource:\s*
      name: memory\s*
      target:\s*
        type: Utilization\s*
        averageUtilization: 70\s*$
checks.msg: metrics: - type: Resource, resource: name: memory, target: type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70.

forbid.msg: The metric TODO is still there - type the snippet in its place.
targetAverageUtilization is the old v2beta1 field.

s2.recap: metrics: Resource memory, target type Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 (a % of the request).
s2.explain: In autoscaling/v2 each metric has a type (Resource, Pods, Object, External, ContainerResource) and a target. Utilization is a percentage of the Pods' memory REQUEST (256Mi here, so about 180Mi on average); AverageValue would take an absolute quantity such as 200Mi.
s2.hint: An autoscaling/v2 metric: type Resource, the resource name, and a target with type and percentage.

s3.prompt: Step 4 - Now the scale-down rules: 600 s of calm, then at most 1 Pod every 120 s. Replace the TODO. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: scaleUp rules slow down GROWTH (1 Pod per 2 minutes under load) while scale-down keeps its default: a 300 s window, then up to 100% of the extra Pods every 15 s.
stabilizationWindowSeconds is an integer number of seconds: '10m' is a string and the manifest is rejected.
The window is a field of scaleDown, not of a policy: unknown field in policies[0], the HPA is rejected.

checks.regex:
^  behavior:\s*
    scaleDown:\s*
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600\s*
      policies:\s*
      - type: Pods\s*
        value: 1\s*
        periodSeconds: 120\s*$
checks.msg: behavior: scaleDown: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600, then policies: - type: Pods, value: 1, periodSeconds: 120.

forbid.msg: The TODO is still there - type the snippet in its place.
scaleUp limits growth; the task is about scale-down.

s3.recap: behavior.scaleDown: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600 + policy type Pods, value 1, periodSeconds 120.
s3.explain: During the 600 s window the HPA keeps the HIGHEST recommendation it saw, so a short dip shrinks nothing. Then the Pods policy removes at most 1 Pod per 120 s. With several policies, selectPolicy (Max by default) picks the one allowing the biggest change.
s3.hint: Under behavior, the shrinking side: a stabilization window in seconds, and a policy of type Pods.

context: NAME     REFERENCE           TARGETS           MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS   AGE
s4.prompt: Step 5 - Check what the HPA stored and decided: its metric, scale-down behavior, conditions and events.

aliases: kubectl get hpa worker -n jobs -o yaml

options.why: kubectl top only knows nodes and pods: it rejects 'hpa' as a resource.

options.cmd: kubectl get hpa worker -n jobs -o wide
options.why: The HPA table stays the same (TARGETS, MINPODS, MAXPODS, REPLICAS): no behavior, no conditions, no events.
The Deployment does not know it is autoscaled: you would see replica changes, not the target or the scale-down rules.

s4.explain: describe shows the metric as current / target, the stored behavior (scale-down window and policies, defaults filled in for scaleUp), the conditions AbleToScale, ScalingActive and ScalingLimited with their reasons, and an event for each rescale.
s4.hint: describe shows the metric, behavior, conditions and events of the HPA.

questions.title: A PVC stuck in Pending
questions.scenario: PVC 'data-pvc' is Pending. PV 'data-pv' exists: capacity 10Gi, accessModes ReadWriteOnce, storageClassName 'manual'. The PVC manifest is pvc.yaml.
questions.tip: To bind, a PV must match the PVC's storageClassName, offer at least the requested size and include the requested access mode.
questions.stakes: A Pending claim keeps the database Pod Pending, and the on-call phone rings.
questions.analogy: A PVC is a rental request and a PV is the flat: nobody moves in until size, mode and class match.

context: NAME       STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show why the claim is not binding (conditions and events).

options.why: A PVC is not a workload: it has no logs.
It only repeats the table columns - no events, no reasons.
The volume is fine; the explanation (events) is on the unbound claim.

s1.explain: 'Pending' tells you nothing: the Events section of 'describe' is where the provisioner or scheduler says what is wrong. First reflex for any Pending object.
s1.hint: A Pending claim explains itself in its conditions and events.

context: no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set
s2.prompt: Step 2 - The claim asks for more than the PV offers (size AND access mode). Type the right snippet over the wrong lines of pvc.yaml.

checks.msg: The PV only offers ReadWriteOnce: the claim must request exactly that.
The size goes in resources.requests.storage.
The PV has 10Gi: request 10Gi or less.

forbid.msg: ReadWriteMany is not offered by the PV.

options.why: The size fits now, but the PV does not offer ReadWriteMany: still no match.
A PVC must state its size in resources.requests.storage; 'limits' alone is rejected.

s2.recap: Set accessModes to ReadWriteOnce and the request to at most 10Gi.
s2.explain: A claim binds only to a PV with the same storageClassName, a capacity >= the request, and access modes that include the requested ones. Here the size and the access mode were both wrong, so the claim never matched 'data-pv'.
s2.hint: Match the PV: its access mode and its size, both under the claim's spec.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Apply the fix. (A PVC's spec cannot be changed in place for these fields.)

options.cmd: kubectl delete pvc data-pvc && kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml

options.why: The API rejects changes to accessModes/size of an existing claim in this state: delete and recreate.
Same immutability problem as apply.

options.cmd: kubectl delete pv data-pv && kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml
options.why: You would delete the volume instead of fixing the claim.

s3.explain: A claim's spec is immutable once created, so you replace it. A Pending claim holds no data, so deleting it loses nothing.
s3.hint: Those fields are immutable on an existing claim: remove it, then create it again from the file.

questions.title: A StorageClass that waits for the Pod
questions.scenario: Create a StorageClass 'local-wait' for pre-created local volumes: no dynamic provisioner, binding delayed until a Pod uses the claim, and volumes kept (not deleted) when released. The manifest is sc.yaml.
questions.tip: A StorageClass has no 'spec': provisioner, reclaimPolicy, volumeBindingMode, parameters and allowVolumeExpansion sit at the top level of the object.
questions.stakes: A claim Pending under WaitForFirstConsumer looks like a hang, and 'fixing' it wastes exam minutes.
questions.analogy: A tailor measures you before cutting: the volume is made once the Pod's place is known.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment: no provisioner, WaitForFirstConsumer, Retain. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: provisioner, binding mode and reclaim policy

checks.msg: 'provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner' must be at the top level (no indentation).
'volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer' must be at the top level.
'reclaimPolicy: Retain' must be at the top level.

forbid.msg: A StorageClass has no 'spec' section.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: provisioner, binding mode and reclaim policy

options.why: StorageClass has no 'spec': these fields live at the top level. The API rejects the manifest (and 'provisioner' is required).
Immediate binds the claim as soon as it is created, before the scheduler knows which node the Pod goes to. The task wants delayed binding.
A StorageClass only accepts Delete or Retain. Recycle is a deprecated PV-only policy.

s1.recap: Top-level provisioner kubernetes.io/no-provisioner, volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer, reclaimPolicy Retain.
s1.explain: no-provisioner = static volumes only: you create the PVs yourself. WaitForFirstConsumer waits for the Pod so the scheduler picks the node first, essential for local volumes tied to one node. Retain keeps the data when the claim goes.
s1.hint: Static local volumes have a special 'no provisioner' name; binding waits for a consumer; data is kept.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Create the StorageClass from sc.yaml.

options.why: There is no 'kubectl create storageclass' generator: StorageClasses are always created from YAML.
A client dry-run only prints what would happen: nothing is created.
'get -f' only reads the objects named in the file: NotFound, nothing is created.

s2.explain: 'apply' creates it. Get it right first: provisioner, reclaimPolicy, volumeBindingMode and parameters cannot be changed afterwards (allowVolumeExpansion can). No imperative generator exists, so keep a skeleton from the docs.
s2.hint: Create the object from the file.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - List the StorageClasses to check the new one and its binding mode.

options.why: This lists PersistentVolumes. No PV exists yet: the class is only a template.
This lists installed CSI drivers, not StorageClasses.
'local-wait' is a StorageClass, not a claim.

s3.explain: 'get sc' shows PROVISIONER, RECLAIMPOLICY, VOLUMEBINDINGMODE and ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION at a glance, so you verify all three settings you just asked for. StorageClasses are cluster-scoped.
s3.hint: The class table shows each binding mode and the default marker.

questions.title: Switch the default StorageClass
questions.scenario: Claims without a storageClassName must now be provisioned by the class 'gp3' instead of the current default.
questions.tip: The default class is marked by the ANNOTATION storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class="true". Remove the old default before setting the new one, so there is only one.
questions.stakes: Two defaults, or none, and claims without a class behave nothing like you expect.
questions.analogy: The default class is the house wine: what you get when you order nothing.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Find the current default StorageClass.

options.why: is-default-class is an annotation, not a label: the selector matches nothing.
There is no --default flag: kubectl rejects it. The plain list already marks the default.
This lists claims, not classes; it does not say which class is the default.

s1.explain: You must know the current default before changing it, and there should be only one. 'get sc' prints '(default)' next to it; 'describe sc' shows 'IsDefaultClass: Yes'.
s1.hint: The default class is marked '(default)' in the class table.

context: NAME            PROVISIONER       RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE      ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - With kubectl patch, set the default-class annotation of gp2 to "false".

options.why: This adds a LABEL; the default flag is read from the annotation, which stays "true".
A StorageClass has no spec: kubectl only warns 'unknown field "spec"' and patches nothing, so gp2 stays the default. The default flag is an annotation in metadata.
The annotation already has a value: without --overwrite kubectl refuses to change it.

s2.explain: Remove the old default first: with two defaults the NEWEST class silently wins, which is rarely what you meant. The default is just an annotation, and annotation values are strings, so write "false" in quotes. Any value other than "true" removes it.
s2.hint: The default marker is an annotation under metadata; a merge patch can set it to the string "false".

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Make gp3 the default class with kubectl patch.

options.why: Wrong annotation key: it must be exactly storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class. This one is ignored.
A label is not read by the admission plugin: gp3 does not become the default.
annotations live under metadata: at the top level kubectl only warns 'unknown field' and nothing changes, so gp3 is still not the default.

s3.explain: The DefaultStorageClass admission plugin gives the default class to new claims that omit storageClassName, and since v1.28 also to existing claims still without one: switching the default can change where old Pending claims land.
s3.hint: Same annotation on the other class, set to the string "true".

questions.title: A hostPath PersistentVolume
questions.scenario: Create PV 'pv-log': 2Gi, access mode ReadWriteOnce, storageClassName 'manual', backed by the node directory /mnt/data/log. The manifest is pv.yaml.
questions.tip: PV = capacity.storage; PVC = resources.requests.storage. Copy the PV skeleton from the docs (Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume).
questions.stakes: hostPath ties data to one node: the Pod moves and the data seems gone.
questions.analogy: hostPath is a note stuck on one desk: change desk and the note is not there.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Type the PV spec in place of the TODO comment (2Gi, ReadWriteOnce, class manual, hostPath /mnt/data/log). Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: capacity, access mode, class and host directory

checks.msg: A PV declares its size in spec.capacity.storage: 2Gi.
accessModes is a LIST: '- ReadWriteOnce' on the next line.
Add 'storageClassName: manual' under spec.
hostPath is an object: 'hostPath:' then 'path: /mnt/data/log' indented 2 more spaces.

forbid.msg: resources.requests is PVC syntax; a PV uses capacity.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: capacity, access mode, class and host directory

options.why: resources.requests is how a PVC asks for space. A PV offers space with 'capacity': the API rejects this PV (capacity is required).
accessModes is a list of strings: a plain scalar is rejected by the API.
hostPath is an object with a 'path' field, not a string: the API rejects it.

s1.recap: spec: capacity.storage 2Gi, accessModes [ReadWriteOnce], storageClassName manual, hostPath.path /mnt/data/log.
s1.explain: The four building blocks of a static PV: capacity, accessModes, storageClassName and a volume source. 'manual' is only a label a claim must repeat to bind here. hostPath ties the data to one node: fine for labs, never for multi-node production.
s1.hint: A PV spec: capacity with storage, the access-mode list, the class name and a hostPath source with its path.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Create the PV from pv.yaml.

options.why: There is no 'kubectl create pv' generator: PVs are created from a manifest.
A server dry-run validates the object but does not persist it: no PV is created.
'replace' fails when the object does not exist yet.

s2.explain: PVs are cluster-scoped: no namespace is needed (or used).
s2.hint: Create the object from the file.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Check that pv-log exists and is Available.

options.why: This lists claims in all namespaces; pv-log is a PersistentVolume: use 'get pv'.
There is no --show-status flag: kubectl rejects it. STATUS is a default column.
No class 'manual' needs to exist for static binding, and a class says nothing about this PV's status.

s3.explain: Available means free to be claimed. Other phases: Bound (claimed), Released (claim deleted, policy Retain), Failed. A static PV can name a class that has no StorageClass object.
s3.hint: PVs are cluster-scoped: get it by name and read STATUS.

questions.title: Mount a claim into nginx
questions.scenario: In namespace 'shop', PVC 'web-data' already exists. Pod 'web' (nginx:1.27) must serve its content from that claim, mounted at /usr/share/nginx/html. The manifest is pod.yaml.
questions.tip: Two halves, linked by name: spec.volumes[].name (pod level) and containers[].volumeMounts[].name (container level). The claim is referenced by persistentVolumeClaim.claimName.

docs.title: Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume for Storage

questions.stakes: Point the Pod at the volume instead of the claim and nothing mounts.
questions.analogy: A Pod shows the claim ticket (PVC), never the keys of the flat (PV).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Check that the claim web-data is Bound before using it.

options.why: No '-n shop': kubectl looks in the current namespace (usually 'default') and finds nothing.
web-data is a claim (pvc). PVs are cluster-scoped and have their own names.
Claims are not linked to Pods by labels: this selector matches nothing.

s1.explain: A Pod using a Pending claim stays Pending too (unless the class is WaitForFirstConsumer, where the Pod itself triggers the binding), so check the claim first.
s1.hint: Check the claim's STATUS in its namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Type the right snippet in place of the two TODO lines: mount volume 'html' at /usr/share/nginx/html, backed by PVC web-data. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: volume 'html' backed by PVC web-data

checks.msg: The container needs volumeMounts: '- name: html' with 'mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html'.
'volumes:' belongs to the Pod spec (2 spaces), next to 'containers:'.
The volume: '- name: html', then 'persistentVolumeClaim:' with 'claimName: web-data'.

forbid.msg: A TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in place of both lines.

target: # TODO: volume 'html' backed by PVC web-data

options.why: The volume is named web-data but the mount refers to 'html': the API rejects the Pod (volumeMounts name not found).
With 4 spaces 'volumes' becomes a field of the container, which does not exist: the Pod is rejected.
The field is claimName, not name: the claim reference is missing and the Pod is rejected.

s2.recap: containers[].volumeMounts (name html, mountPath) + spec.volumes (name html, persistentVolumeClaim.claimName web-data).
s2.explain: A Pod never names the PV: it only knows the claim, and the claim finds the volume. The Pod and the claim must be in the same namespace. The mount name ('html') links volumeMounts to volumes.
s2.hint: Two halves: the container mounts a named volume at a path; the Pod declares that name backed by the claim.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Verify from inside the container that /usr/share/nginx/html is a mounted volume (df).

options.why: No '-n shop': the Pod is searched in the current namespace and not found.
The claim is mounted at /usr/share/nginx/html, not /data: df reports another filesystem (or the path does not exist).

options.cmd: kubectl get pod web -n shop -o wide
options.why: It shows node and IP, not the mounts inside the container.

s3.explain: df on the mount path shows the backing filesystem. 'kubectl describe pod' also lists Volumes and Mounts, and 'describe pvc' shows 'Used By'.
s3.hint: Run df inside the container on that path: a separate filesystem means a mounted volume.

questions.title: Keep the data when the claim goes
questions.scenario: PV 'pv-db' (bound to claim prod/db-data) uses reclaim policy Delete. The database is being decommissioned, but its data must survive the deletion of the claim.
questions.tip: Reclaim policy lives on the PV (spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy) and can be changed at any time; the StorageClass reclaimPolicy only sets it for NEW dynamic PVs.

docs.title: Change the Reclaim Policy of a PersistentVolume

questions.stakes: With policy Delete, removing the claim erases the data: a customer's data, forever.
questions.analogy: Retain keeps the box; Delete shreds it.

context: NAME    CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM          STORAGECLASS   AGE
pv-db   5Gi        RWO            Delete           Bound    prod/db-data   fast           12d
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Switch pv-db to the Retain reclaim policy with kubectl patch.

options.why: 'reclaimPolicy' is the StorageClass field. On a PV it is spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: kubectl only warns 'unknown field' and the policy stays Delete.
The policy is a property of the PV, not of the claim.
reclaimPolicy of a StorageClass is immutable, and it would only apply to future PVs anyway.

s1.explain: With Delete, removing the claim also deletes the volume and its data. Retain keeps them. The policy is mutable on an existing PV, even while it is Bound, so switch it BEFORE you delete the claim.
s1.hint: The reclaim policy is a PV spec field; a merge patch with the new value changes it.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Print only the reclaim policy of pv-db to confirm the change.

options.why: No such field on a PV: the output is empty.
A claim has no reclaim policy: the output is empty.
The policy is in spec, not status: the output is empty.

s2.explain: Never assume a patch worked: read the field back. The RECLAIM POLICY column of 'get pv' shows it too. It must say Retain before you touch the claim.
s2.hint: jsonpath prints a single field of the PV's spec.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The database Pod is gone. Delete the claim db-data (the data must stay on the volume).

options.why: While the claim exists, the pv-protection finalizer keeps the PV in Terminating; and the task is to remove the claim, not the volume.
No '-n prod': the claim is not found in the current namespace.
This deletes every claim of the namespace, not only db-data.

s3.explain: With Retain, deleting the claim moves the PV to Released: the data stays, but the PV keeps spec.claimRef to the old claim, so no new claim can bind it until an admin cleans it up.
s3.hint: Delete the claim in its namespace: with Retain, the PV and its data survive (Released).

questions.title: Give a Released volume a new claim
questions.scenario: PV 'pv-archive' (Retain, class 'manual', 5Gi) is Released since its old claim was deleted. A new claim 'archive-v2' in namespace 'archive' must reuse it and its data. The claim manifest is pvc.yaml.
questions.tip: Released != Available: the PV still points at the deleted claim through spec.claimRef. Removing claimRef makes it Available again (the data is untouched).

docs.title: Change the Reclaim Policy of a PersistentVolume

questions.stakes: A Released volume keeps the old claimRef, so new claims never bind and the admin stares at it.
questions.analogy: The previous tenant's name is still on the door: clear it to rent the flat again.

context: NAME         CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS     CLAIM                 STORAGECLASS   AGE
pv-archive   5Gi        RWO            Retain           Released   archive/old-archive   manual         90d
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Remove spec.claimRef from pv-archive with a JSON patch so that it becomes Available.

options.why: status is a subresource: a patch on the PV itself ignores it, and the controller would compute Released again anyway.
In a merge patch, an empty object changes nothing: claimRef stays. Use null (merge) or op remove (json).
You would lose the PV object; the goal is to reuse it as it is.

s1.explain: A Released PV keeps spec.claimRef to the old claim, so no new claim can bind it, however well it matches. Removing it makes the PV Available again, with its data. A JSON patch is a LIST of operations.
s1.hint: A JSON patch is a list of operations: remove the claimRef path from the PV's spec.

context: NAME         CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS      CLAIM   STORAGECLASS   AGE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Pin the new claim to pv-archive: type the right line in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Add 'volumeName: pv-archive' directly under spec (2 spaces).

forbid.msg: This field does not exist on a PVC: the claim names its PV with spec.volumeName.
The TODO comment is still there - type the line in its place.

options.why: claimRef is the PV-side pointer to a claim. A PVC has no such field: the API rejects it.
There is no persistentVolumeName field: the PVC field is spec.volumeName.
With 6 spaces the line lands under resources.requests as a resource named volumeName: the API rejects it.

s2.recap: spec.volumeName: pv-archive pins the claim to that PV.
s2.explain: volumeName pre-binds the claim to one PV (class, size and access modes must still match). Without it, any other Available PV that matches could be chosen and your data would stay unclaimed.
s2.hint: One claim spec field pre-binds it to a named PV.

s4.prompt: Step 3 - Create the claim from pvc.yaml (its metadata names namespace 'archive').

options.why: The file says archive, the flag says default: kubectl refuses with a namespace mismatch error.
replace only updates an existing object: 'persistentvolumeclaims "archive-v2" not found'.
A client dry run only prints what would be sent: nothing is created, pv-archive stays Available.

s4.explain: Creating the claim starts the binding: the PV controller sees volumeName and binds archive-v2 to pv-archive only, provided class, size and access modes match.
s4.hint: Create the object from the file you just edited.

s3.prompt: Step 4 - Check that the new claim is Bound to pv-archive.

options.why: No '-n archive': the claim is not found in the current namespace.
archive-v2 is the claim; the PV is called pv-archive.
--watch-only prints only future changes: the current Bound state is not shown and the command hangs.

s3.explain: Bound with VOLUME pv-archive proves the old data now belongs to the new claim. If it stays Pending, compare class, size and access modes with the PV.
s3.hint: Check the claim's STATUS and VOLUME in its namespace.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Pod 'reader' (namespace 'archive') mounts archive-v2 at /archive. List the files to prove the old data is there.

options.why: Without '-n archive' kubectl looks for 'reader' in the current namespace: NotFound.
Shows what the container printed, not the content of the volume.
Shows that /archive is mounted from archive-v2, not a single file of what is inside.

s5.explain: Bound proves the binding, the files prove the data: with Retain the disk was never wiped, so the archives written through the old claim are exactly where they were.
s5.hint: Run a command inside the Pod that mounts the claim; mind the namespace.

questions.title: A dynamic claim that waits
questions.scenario: In namespace 'apps', PVC 'cache' (storageClassName 'csi-hostpath') was created 10 minutes ago and is still Pending. No PV was created. The class uses volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer.
questions.tip: WaitForFirstConsumer: a Pending PVC with the event 'waiting for first consumer' is NORMAL. The PV is provisioned when a Pod using the claim is scheduled.
questions.stakes: A claim waiting for its Pod is not broken: 'fixing' it burns your time.
questions.analogy: Like a made-to-order pizza: the oven starts only when someone orders.

context: NAME    STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the events of the claim to see why it is Pending.

options.why: No PV exists yet: with dynamic provisioning the PV is created later, under a generated name (pvc-<uid>).
No '-n apps': the claim is not found in the current namespace.
A claim has no logs; its story is in the events.

s1.explain: The Events say 'waiting for first consumer': binding is delayed on purpose, it is not an error. Reading them first stops you from 'fixing' something that works.
s1.hint: A Pending claim explains itself in its events.

context: Normal  WaitForFirstConsumer  12s (x42 over 10m)  persistentvolume-controller  waiting for first consumer to be created before binding
s2.prompt: Step 2 - This is expected. Trigger provisioning: cache-pod.yaml defines a Pod that mounts the claim 'cache'.

options.why: volumeBindingMode is immutable on a StorageClass: the API rejects the patch.

options.cmd: kubectl delete pvc cache -n apps && kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml
options.why: The new claim would wait exactly the same way: nothing consumes it.
A dry-run creates no Pod, so there is still no consumer.

s2.explain: Once the scheduler picks a node for the Pod, it annotates the claim with that node, and the CSI provisioner creates a volume reachable from there. That is why a claim waits for a Pod: the volume's location depends on where the Pod runs.
s2.hint: WaitForFirstConsumer provisions when a Pod using the claim is scheduled: create that Pod.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - List the PersistentVolumes to see the volume the provisioner just created.

options.why: Provisioned PVs carry no such label: the selector matches nothing.
This shows the class (the template), not the volumes created from it.
VolumeAttachments describe attach operations to nodes, not the PV list.

s3.explain: A dynamically provisioned PV is named pvc-<claim uid>, takes the reclaim policy of its class (Delete by default) and shows CLAIM apps/cache.
s3.hint: PVs are cluster-scoped: list them all and look for the new one bound to the claim.

questions.title: Grow a claim from 2Gi to 5Gi
questions.scenario: PVC 'reports' in namespace 'finance' (class 'standard', CSI driver with expansion support) is full. Grow it from 2Gi to 5Gi. Its manifest was exported to pvc.yaml.
questions.tip: Only spec.resources.requests.storage of a bound claim can be raised, and only if the class has allowVolumeExpansion: true. Shrinking is never allowed.
questions.stakes: The disk is full at 3 a.m.: a claim can grow but never shrink, and the class must allow it.
questions.analogy: A balloon: you can inflate it (allowVolumeExpansion), never deflate it.

context: NAME       PROVISIONER             RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE   ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Allow volume expansion on the class 'standard' with kubectl patch.

options.why: A StorageClass has no spec: allowVolumeExpansion is a top-level field.
allowVolumeExpansion is a StorageClass field, not a claim field.
An annotation is just metadata: the field stays false and resizes are refused.

s1.explain: Without allowVolumeExpansion the API server rejects any request to enlarge a claim. It is one of the few StorageClass fields you can change later (unlike provisioner, reclaimPolicy, volumeBindingMode, parameters).
s1.hint: Expansion is allowed by a top-level StorageClass field (classes have no spec); a merge patch sets it.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Raise the request to 5Gi: type the right snippet over the 'requests' lines. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Set resources.requests.storage to 5Gi (storage indented under requests).

forbid.msg: Only resources.requests.storage can be changed on a bound claim.
The old 2Gi request is still there.

options.why: On a bound claim only requests.storage may change; replacing requests by limits is rejected (and requests are needed).
'storage' at the level of 'requests' becomes an unknown field of resources and requests is empty: rejected.
capacity is the PV (and status) field; the claim asks through resources.requests.

s2.recap: resources.requests.storage: 5Gi, then 'kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml'.
s2.explain: Only the request changes, and only upwards: you can grow a claim, never shrink it. The same in one line: kubectl patch pvc reports -n finance -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"5Gi"}}}}'.
s2.hint: Only the request under resources may change on a bound claim, and only upwards.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Follow the resize: show the claim's Conditions and Events.

aliases: kubectl get pvc reports -n finance -o yaml

options.why: rollout only works for Deployments, DaemonSets and StatefulSets.
reports is the claim; its PV has a generated name (pvc-6f1c...).

options.cmd: kubectl get pvc reports -n finance -o wide
options.why: The table has no Conditions; CAPACITY keeps showing 2Gi until the resize is finished.

s3.explain: Conditions such as Resizing then FileSystemResizePending show the progress: the volume grows first, then the kubelet grows the filesystem on the node. status.capacity shows 5Gi when done.
s3.hint: describe the claim: Conditions and Events show the resize steps.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - The Resizing condition is gone. Check that the claim's capacity now shows 5Gi.

options.why: reports is the CLAIM; its PV has a generated name (pvc-...): NotFound.
That is what you ASKED for (5Gi since your edit), not what was provisioned: it proves nothing.
The class shows ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION, not the size of any claim.

s4.explain: CAPACITY comes from status.capacity, which only changes once the volume really grew, unlike spec, which changed the moment you applied. 5Gi in CAPACITY means the resize is complete.
s4.hint: Compare what was granted (status) with what was requested (spec).

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Pod 'reporter' mounts the claim at /reports. Check the size of the filesystem inside the container.

options.why: du adds up the files you stored, not the size of the filesystem: it cannot show the new 5Gi.
Shows CPU and memory usage, never disk sizes.
Without '-n finance' the Pod is looked up in the current namespace: NotFound.

s5.explain: The claim grows first, then the kubelet grows the filesystem on the node (online for CSI drivers that support it). df inside the container is what the application sees: about 5G total means the space is really usable.
s5.hint: What the application sees is the mounted filesystem's size, seen from inside the container.

questions.title: Share a scratch volume between containers
questions.scenario: Pod 'logger' has two containers: 'app' writes /var/log/app/out.log, 'shipper' must read the same file under /logs. Use an emptyDir volume named 'logs'. The manifest is pod.yaml.
questions.tip: emptyDir lives as long as the Pod: it survives container restarts but is deleted with the Pod. Each container may mount it at a different path.
questions.stakes: emptyDir dies with the Pod: the only copy of your data is gone after a restart.
questions.analogy: A shared whiteboard in a meeting room: everyone in the room sees it, and it is wiped when the meeting ends.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Type the right snippet in place of the two TODO lines: mount 'logs' at /logs in 'shipper' and declare it as an emptyDir. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do date >> /var/log/app/out.log; sleep 5; done"]
# TODO: mount the shared volume at /logs

checks.msg: shipper needs volumeMounts: '- name: logs' with 'mountPath: /logs'.
Declare under spec: 'volumes:', '- name: logs', 'emptyDir: {}'.

forbid.msg: The task asks for an emptyDir, not a hostPath.
A TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in place of both lines.

target: # TODO: mount the shared volume at /logs

options.why: hostPath shares a node directory that outlives the Pod and depends on the node: the task asks for an emptyDir.
Mounts refer to volumes by NAME: 'shipper-logs' does not exist, so the Pod is rejected.
With 4 spaces 'volumes' becomes a (non-existent) container field: the Pod is rejected.

s1.recap: shipper mounts 'logs' at /logs; spec.volumes declares 'logs' as emptyDir: {}.
s1.explain: One volume, two mounts: the same directory appears at /var/log/app in 'app' and at /logs in 'shipper', which is how containers of one Pod share files. The volume name links each mount to the volumes list.
s1.hint: Mount the shared volume in the second container, and declare it once at Pod level as a scratch volume.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Read /logs/out.log from inside the 'shipper' container.

options.why: Without -c kubectl uses the first container, 'app', which mounts the volume at /var/log/app: /logs does not exist there.
In 'app' the volume is at /var/log/app, not /logs.
In 'shipper' the volume is mounted at /logs; /var/log/app does not exist there.

s2.explain: In a multi-container Pod, always pick the container with -c (exec, logs, cp), otherwise kubectl chooses the default one, which may not see the file you expect.
s2.hint: exec into one named container of the Pod and print the file.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Prove the emptyDir lifetime: delete the Pod and recreate it from pod.yaml (out.log will start empty).

options.cmd: kubectl delete pod logger && kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
aliases: kubectl delete pod logger && kubectl create -f pod.yaml

options.why: rollout restart works on Deployments, DaemonSets and StatefulSets, not on a bare Pod.
Without --force the same Pod object is updated in place: nothing is recreated and the emptyDir keeps its content.
There is no 'kubectl restart' command.

s3.explain: emptyDir is created when the Pod is assigned to a node and deleted with the Pod; a container crash or restart keeps it. Use a PVC for data that must outlive the Pod.
s3.hint: An emptyDir lives as long as the Pod: delete the Pod, then create it again from the file.

questions.title: One disk per replica, kept on delete
questions.scenario: StatefulSet 'db' (namespace 'data', 3 replicas, image redis:7.4) must give EACH replica its own 1Gi ReadWriteOnce volume at /data, from the default StorageClass. The data must survive a deletion of the StatefulSet.
questions.tip: Claims are named <template>-<statefulset>-<ordinal> (data-db-0). By default they outlive the StatefulSet; persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy (whenDeleted / whenScaled) changes that.
questions.stakes: Set whenDeleted: Delete and one 'kubectl delete sts' wipes every replica's claim, and with it the data.
questions.analogy: Named lockers: seat db-1 always gets locker data-db-1, even after the classroom is torn down and rebuilt.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Give each replica its own claim 'data' (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce): replace the TODO line. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: Each template is a whole PersistentVolumeClaim: its name goes under metadata. 'name' at item level is an unknown field and the StatefulSet is rejected.
The container mounts a volume named 'data': with a template named db-data that mount matches no volume (volumeMounts[0].name: Not found) and no replica starts.
volumes is a Pod field: at StatefulSet level it is unknown. Even in the template, all 3 replicas would share ONE claim 'data' instead of one each.

checks.msg: volumeClaimTemplates: - metadata: name: data, then spec: (the claim spec).
The claim spec needs accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"].
The claim asks resources.requests.storage: 1Gi.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.
volumes is a Pod field: one claim per replica needs volumeClaimTemplates.

s1.recap: volumeClaimTemplates: - metadata: {name: data}, spec: RWO, requests.storage 1Gi (name = the volumeMount's).
s1.explain: The controller creates one claim per replica from the template and gives each Pod ITS claim by ordinal. A plain volumes/persistentVolumeClaim entry would make all replicas share one RWO claim. Without storageClassName the default class is used.
s1.hint: A StatefulSet field holds a list of PVC templates; each has metadata.name and a claim spec.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Replica db-1 reports a full disk. Show ITS claim, and only that one.

options.why: Wrong order: claims are named <template>-<statefulset>-<ordinal>, so NotFound.
The StatefulSet name is part of the claim name (two StatefulSets may both use a template 'data'): NotFound.
'data' is only the template: no claim has that name, every replica gets its own suffixed copy. NotFound.

s2.explain: Claim name = template + StatefulSet + ordinal: data-db-1 belongs to Pod db-1 for good. Because the name is stable, a rescheduled or recreated db-1 finds the same claim, and the same data, by name.
s2.hint: Claim names are template-statefulset-ordinal.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - New policy: keep the claims if the StatefulSet is deleted, but delete the claim of a replica removed by a scale-down. Patch it.

options.why: That deletes ALL claims when the StatefulSet is deleted (and the data too with a Delete reclaim policy): the opposite of the requirement.
persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy is a PV field: on a claim kubectl only warns 'unknown field' and nothing changes. Claim retention is decided by the StatefulSet.
Only Retain and Delete exist: the API rejects 'Remove' (Unsupported value).

s3.explain: With whenScaled: Delete the controller makes a condemned Pod the owner of its claim, so the garbage collector removes data-db-2 after db-2 is gone on a scale-down. whenDeleted keeps its default Retain. The policy is one of the few StatefulSet fields you may update.
s3.hint: The StatefulSet's claim retention policy has two sides; patch only the scale-down side to Delete.

s5.prompt: Step 4 - Scale 'db' down to 2 replicas: the claim of the removed replica must go, the others stay.

options.why: The StatefulSet still wants 3 replicas: db-2 comes back at once, with its claim.
Without '-n data' kubectl looks for 'db' in the current namespace: NotFound.
replicas is an integer: "2" is a string and the API rejects the patch.

s5.explain: A StatefulSet removes the highest ordinal first: db-2 goes. With whenScaled: Delete, data-db-2 is garbage collected after the Pod, while data-db-0 and data-db-1 stay bound to their replicas.
s5.hint: Change the replica count of the StatefulSet itself, in its namespace.

context: $ kubectl delete sts db -n data && kubectl apply -f sts.yaml
NAME        STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   AGE
s4.prompt: Step 5 - The StatefulSet was deleted and re-applied. Prove that the new Pod db-0 mounts the OLD claim data-db-0.

aliases: kubectl get pod db-0 -n data -o yaml

options.why: The StatefulSet shows the claim TEMPLATE ('Volume Claims: Name: data'), not which claim a given Pod mounts.
PVs are cluster-scoped (-n is ignored): CLAIM shows data/data-db-0 because that binding never changed. It says nothing about the new Pod.

options.cmd: kubectl get pvc data-db-0 -n data -o wide
options.why: The claim table has no column for the Pods using it: 'Used By' only appears in 'kubectl describe pvc'.

s4.explain: The recreated Pod has the same name, so the controller looks for claim data-db-0, finds it (Retain kept it) and reuses it instead of provisioning a new volume: Volumes shows ClaimName: data-db-0, and the claims' AGE proves they were never re-created.
s4.hint: The Pod's Volumes section shows the ClaimName it mounts.

questions.topic: Access modes (RWO, RWOP, ROX) and read-only mounts
questions.title: One writer, read-only readers
questions.scenario: In namespace 'ledger', two Pods on the same node both write to claim 'ledger-data' (ReadWriteOnce, CSI class 'csi-standard') and corrupt it. Only ONE Pod in the cluster may ever write the ledger. Pod 'report' must read claim 'archive' without being able to change it.
questions.tip: RWO = one NODE (its Pods share the volume). RWOP = one Pod cluster-wide (CSI only). Access modes never make a mount read-only: readOnly: true does.
questions.stakes: Two writers on one RWO volume look fine for weeks, until both flush at once and the ledger is corrupted for good.
questions.analogy: RWO locks the house, not the room: everyone inside may write. RWOP hands the only key to one person.

context: NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP            NODE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Confirm which Pods currently use the claim 'ledger-data'.

options.cmd: kubectl get pvc ledger-data -n ledger -o wide
options.why: -o wide adds volume details (VOLUMEMODE...), never a Pod column: the claim table does not say who mounts it.
ledger-data is the CLAIM; its PV has a generated name (pvc-<uid>), so NotFound. A PV does not list Pods either.
Pods support only a few field selectors (spec.nodeName, status.phase...): the API rejects this field label as not supported.

s1.explain: describe pvc shows 'Used By:' with every Pod mounting the claim: both writers. ReadWriteOnce only limits the NODE that mounts the volume read-write; all Pods on that node may use it, so the claim allowed exactly what happened.
s1.hint: describe on a claim lists the Pods using it ('Used By').

s2.prompt: Step 2 - A claim's access modes cannot change: you write a new claim 'ledger-data-v2'. Make it usable by a single Pod in the whole cluster. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: ReadWriteOncePod cannot be combined with other access modes: the API rejects the claim.
RWOP is only the abbreviation kubectl prints: the API takes full names and rejects it (Unsupported value).
ReadOnlyMany lets MANY nodes mount the volume: it limits nothing to one Pod, and the writer is not meant to get a read-only volume.

checks.msg: accessModes must hold ReadWriteOncePod, and nothing else.

forbid.msg: ReadWriteOnce still allows every Pod of the node.
RWOP is an abbreviation: write ReadWriteOncePod.

s2.recap: accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod] alone, on a NEW claim (access modes are immutable).
s2.explain: ReadWriteOncePod (GA since v1.29, CSI volumes only) lets a single Pod in the whole cluster use the volume, and the scheduler enforces it: a second Pod using the claim is not scheduled. ReadWriteOnce would again let every Pod on the same node write.
s2.hint: One access mode restricts a volume to a single Pod in the whole cluster, not just one node.

context: $ kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml -f writers.yaml   # both writers now use ledger-data-v2
s3.prompt: Step 3 - ledger-writer-2 stays Pending, as intended. Show the scheduler's reason.

options.why: A Pending Pod has no started container: logs returns an error, not the reason. The scheduler's verdict is an event of the Pod.
The Pod was never placed on a node: node01's description knows nothing about it.

options.cmd: kubectl get pod ledger-writer-2 -n ledger -o wide
options.why: The table only says Pending with NODE <none>: it shows that it waits, not why.

s3.explain: The FailedScheduling event names the ReadWriteOncePod conflict: a Pod already uses the claim, so the scheduler refuses a second user on ANY node, not only node01. ledger-writer-2 can only be scheduled once ledger-writer is gone.
s3.hint: A Pending Pod's scheduling reason is an event: describe the Pod.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Claim 'archive' is ReadOnlyMany, yet 'report' could write to it. Make its mount read-only. Ctrl+D to submit.

options.why: ':ro' is Docker syntax: here it is part of the path, and the volume is mounted read-write at a directory literally named '/archive:ro'.
Field names are case-sensitive: 'readonly' is an unknown field and the Pod is rejected (strict field validation).
Access modes belong to claims and PVs, not to mounts: unknown field, the Pod is rejected.

checks.msg: The volumeMount needs readOnly: true (camelCase), under mountPath: /archive.

forbid.msg: The field is readOnly (camelCase).
':ro' is not Kubernetes syntax.
A volumeMount has no accessModes.

s4.recap: volumeMounts: readOnly: true (an access mode alone never makes a mount read-only).
s4.explain: Access modes are matching rules between claims and volumes; the docs warn they do not enforce write protection once mounted. readOnly: true on the volumeMount makes the kubelet mount it read-only for this container (persistentVolumeClaim.readOnly does it for the whole volume).
s4.hint: The access mode does not stop writes: the container's volumeMount has a flag for that.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Prove that 'report' really cannot write to /archive.

aliases: kubectl exec report -n ledger -- sh -c 'echo x > /archive/probe'

options.why: ls shows permission bits, not mount options: a read-only mount still lists rw- files. Only a write attempt proves it.
It shows Access Modes: ROX, which the docs say does not enforce write protection: no proof at all.

options.cmd: kubectl get pod report -n ledger -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes}'
options.why: volumes only names the claim: readOnly sits on the container's volumeMounts, so no flag is shown, and a setting is not a proof anyway.

s5.explain: The write must fail with 'Read-only file system' and a non-zero exit code: the kernel refuses it whatever the file permissions or the claim's access mode. If the file gets created, the mount is still read-write.
s5.hint: Try to create a file there from inside the container: a read-only mount must refuse it.

questions.title: Allow API -> DB on port 5432
questions.scenario: Namespace 'prod' has a default-deny ingress policy. Pods labelled app=db must accept TCP 5432 only from Pods labelled app=api (same namespace).
questions.tip: Within one 'from' list, separate items are OR-ed; selectors inside ONE item are AND-ed. An empty rule '- {}' allows everything!
questions.stakes: A database open to every Pod: one compromised front-end reads all customer data.
questions.analogy: A NetworkPolicy is a bouncer with a guest list: once a list exists, everyone not on it stays out.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Add the ingress rule: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Add 'ingress:' directly under 'spec:' (2 spaces).
Allow traffic 'from' a podSelector with matchLabels app: api.
Restrict the rule with 'ports:' -> 'port: 5432'.

forbid.msg: An empty ingress rule allows (or denies) the wrong traffic - it must name the source and the port.
'- ports:' starts a SECOND rule: 'ports' must belong to the same rule as 'from' (no dash).
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: '- ports' starts a second rule. Rules are OR-ed: api may reach ANY port, and EVERYONE may reach 5432.
namespaceSelector selects NAMESPACES labelled app=api, not the api Pods.

s1.recap: Add ingress: from podSelector app=api + ports TCP 5432.
s1.explain: The namespace already denies all ingress, so this rule opens exactly one door. Two selectors: spec.podSelector = who is PROTECTED (db); from.podSelector = who is ALLOWED (api). Anything not listed, such as other Pods or other ports, stays blocked.
s1.hint: An ingress rule: a 'from' list (Pods selected by label) and a 'ports' list (protocol and port), as siblings.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The policy is applied. Show the rules it enforces.

options.cmd: kubectl get netpol allow-api-to-db -n prod -o wide
options.why: 'wide' only shows name, pod-selector and age - not the rules.
A NetworkPolicy has no logs.
'explain' documents the API schema; it does not read live objects.

s2.explain: Verify what the policy really enforces: 'describe' prints the allowed sources and ports in plain language, so you catch a wrong selector or port before an application does. 'netpol' is the short name of networkpolicies.
s2.hint: describe on a NetworkPolicy prints its rules in plain words; mind the namespace.

questions.title: Expose a Deployment outside the cluster
questions.scenario: Deployment 'web' (label app=web) listens on container port 8080. Expose it as Service 'web-svc' on port 80, reachable from outside through every node.
questions.tip: port = Service port, targetPort = container port. A Service without endpoints means the selector matches no Ready Pod.

docs.title: Using a Service to Expose Your App

questions.stakes: A Service with no endpoints looks healthy and answers nothing.
questions.analogy: A Service is a forwarding number; endpoints are the phones actually plugged in.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the Service imperatively.

options.why: port and target-port are swapped: the container listens on 8080.
The default type is ClusterIP: internal only.
Needs a cloud load balancer (stays <pending> on kubeadm clusters). The task asks for NodePort.

s1.explain: NodePort opens a port on every node, which is what 'reachable from outside through every node' asks for. 'expose' copies the Deployment's selector, so you never write it by hand; --port is the Service port, --target-port the container's.
s1.hint: expose builds a Service from the Deployment's selector: name, port, target port and type.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Check that the Service actually targets Ready Pods (list its endpoints).

options.why: That flag does not exist.
'web-svc' is a Service, not a Pod.
EndpointSlices have a random suffix (web-svc-xxxxx), so the exact name is not found; use -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-svc.

s2.explain: A Service with no endpoints answers nothing, even though it looks healthy. <none> means a wrong selector, a wrong namespace or Pods that are not Ready.
s2.hint: The Ready Pod IPs behind a Service are listed by its endpoints object, same name.

questions.title: Expose a Pod inside the cluster
questions.scenario: Pod 'nginx' (label run=nginx) runs in namespace 'web' and listens on port 80. Expose it inside the cluster as Service 'nginx-svc' on port 8080, then test it.
questions.tip: kubectl expose copies the Pod's labels into the Service selector. 'kubectl create service' does NOT: it uses app=<service-name>.
questions.stakes: The wrong Service type and your test client cannot reach it from where it stands.
questions.analogy: ClusterIP is the office intercom: it works inside the building only.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the ClusterIP Service 'nginx-svc' (port 8080 -> container port 80).

options.cmd: kubectl create service clusterip nginx-svc --tcp=8080:80 -n web
options.why: create service sets the selector app=nginx-svc, which matches no Pod: the Service has no endpoints.
No '-n web': kubectl looks for Pod 'nginx' in the current namespace and fails with NotFound.
port and target-port are swapped: nothing listens on 8080 inside the container.

s1.explain: No --type means ClusterIP: a stable virtual IP reachable only from inside the cluster, which is exactly what the task asks for. --port is what clients use (8080), --target-port is the container's port (80).
s1.hint: expose works on a single Pod too (it needs labels); Service port first, container port as target.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - From a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod in 'web', fetch the page through the Service (short name).

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n web -- wget -qO- nginx-svc:8080

options.why: The short name 'nginx-svc' only resolves from Pods in the same namespace; this Pod lands in 'default'.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n web -- ping -c 3 nginx-svc
options.why: A ClusterIP is virtual (iptables/IPVS rules): it does not answer ICMP. Test the TCP port instead.

options.cmd: kubectl exec nginx-svc -n web -- wget -qO- localhost:8080
options.why: You cannot exec into a Service; and localhost inside the Pod would bypass the Service anyway.

s2.explain: Test like a real client: from a Pod inside the cluster, through the Service name and the Service port (8080). kube-proxy translates it to the Pod's targetPort (80). A test from your laptop would prove nothing for a ClusterIP.
s2.hint: A throw-away busybox Pod in the same namespace fetches the short name on the Service port.

questions.title: Pin a NodePort to 30080
questions.scenario: Deployment 'shop' (label app=shop) in namespace 'shop' listens on port 80. Expose it as NodePort Service 'shop-np' on port 80, and the node port MUST be 30080.
questions.tip: kubectl expose has no --node-port flag: generate YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml and add spec.ports[].nodePort. Default range: 30000-32767.
questions.stakes: A NodePort outside the allowed range is rejected: an exam point lost for nothing.
questions.analogy: NodePort is a side door numbered by the building (30000-32767) that opens on every node.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Generate the Service manifest into np.yaml without creating it.

options.cmd: kubectl expose deploy shop -n shop --name=shop-np --type=NodePort --port=80 --dry-run=client -o yaml > np.yaml

options.why: kubectl expose has no --node-port flag (only 'kubectl create service nodeport' has one).

options.cmd: kubectl create service nodeport shop-np -n shop --tcp=80:80 --node-port=30080
options.why: create service sets the selector app=shop-np, which matches no Pod of Deployment 'shop'.
--port is the Service (ClusterIP) port, not the node port; and the Service is created at once with a random node port.

s1.explain: --dry-run=client -o yaml = a correct skeleton with the right selector, ready to edit.
s1.hint: expose with a client-side dry run, printed as YAML and redirected into the file.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Pin the node port: type the right snippet over the line '    targetPort: 80'. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: nodePort: 30080 belongs to the port entry (4 spaces, next to targetPort).
Keep 'targetPort: 80': the container listens on 80.

forbid.msg: nodePort is a field of a port entry (spec.ports[]), not of spec.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: At 2 spaces nodePort lands directly under spec: unknown field, the port stays random.
38080 is outside the default node port range 30000-32767: the API server rejects it.
hostPort is a container field (Pod spec), not a Service port field.

s2.recap: Add 'nodePort: 30080' to the port entry, next to targetPort.
s2.explain: port = Service port, targetPort = container port, nodePort = the port opened on every node. Without nodePort Kubernetes picks a random one in 30000-32767, but the task demands 30080.
s2.hint: Keep the target port line and add the fixed node port under it, in the same port item.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Before applying, check whether this kubeadm cluster overrides the node port range (flag on the API server).

options.why: Node ports are allocated by the API server when the Service is created; the controller manager has no such flag.
The kubelet never allocates Service ports.

options.cmd: kubectl get cm kube-proxy -n kube-system -o yaml | grep nodePortRange
options.why: kube-proxy only programs the rules for ports already allocated; the range is an API server flag.

s3.explain: No match = default 30000-32767. A nodePort outside the range is rejected: 'provided port is not in the valid range'.
s3.hint: The node port range is an API server flag in its static Pod manifest: search for it.

questions.title: Stable DNS names for StatefulSet Pods
questions.scenario: StatefulSet 'db' (label app=db, 3 replicas) in namespace 'data' needs a headless Service so each Pod gets its own DNS name. Check the name it expects, create it, then resolve Pod db-0.
questions.tip: Pod DNS in a StatefulSet: <pod>.<serviceName>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local - it only exists if spec.serviceName names a headless Service (clusterIP: None).
questions.stakes: A database that needs 'db-0' by name breaks behind a normal ClusterIP.
questions.analogy: Headless is a phone book with every direct line, not a switchboard.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Print the governing Service name the StatefulSet expects (spec.serviceName).

options.cmd: kubectl get sts db -n data -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceName}'
aliases: kubectl get sts db -n data -o jsonpath="{.spec.serviceName}"
kubectl get statefulset db -n data -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceName}'

options.cmd: kubectl get sts db -n data -o jsonpath='{.metadata.serviceName}'
options.why: serviceName is part of the spec, not of metadata: the output is empty.
Lists existing Services with that label; the Service you need may not exist yet.

options.cmd: kubectl get sts db -n data -o wide
options.why: The wide columns show containers and images, not spec.serviceName.

s1.explain: The StatefulSet gives its Pods DNS names under a governing Service, but does not create it: you must, with exactly the name in spec.serviceName, or the per-Pod names never resolve.
s1.hint: jsonpath prints one field of the StatefulSet's spec: the governing Service's name.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - It prints 'db-hl'. Make svc.yaml headless: type the right line in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: A headless Service has 'clusterIP: None' directly under spec.

forbid.msg: There is no 'Headless' or 'None' Service type: keep the default type (ClusterIP).
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: 'Headless' is not a Service type (valid: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName).
An empty clusterIP means 'allocate one for me': you get a normal ClusterIP Service.
'None' is a value for clusterIP, not a Service type: the API rejects it.

s2.recap: Add 'clusterIP: None' under spec.
s2.explain: clusterIP: None makes the Service headless: no virtual IP, so DNS returns the Pod IPs directly and each StatefulSet Pod gets its own A record. A normal ClusterIP would hide the Pods behind one address.
s2.hint: A headless Service has no virtual IP: one field of its spec says so.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - From a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod, resolve the FQDN of Pod db-0.

options.why: The middle label is the Service name (serviceName 'db-hl'), not the StatefulSet name.
Pod records live under the Service: <pod>.<service>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local.
The Pod is called db-0 (StatefulSet name + ordinal); and the Service part is missing.

s3.explain: <pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local points to ONE Pod and stays the same after restarts even when the IP changes. That is why a database can ask for 'db-0' by name.
s3.hint: Pod DNS names: pod.service.namespace.svc.cluster.local, through the headless Service.

questions.title: Resolve a Service across namespaces
questions.scenario: Service 'api' (port 8080) lives in namespace 'backend'. Pod 'web' in namespace 'ui' cannot reach 'http://api:8080'. Investigate DNS.
questions.tip: Service FQDN: <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local. A bare name only resolves in the client Pod's own namespace (resolv.conf search list).
questions.stakes: The short name resolves in your namespace only: across namespaces you hit the wrong Service or none.
questions.analogy: Like a first name: fine in your family, across towns you need the full address.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - From a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod in 'ui', resolve the Service by its FQDN.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n ui -- nslookup api.backend.svc.cluster.local
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n ui -- nslookup api
options.why: That is exactly what fails: 'api' expands to api.ui.svc.cluster.local, which does not exist.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n ui -- nslookup api.backend.cluster.local
