options.why: The 'svc' label is missing: Service records live under <ns>.svc.cluster.local.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n ui -- nslookup backend.api.svc.cluster.local
options.why: Wrong order: the Service name comes first, then the namespace.

s1.explain: The FQDN (service.namespace.svc.cluster.local) works from any namespace: it names the exact Service. 'api.backend' also works thanks to the search list.
s1.hint: From a throw-away Pod in 'ui', resolve service.namespace.svc.cluster.local.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Show the DNS config of Pod 'web' to understand why the bare name failed.

options.why: No '-n ui': kubectl looks for 'web' in the current namespace.
Application logs, not the Pod's resolver configuration.

options.cmd: kubectl describe pod web -n ui | grep nameserver
options.why: describe shows the Pod's spec and events, not the resolv.conf generated by the kubelet: no match.

s2.explain: A bare name is tried through the search list: 'api' becomes api.ui.svc.cluster.local first, which does not exist, so the lookup fails. That is why a name that works inside 'backend' fails from 'ui': add the namespace ('api.backend').
s2.hint: A Pod's DNS settings are in a file under /etc: print it from inside the container.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - resolv.conf says 'nameserver 10.96.0.10'. Show the Service behind that IP.

options.why: The Deployment is 'coredns', but the Service keeps the historic name 'kube-dns'.
No '-n kube-system': there is no kube-dns Service in 'default'.
10.96.0.10 is a Service ClusterIP, not a Pod; CoreDNS Pods are named coredns-<hash>.

s3.explain: The kubelet writes the kube-dns Service's ClusterIP (its clusterDNS setting) into every Pod's resolv.conf. If DNS fails everywhere, check this Service and its endpoints next.
s3.hint: The cluster DNS Service in kube-system keeps a historical name.

questions.title: Pod-to-pod across namespaces
questions.scenario: Pod 'client' (namespace 'team-a', busybox image) must reach Pod 'server' (namespace 'team-b', nginx on port 80) directly - there is no Service.
questions.tip: Every Pod gets a routable IP; any Pod can reach any Pod IP, across nodes and namespaces, without NAT - unless a NetworkPolicy says otherwise.
questions.stakes: Assume namespaces isolate the network and you over-trust them: by default they do not.
questions.analogy: Namespaces are labelled rooms with no walls.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the IP address of Pod 'server'.

options.cmd: kubectl get pod server -n team-b -o wide
aliases: kubectl get po server -n team-b -o wide

options.why: No '-n team-b': the Pod is not in the current namespace.
Endpoints exist only for Services, and there is no Service here.

options.cmd: kubectl get pod server -n team-b -o jsonpath='{.status.hostIP}'
options.why: hostIP is the IP of the node running the Pod; the Pod's own IP is status.podIP.

s1.explain: Pods talk to each other by IP, so you need the target's address. -o wide adds IP and NODE columns.
s1.hint: The wide Pod listing adds the IP column; mind the server's namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - From Pod 'client', fetch the nginx page using the Pod IP.

options.cmd: kubectl exec server -n team-b -- wget -qO- -T 3 localhost:80
options.why: Tests nginx from inside its own Pod: no packet crosses the Pod network.
Pod 'client' lives in team-a: -n selects where the exec'd Pod is, not the target.

options.cmd: kubectl exec client -n team-a -- wget -qO- -T 3 server.team-b:80
options.why: Pods have no DNS name of their own like this: <name>.<ns> resolves only for Services.

s2.explain: The network is flat: a Pod IP is reachable from any namespace and any node, because namespaces do not isolate traffic by themselves. If it fails, something filters it.
s2.hint: exec in the client Pod and fetch the server's Pod IP directly, with a short timeout.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - wget times out. Namespace 'team-a' has no policies at all. Look for what could block the traffic on the server side.

options.why: The statement says team-a has none; ingress to 'server' is governed by policies in ITS namespace, team-b.
No Service is involved in Pod-IP traffic: kube-proxy rules play no role here.
kube-proxy only handles Service IPs; direct Pod-to-Pod traffic never goes through it.

s3.explain: Nothing blocks on the client side (no policy in team-a), so look at the server side: a policy that selects 'server' with policyTypes Ingress drops everything it does not explicitly allow, silently.
s3.hint: Ingress policies are enforced where the TRAFFIC ARRIVES: list the policies of the server's namespace.

questions.title: Default-deny ingress for a namespace
questions.scenario: Namespace 'secure' must block all incoming traffic to every Pod by default. Pods there include 'web' behind Service 'web' (port 80).
questions.tip: podSelector: {} selects ALL Pods of the namespace. policyTypes [Ingress] with no ingress rules = deny all ingress.
questions.stakes: Without a default deny, every new Pod is open to the whole cluster.
questions.analogy: Lock the front door first, then hand out keys.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: select every Pod and deny all ingress

checks.msg: Select every Pod with 'podSelector: {}' directly under spec.
Declare 'policyTypes:' with '- Ingress'.

forbid.msg: Any ingress rule allows something; default deny has NO ingress rules.
Egress is not asked: denying it would also break DNS lookups from these Pods.
Label selectors have no wildcards.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: select every Pod and deny all ingress

options.why: '- {}' is one empty rule = allow from everywhere: the exact opposite.
This denies outgoing traffic; incoming traffic stays open.
Selectors have no wildcards ('*' is not even a valid label value): use podSelector: {}.

s1.explain: podSelector: {} selects every Pod of the namespace, and policyTypes: [Ingress] with no ingress rules allows nothing in. Policies are additive allow-lists: once a Pod is selected for Ingress, only explicitly allowed traffic gets in.
s1.hint: An empty Pod selector selects every Pod; declare the Ingress type with no rules.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Prove that ingress is blocked: from a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod in 'secure', call the Service with a 3 s timeout.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n secure -- wget -qO- -T 3 web
kubectl exec web -n secure -- wget -qO- -T 3 localhost
options.why: Traffic from a Pod to itself on localhost never crosses the Pod network: policies do not apply, it succeeds.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n secure -- nslookup web
options.why: DNS is egress to CoreDNS in kube-system: an ingress deny in 'secure' does not affect it, it proves nothing.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i get pods -n secure
options.why: That tests RBAC (API permissions), not network traffic.

s2.explain: A timeout is the proof: the policy drops packets silently, so you see 'download timed out', not 'connection refused'. A test from inside 'secure' also shows that namespace members are blocked too.
s2.hint: From a throw-away Pod inside 'secure', call the Service with a short timeout: it should fail.

questions.title: Let the monitoring namespace in
questions.scenario: Namespace 'prod' has a default-deny ingress policy. Pods labelled app=web (Service 'web', port 80) must accept TCP 80 from every Pod of namespace 'monitoring' - and nothing else.
questions.tip: Every namespace automatically carries kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<name>: the safest label to select a namespace by name.
questions.stakes: Monitoring cannot scrape and the dashboard goes dark in the middle of an incident.
questions.analogy: Admit by 'which building' (namespaceSelector), not 'which person' (podSelector).

s0.prompt: Step 1 - Before adding a rule, list the policies that already apply in namespace 'prod'.

options.why: Without '-n prod' you list the current namespace: the default-deny of prod is not shown.
Shows the Pods and their labels, not the policies selecting them.
The Service is not filtered by policies: policies act on the Pods behind it.

s0.explain: NetworkPolicies add up: a new allow rule only opens what the existing default-deny closes, it cannot loosen another allow. Listing them first shows what you are building on (here: default-deny-ingress, podSelector {}).
s0.hint: Policies are namespaced objects; mind which namespace you list.

s1.prompt: Step 2 - Show the labels of namespace 'monitoring'.

options.why: These are Pod labels; namespaceSelector matches labels of the Namespace object.
For namespaces -o wide adds nothing: name, status and age only.
'-l monitoring' filters namespaces having a label KEY 'monitoring': it does not show labels.

s1.explain: namespaceSelector matches namespace LABELS, so you must know them before writing the rule. Since v1.21 every namespace carries kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<its name>, a safe label to match.
s1.hint: Namespaces carry labels too; show them for monitoring.

s2.prompt: Step 3 - Type the right source in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: allow every Pod of namespace monitoring

checks.msg: Use a namespaceSelector (item of 'from', 4 spaces + dash) matching kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring.

forbid.msg: A separate '- podSelector' item is OR-ed: it allows Pods of 'prod' too.
The namespace has no 'name' label - only kubernetes.io/metadata.name.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: allow every Pod of namespace monitoring

options.why: podSelector alone selects Pods of the policy's OWN namespace (prod) carrying that label: none.
The namespace has no 'name' label (see --show-labels): the selector matches nothing.
Two items of 'from' are OR-ed: '- podSelector: {}' also lets in every Pod of prod.

s2.recap: from: namespaceSelector kubernetes.io/metadata.name=monitoring.
s2.explain: namespaceSelector alone allows ALL Pods of the matching namespaces. To restrict to some Pods there, put a podSelector in the SAME item (no dash): with a dash they become two separate sources and the rule widens.
s2.hint: Select the source namespace by the label Kubernetes sets on every namespace automatically: its name.

s3.prompt: Step 4 - Prove it: from a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod in 'monitoring', call Service 'web' of 'prod' (3 s timeout).

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n monitoring -- wget -qO- -T 3 web.prod
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n monitoring -- wget -qO- -T 3 web
options.why: From 'monitoring' the bare name means web.monitoring.svc...: DNS fails, it tests nothing.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n prod -- wget -qO- -T 3 web
options.why: A Pod in 'prod' is still denied (time-out): that tests the default deny, not the new allow.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n monitoring -- ping -c 3 web.prod
options.why: Service IPs do not answer ICMP, and the policy only allows TCP 80 anyway.

s3.explain: Prove the rule from the allowed side: web.prod expands to web.prod.svc.cluster.local through the search list. The same call from another namespace must still time out.
s3.hint: From a throw-away Pod in monitoring, call service.namespace with a short timeout.

s4.prompt: Step 5 - Now prove the 'nothing else' part: the same call from a Pod in namespace 'default' must time out.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n default -- wget -qO- -T 3 web.prod
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n monitoring -- wget -qO- -T 3 web.prod
options.why: That repeats the ALLOWED call from monitoring: it succeeds and says nothing about other namespaces.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n default -- nslookup web.prod
options.why: DNS goes to CoreDNS in kube-system, which the ingress policy of prod does not touch: the name resolves whatever the policy says.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n default -- ping -c 2 web.prod
options.why: A Service ClusterIP does not answer ping, policy or not: the failure proves nothing.

s4.explain: A policy test has two halves: the allowed source gets through, any other source does not. 'wget: download timed out' from 'default' shows the namespaceSelector admits monitoring only. A typo in the selector would have opened prod to everyone.
s4.hint: Same request, from a namespace the rule must NOT admit.

questions.title: Lock down egress, keep DNS
questions.scenario: In namespace 'app', Pods labelled app=frontend (busybox-based image) may only open connections to Pods app=backend on TCP 8080, plus DNS (UDP and TCP 53) to any destination.
questions.tip: Once a policy selects a Pod for Egress, DNS is blocked too unless you allow port 53. A rule with 'ports' but no 'to' allows those ports to any destination.
questions.stakes: Block all egress and forget DNS: every lookup times out and the app looks dead.
questions.analogy: You banned every outgoing call, including directory enquiries (DNS).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the Pods the policy will select, to check the label.

options.why: -L (capital) adds a label COLUMN; it does not filter (and expects a key, not key=value).
Selector syntax is key=value; 'app:frontend' is rejected.
No '-n app': this filters the current namespace.

s1.explain: spec.podSelector uses the same label logic as -l: if this list is empty, the policy selects no Pod and protects nothing.
s1.hint: List the Pods in 'app' that carry the label the policy selects.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Add the DNS rule: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: DNS needs its own rule ('  - ports:', no 'to': any destination).
Allow UDP 53 (normal DNS queries).
Allow TCP 53 too (large answers fall back to TCP).
Keep the backend rule unchanged.

forbid.msg: A bare podSelector only looks in namespace 'app': CoreDNS Pods live in kube-system.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: At this indentation the ports join the backend rule: DNS is only allowed towards backend Pods.
Only UDP: the task requires TCP 53 too (truncated answers retry over TCP).
Without a namespaceSelector, podSelector matches Pods of 'app' only: CoreDNS (kube-system) stays blocked.

s2.recap: Add a second egress rule '- ports' UDP 53 + TCP 53 (no 'to').
s2.explain: Denying egress also blocks DNS: every name lookup would time out and the app would look dead. So allow port 53 over UDP and TCP. Each '- ' under egress is a rule; rules are ORed, and inside one rule 'to' AND 'ports' must both match.
s2.hint: An egress rule without 'to' allows any destination; list port 53 for both UDP and TCP.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Applied. Prove that DNS still works for the frontend Pods.

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- nslookup backend
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n app -- nslookup backend
options.why: The throw-away Pod has label run=t, not app=frontend: the policy does not apply to it.
Reads a local file: no network traffic, it proves nothing about the policy.
ICMP is not allowed by the policy and a Service IP never answers ping anyway.

s3.explain: Always test from a Pod the policy actually selects: a test from another Pod proves nothing. Resolving 'backend' shows that DNS still works while everything else stays locked.
s3.hint: From a frontend Pod (exec through its Deployment), resolve the backend's name.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Prove the allowed path: from the frontend, fetch Service 'backend' on port 8080 (3 s timeout).

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- wget -qO- -T 3 backend:8080
aliases: kubectl -n app exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T 3 backend:8080
kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://backend:8080

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- wget -qO- -T 3 backend
options.why: Port 80 is not allowed (and the Service listens on 8080): it times out and wrongly suggests the policy blocks the backend.

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- curl -s backend:8080
options.why: The busybox-based image has no curl: 'executable file not found', not a network answer.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n app -- wget -qO- -T 3 backend:8080
options.why: The throw-away Pod has no app=frontend label: the egress policy does not select it, so its success proves nothing about the frontend.

s4.explain: Testing from a real frontend Pod uses the exact labels the policy selects. Egress to app=backend on TCP 8080 is allowed and DNS resolves 'backend', so the page comes back.
s4.hint: Test from a Pod the policy selects, to the allowed port.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Prove the rest is cut: from the frontend, fetching http://example.com must time out after DNS succeeds.

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://example.com
aliases: kubectl -n app exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://example.com

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- nslookup example.com
options.why: DNS is explicitly allowed: it succeeds and proves nothing about other traffic.

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/backend -n app -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://example.com
options.why: backend Pods are not selected by this policy: their result says nothing about the frontend.

options.cmd: kubectl exec deploy/frontend -n app -- wget -qO- -T 3 backend:8080
options.why: That is the allowed path again: it succeeds and tests nothing new.

s5.explain: The name resolves (UDP/TCP 53 allowed), then the TCP connection to port 80 is dropped: 'download timed out'. That is the egress allow-list working: only backend:8080 and DNS leave the frontend Pods.
s5.hint: Same Pod, a destination the policy does not list.

questions.title: Create an Ingress in one command
questions.scenario: In namespace 'shop', Service 'shop-svc' (port 80) must be published by the 'nginx' ingress controller for host shop.example.com, for every path.
questions.tip: kubectl create ingress --rule="host/path=svc:port": the path is Exact by default; end it with '*' (e.g. '/*') for a Prefix match.
questions.stakes: Hand-writing YAML eats exam minutes: one imperative command does the job.
questions.analogy: Ingress is a receptionist who routes visitors by name (host) and floor (path).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create Ingress 'shop' (class nginx) routing every path of shop.example.com to shop-svc:80.

options.why: The flag is --class (it fills spec.ingressClassName); --ingress-class does not exist.
Reversed: the rule is host/path=service:port.
A default backend catches every host: the task asks for host shop.example.com only.

s1.explain: '/*' gives path '/' with pathType Prefix, so every path is routed; a plain '/' would be Exact and /cart would get a 404. --class=nginx says which controller must serve it.
s1.hint: The ingress generator takes the class and a quoted rule host/path=service:port (* matches every path).

context: NAME   CLASS   HOSTS              ADDRESS         PORTS   AGE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Test from your terminal through the controller (address 192.168.1.240) without touching DNS: fetch /cart.

options.why: Without the Host header no rule matches: the controller answers 404 from its default backend.
Cluster DNS names do not resolve outside the cluster - and that bypasses the Ingress.
The Host header must be the rule's host, not the Service name.

s2.explain: An Ingress routes on the HTTP Host header plus the path, so send the Host header yourself and no DNS change is needed. curl --resolve shop.example.com:80:IP also works.
s2.hint: Send the request to the controller's IP while setting the Host header to the site's name.

questions.title: Route /api to a second Service
questions.scenario: Ingress 'store' (namespace 'store', host store.example.com) sends everything to web-svc:80. Requests to /api and below (e.g. /api/orders) must go to api-svc:8080.
questions.tip: pathType Prefix matches whole path elements (/api matches /api and /api/orders, not /apix); Exact matches one path only. The longest match wins.
questions.stakes: The wrong pathType and /api swallows /api2, or matches nothing.
questions.analogy: Paths are street signs: Prefix means 'this whole street', Exact means 'only this house'.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Add the /api path: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: send /api and below to api-svc:8080

checks.regex:
^      - path: /api\s*
        pathType: Prefix\s*
        backend:\s*
          service:\s*
            name: api-svc\s*
            port:\s*
              number: 8080\s*$
checks.msg: Add a path item '/api', pathType Prefix, backend.service name api-svc + port.number 8080 (same indentation as the '/' item).

forbid.msg: Exact would only match /api itself: /api/orders would fall to web-svc.
serviceName/servicePort is the removed v1beta1 format.
In networking.k8s.io/v1 the port is an object: port.number (or port.name).
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: send /api and below to api-svc:8080

options.why: Exact matches only '/api': /api/orders goes to web-svc through the '/' Prefix path.
That is the old extensions/v1beta1 syntax, rejected by networking.k8s.io/v1.
port must be an object: 'port:' then 'number: 8080' (strict decoding rejects an integer).

s1.recap: Add path /api, pathType Prefix -> api-svc port.number 8080.
s1.explain: Prefix /api matches /api and everything below, such as /api/orders; Exact would match only /api. Ingress v1 needs pathType and a backend as service.name + service.port. Keep the '/' rule last in the file.
s1.hint: A new item in the paths list: path, pathType, and a backend service with name and port number.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Applied. Show the host/path -> backend table, including the backend Pod IPs.

options.cmd: kubectl get ingress store -n store -o wide
options.why: get only shows class, hosts, address and ports - no paths or backends.
An IngressClass describes a controller, not your routes - and none is named 'store'.
An Ingress is configuration, not a workload: it has no logs.

s2.explain: 'describe' shows each Host / Path -> backend with the endpoint IPs, so you see that /api really reaches api-svc. An empty endpoint list means the Service selects no Ready Pod.
s2.hint: describe on the Ingress shows rules with their backends and endpoints.

questions.title: An Ingress nobody serves
questions.scenario: Ingress 'blog' (namespace 'blog') has no ADDRESS: no controller picked it up. Several controllers are installed. It must be served by the ingress-nginx controller.
questions.tip: spec.ingressClassName holds the IngressClass NAME (not the controller string). The annotation ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class="true" on an IngressClass makes it the default.
questions.stakes: An Ingress with no class is accepted happily and served by nobody.
questions.analogy: A letter with no courier assigned: stamped, never delivered.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the available ingress classes and their controllers.

options.why: Lists Ingress objects, not the classes you can use.
Shows controller Pods, not the class name they serve.
There is no 'ingresscontroller' resource in Kubernetes.

s1.explain: Several controllers are installed, so you must pick the right one. An IngressClass links a name (used by Ingresses) to a controller (spec.controller).
s1.hint: Ingress classes are cluster-scoped objects naming their controller.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Bind the Ingress to the right class: type the right line in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: let ingress-nginx serve this Ingress

checks.msg: Set 'ingressClassName: nginx' directly under spec (the class NAME).

forbid.msg: That is the controller string, not the class name.
The field is ingressClassName.
That is a (deprecated) annotation: it belongs in metadata.annotations, not in spec.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: let ingress-nginx serve this Ingress

options.why: That is the CONTROLLER column; ingressClassName needs the class NAME 'nginx'.
No such field: the API rejects 'className' (strict decoding).
The old annotation is not a spec field; use spec.ingressClassName.

s2.recap: Add 'ingressClassName: nginx' under spec.
s2.explain: Without a class (and without a default class) every controller ignores the Ingress, so no ADDRESS ever appears. ingressClassName tells the ingress-nginx controller that this one is its job.
s2.hint: An Ingress spec field names its class.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Make 'nginx' the default class, so future Ingresses without a class use it.

options.why: It must be an ANNOTATION; a label with that key is ignored.
The annotation goes on the IngressClass, not on an Ingress.
Wrong key: the default marker is ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class.

s3.explain: Only NEW Ingresses without ingressClassName get the default class, and existing ones are unchanged. Keep a single default class: with several, behaviour is ambiguous.
s3.hint: The default class is chosen by an annotation on the IngressClass, set to true.

questions.title: Create a Gateway listener
questions.scenario: The Gateway API CRDs and a controller are installed. Create Gateway 'web-gw' in namespace 'infra' with one HTTP listener on port 80 for *.example.com.
questions.tip: GatewayClass = which controller (cluster-scoped, like IngressClass); Gateway = listeners (name, protocol, port, hostname); routes attach to it.
questions.stakes: A listener with the wrong port or protocol and nothing connects, with no error.
questions.analogy: A Gateway is the building's entrance; routes are the signs inside.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Find the GatewayClass to use (and check it is ACCEPTED).

options.why: IngressClass belongs to the Ingress API; a Gateway needs a GatewayClass.
Lists Gateways, not the classes (controllers) available.
CRD names are plural + group (gatewayclasses.gateway.networking.k8s.io): NotFound.

s1.explain: A Gateway needs a GatewayClass, which names the controller that implements it. ACCEPTED=True means the controller listed in CONTROLLER watches this class.
s1.hint: GatewayClasses are cluster-scoped; their table shows ACCEPTED.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Add the listener: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: one HTTP listener on port 80 for *.example.com

checks.msg: Add 'listeners:' directly under spec.
Each listener needs a 'name' (e.g. '- name: http').
The protocol must be HTTP (HTTPS needs a tls section).
Listen on port 80.
Quote the wildcard hostname: "*.example.com".

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: one HTTP listener on port 80 for *.example.com

options.why: Unquoted, a leading '*' is a YAML alias: the file does not even parse.
listeners[].name is required (routes can target it via sectionName).
HTTPS needs a tls section with a certificate: without one the listener cannot serve TLS and is not programmed, and the task asks for HTTP.

s2.recap: listeners: name http, protocol HTTP, port 80, hostname "*.example.com".
s2.explain: A listener says which traffic the Gateway accepts: protocol, port and hostname. The hostname filters Host headers, and routes attached later must intersect it.
s2.hint: A listener: name, protocol, port and a wildcard hostname (quoted: YAML treats '*' specially).

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Applied. Check that the controller programmed the Gateway (ADDRESS and PROGRAMMED columns).

options.why: No '-n infra': the Gateway is namespaced.
web-gw is a Gateway; GatewayClasses are cluster-scoped and named 'envoy' here.
A Gateway is a configuration object: no logs. Its state is in status.conditions.

s3.explain: PROGRAMMED=True with an ADDRESS means the controller configured its data plane. If not, 'kubectl describe gateway' shows the reason.
s3.hint: The Gateway table has ADDRESS and PROGRAMMED columns; mind its namespace.

questions.title: Route /cart through a Gateway
questions.scenario: Gateway 'shop-gw' (namespace 'shop') has an HTTP listener. Requests for shop.example.com/cart (and below) must reach Service 'cart' (port 8080) in the same namespace.
questions.tip: HTTPRoute = parentRefs (which Gateway) + rules: matches (path type PathPrefix/Exact) and backendRefs (Service name + port).
questions.stakes: A route not attached through parentRefs is ignored: no error, no traffic.
questions.analogy: The route is a signpost; parentRefs is the nail that fixes it to the wall.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Add the rule: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: send /cart (and below) to Service cart, port 8080

checks.msg: Match with '- matches:' -> '- path:' type PathPrefix, value /cart.
In the SAME rule (no dash before backendRefs), add backendRefs: name cart, port 8080.

forbid.msg: '- backendRefs' starts a second rule: the /cart rule would have no backend.
Gateway API uses PathPrefix (Prefix is the Ingress term).
backendRefs take name/port directly - no 'service:' wrapper.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: send /cart (and below) to Service cart, port 8080

options.why: 'Prefix' is an Ingress pathType; HTTPRoute accepts PathPrefix, Exact or RegularExpression.
Two rules: /cart matches a rule with no backend, so it gets an error response (5xx) instead of reaching the cart Service; the other rule catches everything else.
That is the Ingress backend shape; a backendRef is name + port (kind defaults to Service).

s1.recap: rules: matches path PathPrefix /cart + backendRefs name cart port 8080.
s1.explain: matches chooses which requests the rule catches (PathPrefix /cart also covers /cart/items); backendRefs says where they go, and a Service backend must give the port. The route is attached to the Gateway by parentRefs, already in the file.
s1.hint: A rule: matches with a path (prefix type and value) and backendRefs naming the Service and port.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Applied. Check the route's conditions (Accepted by the Gateway, ResolvedRefs for the backend).

aliases: kubectl get httproute cart-route -n shop -o yaml

options.cmd: kubectl get httproute cart-route -n shop -o wide
options.why: The table only shows hostnames and age - not status.parents[].conditions.
No 'route' resource in Kubernetes (that is OpenShift); the kind is httproute.
A route is configuration: no logs. Its status is in status.parents.

s2.explain: A route can be accepted or silently ignored. Accepted=False: the listener refuses it (hostname, allowedRoutes). ResolvedRefs=False: wrong Service name or port, or a missing ReferenceGrant for another namespace.
s2.hint: describe on the HTTPRoute shows its parents' conditions.

questions.title: Canary 90/10 with an HTTPRoute
questions.scenario: HTTPRoute 'checkout' (namespace 'shop') sends all traffic to Service checkout-v1:8080. Send 10% of it to checkout-v2:8080 (canary). shop.example.com resolves to the Gateway.
questions.tip: Weights are relative within ONE rule's backendRefs (weight defaults to 1). 90/10 = 9/1 = 900/100.
questions.stakes: A weight typo sends everyone to the untested version instead of 10 %.
questions.analogy: A tap with two outlets: the weights decide how the flow splits.

s0.prompt: Step 1 - Before sending traffic to it, check that Service checkout-v2 exists in 'shop' and exposes port 8080.

options.why: Shows the route (HOSTNAMES, AGE), not whether the new backend exists.
Shows Pods, but the route points at a SERVICE: a missing Service would still break the canary.
Without '-n shop' you search the current namespace: NotFound, though it may exist.

s0.explain: A backendRef to a missing Service makes the route report ResolvedRefs=False and that share of traffic fails with 500s. Checking the Service and its port first avoids sending 10 % of users to an error.
s0.hint: A backendRef names a Service and a port in the route's namespace.

s1.prompt: Step 2 - Replace the backend lines (the '- name: checkout-v1' item) with the right snippet. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Give checkout-v1 'weight: 90'.
Add checkout-v2 (port 8080) with 'weight: 10' in the same backendRefs list.

forbid.msg: Two rules with the same match: only one wins; weights work inside ONE rule.
weight is an integer, no percent sign.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: Two rules with identical (default) matches: one takes all traffic; weights only split inside one rule.
checkout-v1 keeps the default weight 1: 1/11 vs 10/11 - the canary gets ~91%!
weight is an integer (0-1000000): a percent string is rejected.

s1.recap: One rule, two backendRefs: v1 weight 90, v2 weight 10.
s1.explain: Weights are relative inside one rule's backendRefs: 90 and 10 give 90/10 (9 and 1 would too; the default weight is 1). A weight of 0 keeps a backend listed but sends it nothing, handy to roll back instantly.
s1.hint: Two backendRefs side by side, each with a weight: the weights are relative shares.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Apply the edited route (its metadata names namespace 'shop').

options.why: The route already exists: 'AlreadyExists', nothing changes.
The server validates the change but stores nothing: all traffic still goes to v1.
The file says shop, the flag says default: kubectl refuses with a namespace mismatch.

s3.explain: apply updates the existing HTTPRoute in place: the Gateway controller sees the new backendRefs and reprograms the data plane within seconds, without dropping connections to v1.
s3.hint: Update an existing object from the edited file.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Check that the Gateway accepted the route and resolved both backends (its status conditions).

aliases: kubectl get httproute checkout -n shop -o yaml

options.why: The table shows HOSTNAMES and AGE only: no Accepted or ResolvedRefs condition.
Shows the Gateway's listeners and attached route COUNT, not whether this route's backends resolved.
Lists Service endpoints; the Gateway's verdict on the route is not there.

s4.explain: The controller writes status.parents[].conditions on the route: Accepted=True (the Gateway took it) and ResolvedRefs=True (both Services exist). A False condition comes with a reason, such as BackendNotFound.
s4.hint: The verdict of the Gateway controller is written in the route's status.

s2.prompt: Step 5 - Observe the split from outside (each version answers /version with its name).

options.cmd: for i in $(seq 20); do curl -s http://shop.example.com/version; done

options.why: One request hits one backend: a single sample cannot show a ratio.

options.cmd: for i in $(seq 20); do curl -s http://checkout-v2.shop:8080/version; done
options.why: Bypasses the Gateway (and cluster DNS does not resolve outside the cluster): no split involved.

options.cmd: kubectl get endpoints checkout-v1 checkout-v2 -n shop
options.why: Shows that both Services have Pods, not how the route splits requests.

s2.explain: Weighting is statistical, per request (or per connection, depending on the implementation), so expect about 18 v1 and 2 v2 out of 20, not exactly that.
s2.hint: Repeat the request in a shell loop and look at the mix of answers.

questions.title: Forward a corporate domain
questions.scenario: Pods must resolve names under corp.example (e.g. git.corp.example) through the company DNS server 10.0.0.53. Everything else keeps using the node's resolvers.
questions.tip: A stub domain = an extra server block in the Corefile: 'corp.example:53 { forward . 10.0.0.53 }'. One forward plugin per server block.
questions.stakes: Break the Corefile and cluster DNS dies for every Pod at once.
questions.analogy: A stub domain is a contacts-list rule: 'for this name, ask that operator'.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Open the CoreDNS configuration for editing.

options.why: The Deployment only mounts the config; the Corefile itself is in the ConfigMap.
kube-dns is the Service name; the ConfigMap is called 'coredns'.
That path exists inside the CoreDNS containers (mounted from the ConfigMap), not on the node.

s1.explain: CoreDNS reads its configuration (the Corefile) from a ConfigMap, not from a file in the Pod, so you edit the ConfigMap. On kubeadm clusters it is the 'Corefile' key of 'coredns' in kube-system.
s1.hint: CoreDNS reads its Corefile from a ConfigMap in kube-system: edit it live.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Add a server block for corp.example: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment (end of the Corefile). Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Open a new server block 'corp.example:53 {' at column 0.
Inside it, 'forward . 10.0.0.53', then close the block with '}'.
Keep the main block's forward to /etc/resolv.conf.

forbid.msg: The 'proxy' plugin was removed from CoreDNS long ago: use 'forward'.
'hosts' serves entries from a hosts file; it does not forward queries.
A directive outside any server block breaks the Corefile parsing.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: Plugins must live inside a server block: CoreDNS fails to parse the file and crash-loops.
'proxy' no longer exists in CoreDNS: unknown directive, CoreDNS fails to start.
hosts expects a file path (or inline entries), it does not query another server.

s2.recap: Add server block 'corp.example:53 { errors; cache 30; forward . 10.0.0.53 }'.
s2.explain: CoreDNS picks the most specific server block for each query zone: corp.example goes to 10.0.0.53, everything else stays on '.:53'. So the company DNS only sees queries for its own domain.
s2.hint: A new server block for the domain on port 53, ending in a forward to the company server.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Saved. Make sure CoreDNS runs with the new Corefile now, without deleting anything.

options.cmd: kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system
aliases: kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment coredns

options.cmd: kubectl rollout restart daemonset coredns -n kube-system
options.why: On kubeadm, CoreDNS is a Deployment, not a DaemonSet.
CoreDNS runs as Pods, not as a systemd unit on the node.
That deletes the configuration you just fixed: CoreDNS Pods could not start again.

s3.explain: A ConfigMap change does not reach running Pods at once. The 'reload' plugin re-reads it within about two minutes; a rollout restart is immediate. Check the Pod logs for syntax errors: a broken Corefile takes cluster DNS down.
s3.hint: Restart the Deployment's Pods gracefully, one by one.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Wait until the restarted CoreDNS Pods are all ready.

options.cmd: kubectl rollout status deployment coredns -n kube-system
aliases: kubectl rollout status deploy coredns -n kube-system
kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deployment coredns

options.cmd: kubectl rollout history deployment coredns -n kube-system
options.why: Lists past revisions; it does not wait for the new Pods to be ready.
A snapshot: during a rollout old and new Pods mix and you cannot tell when it is over.
Without '-n kube-system' kubectl looks in the current namespace: 'deployments.apps "coredns" not found'.

s4.explain: rollout status follows the Deployment until every new Pod is ready and the old ones are gone, then exits 0. A Corefile syntax error would show here as new Pods crashing instead of a finished rollout.
s4.hint: One command follows a Deployment until its new Pods are ready.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - From a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod, resolve git.corp.example.

options.why: Runs on your shell host with ITS resolvers, not through CoreDNS: it tests the wrong path.
Asks the company server directly, bypassing CoreDNS: it works even if the stub domain is broken.
Mixes DNS and ICMP: a firewall dropping ping would look like a DNS failure.

s5.explain: A Pod's resolv.conf points at the kube-dns Service, so its lookup goes through CoreDNS and its new corp.example block, which forwards to 10.0.0.53. An answer here proves the whole chain.
s5.hint: Ask from inside a Pod, so the query goes through the cluster DNS.

questions.title: Find the Service and Pod CIDRs
questions.scenario: On kubeadm cluster 'k8s-prod' (you are on the control-plane node), report the Service IP range and the Pod CIDR, then the Pod CIDR of node worker1.
questions.tip: Service range = kube-apiserver --service-cluster-ip-range. Pod range = kube-controller-manager --cluster-cidr; per node: spec.podCIDR.
questions.stakes: Overlapping Pod, Service and node ranges cause unreachable IPs that make no sense.
questions.analogy: CIDRs are postcodes: two towns with the same one lose each other's mail.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Find the Service ClusterIP range.

options.why: --cluster-cidr is the Pod range, and it is a kube-controller-manager flag: no match here.
The kubelet does not know the Service range (it only has clusterDNS).
Shows one IP (usually the first of the range), not the range and its mask.

s1.explain: The cluster does not store its CIDRs in an API object, so read them from where kubeadm wrote them: the API server's static Pod manifest. It comes from networking.serviceSubnet (default 10.96.0.0/12).
s1.hint: The Service range is an API server flag in its manifest: search for it.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Find the cluster-wide Pod CIDR.

options.why: The scheduler places Pods; it does not allocate their IP ranges.
The API server has no Pod CIDR flag.
Shows individual Pod IPs (and hostNetwork Pods use node IPs): not the configured range.

s2.explain: The Pod CIDR is the controller-manager's business: with --allocate-node-cidrs=true it carves a per-node subnet out of --cluster-cidr.
s2.hint: The cluster-wide Pod range is a controller-manager flag in its manifest.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Print the Pod CIDR allocated to node worker1.

options.why: podCIDR is in the node's spec, not its status: the output is empty.
Lists the Pods on worker1 with their IPs, not the allocated range.

options.cmd: kubectl describe node worker1 | grep -i InternalIP
options.why: InternalIP is the node's own address, not its Pod subnet.

s3.explain: Each node gets a slice of the cluster CIDR in spec.podCIDR. Some CNIs (e.g. Calico IPAM) ignore it and manage their own blocks, so check the CNI configuration too.
s3.hint: Each Node's spec records the Pod range allocated to it: print it with jsonpath.

questions.title: Reach Grafana from your laptop
questions.scenario: Service 'grafana' (namespace 'monitoring') listens on port 3000 and is ClusterIP only. You need it at http://localhost:8080 for a quick test.
questions.tip: port-forward LOCAL:REMOTE tunnels through the API server to ONE Pod picked at start: no load balancing, and it dies with that Pod or with kubectl.
questions.stakes: Publish Grafana through a public Service for a quick look and you have a security incident.
questions.analogy: port-forward is a private tunnel from your laptop that closes with Ctrl+C.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Forward local port 8080 to the Service's port 3000.

options.why: Swapped: the order is LOCAL:REMOTE, so this listens on 3000 locally and targets 8080.
Without a type, 'grafana' is a Pod name - and the Pods are called grafana-<hash>: NotFound.
kubectl proxy exposes the API server locally, not the Grafana port.

s1.explain: With svc/NAME kubectl resolves the Service's selector and target port, then forwards to one of its Pods: a private tunnel for a quick test that closes with Ctrl+C. Local port first, then remote (8080:3000).
s1.hint: port-forward can target a Service: local port first, then the Service's port.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - A teammate on another machine must reach it too: listen on all interfaces.

options.why: There is no --bind flag; the flag is --address.
The port spec has no address part: use --address.
Creates another ClusterIP Service: still unreachable from outside the cluster.

s2.explain: The default --address is localhost, so only your machine can use the tunnel. 0.0.0.0 opens it to the network: acceptable for a short test, never for anything lasting (use a NodePort, LoadBalancer, Ingress or Gateway instead).
s2.hint: By default it listens on localhost only: one flag sets the listening address.

questions.title: An in-cluster name for an external API
questions.scenario: Apps in namespace 'payments' must call the partner API as 'billing' (in-cluster name). The real host is billing.partner.example.com.
questions.tip: ExternalName = a DNS CNAME only: no ClusterIP, no endpoints, no proxying, ports are ignored. HTTP Host/TLS names still see 'billing'.
questions.stakes: ExternalName is only a DNS alias: no ports, no proxy, no health checks.
questions.analogy: A contact card that points to someone else's number.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the ExternalName Service 'billing'.

options.cmd: kubectl create service externalname billing --external-name=billing.partner.example.com -n payments
aliases: kubectl create service externalname billing --external-name billing.partner.example.com -n payments
kubectl create svc externalname billing --external-name=billing.partner.example.com -n payments

options.cmd: kubectl create service externalname billing --external-name=https://billing.partner.example.com -n payments
options.why: externalName must be a DNS name, not a URL: validation rejects the scheme.

options.cmd: kubectl create service clusterip billing --external-name=billing.partner.example.com -n payments
options.why: --external-name only exists for the externalname subcommand.
expose needs an existing resource with a selector, and has no way to set the external name.

s1.explain: ExternalName only maps a name: the Service has no ClusterIP and no proxying, and CoreDNS answers billing.payments.svc.cluster.local with a CNAME to the real host. So ports and health checks are the caller's business.
s1.hint: The service generator has an ExternalName type that takes the external DNS name.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Prove that cluster DNS returns the CNAME, from a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod in 'payments'.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n payments -- nslookup billing

options.why: An ExternalName Service has no endpoints: this shows nothing either way.
Shows the configured External Name, not what DNS actually answers.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n payments -- ping -c 3 billing
options.why: ping tests ICMP to the partner host (often blocked); nslookup tests the DNS answer itself.

s2.explain: The answer must be a CNAME: 'billing.payments.svc.cluster.local canonical name = billing.partner.example.com'. An IP here would mean a normal Service, not an ExternalName.
s2.hint: From a throw-away Pod in 'payments', look up the short name: DNS should answer with a CNAME.

questions.title: A LoadBalancer stuck in <pending>
questions.scenario: Bare-metal kubeadm cluster: no cloud controller manager, no MetalLB. Deployment 'shop-api' (namespace 'shop') listens on 8080. Expose it as LoadBalancer Service 'shop-lb' on port 80, then find a way in while the external IP is missing.
questions.tip: type LoadBalancer = ClusterIP + NodePort + an external IP that SOMEONE must provide (cloud controller, MetalLB). Without one: <pending> forever, NodePort still works.
questions.stakes: You wait for an external IP that no controller will ever assign, while the NodePort already worked.
questions.analogy: Ordering a taxi in a town with no taxi company: the booking is saved, the car never comes. Walk (NodePort).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create Service 'shop-lb' (type LoadBalancer, port 80 -> container port 8080) for Deployment 'shop-api'.

options.cmd: kubectl create service loadbalancer shop-lb --tcp=80:8080 -n shop
options.why: create service sets the selector app=shop-lb, which matches none of the shop-api Pods: the Service has no endpoints.
No '-n shop': kubectl looks for Deployment shop-api in 'default' and answers NotFound.
Ports swapped: the Service listens on 8080 and sends to container port 80, where nothing listens.

s1.explain: expose copies the Deployment's selector, so the Service reaches the shop-api Pods; --port is the Service port, --target-port the container's. 'create service loadbalancer' would invent the selector app=shop-lb and match nothing.
s1.hint: expose with a type that asks the cloud for an external IP; Service port 80, target the container's 8080.

context: NAME      TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)        AGE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - EXTERNAL-IP is still <pending> after 6 minutes. Show the Service's NodePort, Endpoints and Events in one view.

options.cmd: kubectl get svc shop-lb -n shop -o wide
options.why: Adds only the SELECTOR column: no endpoints and no events, so you cannot see that no controller ever acted.
No '-n shop': the Service lives in 'shop', so 'default' answers NotFound.
Service events are recorded in the Service's own namespace ('shop'), and there are none for it here anyway.

s2.explain: On a cloud, the service controller of the cloud controller manager logs EnsuringLoadBalancer / EnsuredLoadBalancer events and fills status.loadBalancer. Here describe shows a NodePort and Endpoints but no such events: nobody provisions load balancers, so <pending> never ends.
s2.hint: describe on the Service shows its NodePort, endpoints and events in one view.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Until MetalLB is installed, users will connect to <node-IP>:<port>. Print the port that is open on every node.

options.cmd: kubectl get svc shop-lb -n shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}'
aliases: kubectl get svc shop-lb -n shop -o jsonpath="{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}"
kubectl get service shop-lb -n shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}'

options.why: status.loadBalancer is filled by a load balancer controller: with none, it is empty and prints nothing.

options.cmd: kubectl get svc shop-lb -n shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].targetPort}'
options.why: Prints 8080, the container port: it is reachable only on the Pod IPs, not on the nodes.

options.cmd: kubectl get svc shop-lb -n shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'
options.why: The ClusterIP is virtual and answers only inside the cluster: outside users cannot reach it.

s3.explain: A LoadBalancer Service is built on a NodePort Service: the node port (31547 here) is allocated at once, unless allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts is false, so http://<any-node-IP>:31547 works already. An external load balancer would only forward to those node ports.
s3.hint: The node port is a field of the Service's first port: print it with jsonpath.

questions.title: A stable name for an external database
questions.scenario: Apps in namespace 'shop' must reach the legacy PostgreSQL at 10.20.30.40:5432 (outside the cluster, no DNS name) as 'legacy-db:5432'. Use a Service WITHOUT selector, port named 'postgres', and an EndpointSlice you write yourself.
questions.tip: No selector = you own the endpoints. The EndpointSlice needs the label kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> and a port whose name matches the Service port's name.
questions.stakes: One wrong label or port name and the Service answers nothing, with no error anywhere: the database seems down to every app.
questions.analogy: A switchboard extension wired by hand: the number (Service) works only once you plug the cable (EndpointSlice) into it.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Generate a Service manifest 'legacy-db' (port 5432) in svc.yaml without creating it yet.

options.cmd: kubectl create service clusterip legacy-db --tcp=5432:5432 -n shop --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml
aliases: kubectl create svc clusterip legacy-db --tcp=5432:5432 -n shop --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml

options.cmd: kubectl create service externalname legacy-db --external-name=10.20.30.40 -n shop
options.why: ExternalName takes a DNS name: the IP is accepted but treated as a name made of digits, so CoreDNS returns a CNAME that never resolves.

options.cmd: kubectl expose deployment legacy-db --port=5432 -n shop --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml
options.why: expose needs an existing object to copy a selector from: there is no Deployment legacy-db, so it fails with NotFound.

options.cmd: kubectl create service clusterip legacy-db --tcp=5432:5432 -n shop
options.why: Creates the Service at once WITH the selector app=legacy-db: you need a file first, to remove that selector.

s1.explain: kubectl cannot create a Service without selector: 'create service clusterip' always adds app=<name>. A dry-run file gives the right skeleton (port, namespace) to edit. ExternalName would only be a CNAME, and an IP is not a DNS name.
s1.hint: The service generator for a ClusterIP takes --tcp port:targetPort; dry run on the client into svc.yaml.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Name the port 'postgres' and remove the selector: retype the ports/selector block. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Keep 'ports:' with one item '- name: postgres' and 'port: 5432'.

forbid.msg: Remove the selector: with one, the control plane manages (empty) endpoints for this Service.
externalIPs captures traffic sent TO an IP; it does not send traffic there.
Rename the port to 'postgres' (the EndpointSlice will use that name).

options.why: The selector app=legacy-db stays: Kubernetes keeps managing this Service's endpoints from Pods, and no Pod matches.
externalIPs makes kube-proxy capture traffic sent TO 10.20.30.40:5432 and send it to the Service's endpoints: it creates no endpoint and hijacks the real DB IP in-cluster.

s2.recap: Service legacy-db: port 'postgres' 5432, no selector.
s2.explain: A Service without selector tells the control plane not to compute endpoints: you supply them in an EndpointSlice. The port name matters because kube-proxy matches the slice's ports to the Service's ports by name.
s2.hint: Name the port in the ports item and delete the selector lines: no selector means no automatic endpoints.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - svc.yaml is applied. Write the EndpointSlice body in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: link to Service legacy-db; IPv4 endpoint 10.20.30.40, port 'postgres' 5432
target: # TODO: link to Service legacy-db; IPv4 endpoint 10.20.30.40, port 'postgres' 5432

checks.msg: Label the slice kubernetes.io/service-name: legacy-db (that label links it to the Service).
Set addressType: IPv4 at the top level.
The slice port must be named 'postgres', like the Service port, with port 5432.
One endpoint: '- addresses: ["10.20.30.40"]' (an IP only, no port).

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: app=legacy-db links nothing: Services find their slices only by kubernetes.io/service-name, so legacy-db keeps no endpoints.
Port 'db' does not match the Service port 'postgres': kube-proxy finds no endpoint for that port and connections are rejected.
addresses holds bare IPs: '10.20.30.40:5432' is not a valid IPv4 address, so the API server rejects the slice.

s3.recap: EndpointSlice: label kubernetes.io/service-name, addressType IPv4, port 'postgres' 5432, address 10.20.30.40.
s3.explain: kube-proxy builds the Service's rules from every slice labelled kubernetes.io/service-name=legacy-db, matching ports by name. The address is a bare IP and the port lives in 'ports', so legacy-db.shop:5432 now leads to 10.20.30.40:5432.
s3.hint: The slice links to the Service through a well-known label; then addressType, a named port and the address.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Applied. List the EndpointSlices that back Service legacy-db (expect 10.20.30.40 and port 5432).

options.why: Nothing creates an Endpoints object from a hand-written slice: NotFound (and the Endpoints API is deprecated).
The slice carries kubernetes.io/service-name, not app: 'No resources found'.
No '-n shop': the slice is namespaced, so 'default' shows 'No resources found'.

s4.explain: Selecting by kubernetes.io/service-name shows exactly what the Service uses, whatever the slices are named. ENDPOINTS 10.20.30.40 and PORTS 5432 prove the link; an empty list means the label or the namespace is wrong.
s4.hint: Find the slices of a Service by that well-known label, in its namespace.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - From a throw-away postgres:17 Pod in 'shop', check that the database answers as legacy-db:5432.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=postgres:17 --restart=Never -n shop -- pg_isready -h legacy-db -p 5432
aliases: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=postgres:17 --restart=Never -n shop -- pg_isready -h legacy-db

options.why: Talks to the IP directly: it proves the database is up, not that the Service and its EndpointSlice work.
Without '-n shop' the Pod lives in 'default', where the short name legacy-db does not resolve.

options.cmd: kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n shop -- ping -c 2 legacy-db
options.why: A ClusterIP does not answer ping: it fails even when everything is right.

s5.explain: pg_isready opens a real PostgreSQL connection through the name: DNS gives the ClusterIP, kube-proxy forwards it to 10.20.30.40:5432 from your EndpointSlice. 'accepting connections' proves the whole path.
s5.hint: Use a client that speaks the database's protocol, through the Service name.

questions.title: HTTPS Gateway shared with another namespace
questions.scenario: GatewayClass 'envoy' is installed. The platform team owns Gateway 'secure-gw' in namespace 'infra'; the app team in namespace 'shop' must attach its HTTPRoute. Terminate HTTPS for shop.example.com with tls.crt/tls.key (current directory).
questions.tip: HTTPS listener = tls.mode Terminate + certificateRefs to a kubernetes.io/tls Secret in the Gateway's namespace. Routes from other namespaces need allowedRoutes AND parentRefs.namespace.
questions.stakes: allowedRoutes left at Same and the app team's route is silently refused: the site is down and their YAML looks perfect.
questions.analogy: A shared building entrance: the owner holds the keys (certificate) and keeps the list of tenants allowed to put up their signs.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Store the certificate and key as Secret 'shop-tls' where the Gateway can use it.

options.cmd: kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n infra
aliases: kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --key=tls.key --cert=tls.crt -n infra

options.cmd: kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n shop
options.why: A Secret in 'shop' is in another namespace than the Gateway: without a ReferenceGrant the listener reports ResolvedRefs=False.

options.cmd: kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --from-file=tls.crt --from-file=tls.key -n infra
options.why: 'secret tls' has no --from-file flag (that is 'secret generic'): kubectl stops with 'unknown flag'.

options.cmd: kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert=tls.key --key=tls.crt -n infra
options.why: Cert and key swapped: kubectl checks the pair and fails (PEM inputs may have been switched).

s1.explain: 'create secret tls' checks that the pair matches and stores it as type kubernetes.io/tls with keys tls.crt and tls.key, the format certificateRefs expects. The Secret belongs in the Gateway's namespace (infra): another namespace would need a ReferenceGrant.
s1.hint: A TLS Secret is created from the certificate and key files, in the Gateway's namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Configure TLS on the https listener: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: terminate TLS here with Secret shop-tls
target: # TODO: terminate TLS here with Secret shop-tls

checks.regex:
^    tls:\s*
      mode: Terminate\s*
      certificateRefs:\s*
      - name: shop-tls\s*$
checks.msg: Under the listener: tls -> mode Terminate -> certificateRefs -> '- name: shop-tls'.

forbid.msg: Passthrough is for protocol TLS; an HTTPS listener terminates TLS.
secretName is the Ingress field; a Gateway uses certificateRefs.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: Passthrough does not decrypt (it is for protocol TLS with TLSRoute): the API rejects it on an HTTPS listener, and paths could not be matched.
secretName is the Ingress syntax: kubectl reports an unknown field, and Terminate without certificateRefs fails validation.

s2.recap: listener tls: mode Terminate, certificateRefs - name: shop-tls.
s2.explain: Terminate means the Gateway decrypts with the certificate from certificateRefs (kind Secret and the Gateway's namespace by default), then reads the HTTP request so HTTPRoutes can match hosts and paths. Passthrough sends encrypted bytes on untouched.
s2.hint: Under the listener's tls: terminate TLS at the Gateway and reference the Secret by name.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - By default only routes from 'infra' may attach. Allow routes from namespace 'shop' only. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: accept routes from namespace 'shop' only
target: # TODO: accept routes from namespace 'shop' only

checks.regex:
^    allowedRoutes:\s*
      namespaces:\s*
        from: Selector\s*
        selector:\s*
          matchLabels:\s*
            kubernetes\.io/metadata\.name: "?shop"?\s*$
checks.msg: allowedRoutes -> namespaces -> from: Selector + selector.matchLabels kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop.

forbid.msg: All lets every namespace attach routes for shop.example.com.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: Works for 'shop' but also for every other namespace: any team could attach a route and capture shop.example.com traffic.
The namespace has no label 'name' (see the context): the selector matches nothing and the route is NotAllowedByListeners.
Without 'from: Selector', from keeps its default Same: the selector is not used and routes from 'shop' are still refused.

s3.recap: allowedRoutes.namespaces: from Selector, matchLabels kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop.
s3.explain: A listener accepts routes only from its own namespace by default (from: Same). from: Selector with the automatic label kubernetes.io/metadata.name opens it to 'shop' alone; All would let any namespace claim the hostname.
s3.hint: Under allowedRoutes, admit only namespaces matching a selector on the automatic name label.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - In namespace 'shop', attach the route to the https listener of secure-gw. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: attach to listener 'https' of Gateway secure-gw (namespace infra)
target: # TODO: attach to listener 'https' of Gateway secure-gw (namespace infra)

checks.regex:
^  parentRefs:\s*
  - name: secure-gw\s*
    namespace: infra\s*
    sectionName: https\s*$
checks.msg: parentRefs: '- name: secure-gw', 'namespace: infra', 'sectionName: https'.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: Without namespace, the parent is looked up in the route's own namespace (shop): no Gateway secure-gw there, so nothing attaches.
parentRefs has no 'namespace/name' form: it points to a Gateway literally named 'infra/secure-gw' in shop, which does not exist.
sectionName is the listener's name, matched exactly: the listener is 'https', not 'HTTPS', so the route finds no matching parent.

s4.recap: parentRefs: name secure-gw, namespace infra, sectionName https.
s4.explain: parentRefs defaults to the route's own namespace, so a cross-namespace Gateway needs namespace: infra. sectionName pins the route to the listener named 'https'. Both sides must agree: the listener's allowedRoutes admits 'shop'.
s4.hint: parentRefs points at the Gateway by name, in its namespace, and at one listener by its section name.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Applied. From the Gateway side, check the https listener: its conditions (ResolvedRefs for the certificate) and its attached routes.

aliases: kubectl get gateway secure-gw -n infra -o yaml

options.why: The table shows CLASS, ADDRESS and PROGRAMMED only: no listener conditions, no attached route count.
The Gateway lives in 'infra'; the route is in 'shop': NotFound.
Shows the controller and whether the class is accepted, nothing about this Gateway's listeners.

s5.explain: status.listeners reports per listener: Attached Routes (1 once shop-route is admitted), ResolvedRefs (False if the Secret is missing, in another namespace or not kubernetes.io/tls) and Programmed. The route's own view is in 'describe httproute'.
s5.hint: describe on the Gateway shows each listener's conditions and attached routes.

questions.title: Serve an Ingress over HTTPS
questions.scenario: Ingress 'store' (namespace 'store', class nginx) routes store.example.com to web-svc:80 over plain HTTP. The certificate and key are in store.crt and store.key. Serve the site over HTTPS.
questions.tip: Ingress TLS = a kubernetes.io/tls Secret in the Ingress's namespace + spec.tls: - hosts: [same host as the rule], secretName. describe shows 'SECRET terminates HOST'.
questions.stakes: A wrong host or Secret and the controller serves its default self-signed certificate: every browser shows a warning.
questions.analogy: The ID badge only opens doors for the names printed on it: tls.hosts must list the host the rule serves.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Store the certificate and key as Secret 'store-tls' where the Ingress can use it.

options.cmd: kubectl create secret tls store-tls --cert=store.crt --key=store.key -n store
aliases: kubectl create secret tls store-tls --key=store.key --cert=store.crt -n store

options.cmd: kubectl create secret generic store-tls --from-file=store.crt --from-file=store.key -n store
options.why: Keys are named store.crt/store.key and the type is Opaque: the controller looks for tls.crt/tls.key and serves its default certificate.
No '-n store': the Secret lands in 'default', and an Ingress can only use Secrets of its own namespace.

s1.explain: 'create secret tls' stores the pair as type kubernetes.io/tls under the keys tls.crt and tls.key, the format Ingress controllers read, after checking that key and certificate match. It must sit in the Ingress's namespace: secretName has no namespace field.
s1.hint: A TLS Secret from the certificate and key files, in the Ingress's namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Add the TLS section: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: serve store.example.com over HTTPS with Secret store-tls
target: # TODO: serve store.example.com over HTTPS with Secret store-tls

checks.msg: tls is a list: '- hosts:' with '- store.example.com', then 'secretName: store-tls' in the same item.

forbid.msg: certificateRefs is Gateway API; an Ingress uses secretName.
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: spec.tls is a list of items: without the dash it is an object and the API server rejects the Ingress.
tls.hosts must name the rule's host: store.example.com is not covered, so the controller serves its default certificate for it.
certificateRefs belongs to the Gateway API: kubectl reports an unknown field, and without secretName no certificate is set.

s2.recap: spec.tls: - hosts: [store.example.com], secretName: store-tls.
s2.explain: Each spec.tls item says: for these hosts, terminate TLS with this Secret. The hosts must match the rules' host, or the controller falls back to its default certificate; the Secret is looked up in the Ingress's own namespace.
s2.hint: spec.tls is a LIST: each item names hosts and the Secret; the host must match the rule.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Applied. Show which Secret terminates TLS for which host on this Ingress.

options.why: PORTS '80, 443' only says that a tls section exists: not which Secret or which hosts.
Shows the Secret's type and key sizes, not whether an Ingress uses it.
No '-n store': the Ingress lives in 'store', so 'default' answers NotFound.

s3.explain: describe prints a TLS line 'store-tls terminates store.example.com' next to the rules, so a host mismatch is visible at once. Then test from outside with curl -v https://store.example.com and read the certificate subject.
s3.hint: describe on the Ingress shows which Secret terminates which host.

questions.title: A Pod in CrashLoopBackOff
questions.scenario: Pod 'cache' (namespace default) keeps restarting.
questions.tip: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom, not a cause: 'describe' for the reason/exit code, 'logs --previous' for the app's last words.

docs.title: Determine the Reason for Pod Failure
Resource Management for Pods and Containers

questions.stakes: Restart blindly and it loops again at 3 a.m.: read 'Last State' first.
questions.analogy: 'describe' is the black-box recorder: exit code 137 and OOMKilled name who brought the plane down.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the container's last termination reason and exit code.

options.why: Prints application output, not the termination reason or exit code.
Only adds the node and IP columns.
Shows live usage; a crash-looping Pod usually has no metrics.

s1.explain: A restarting Pod hides its cause: the previous run's reason and exit code are in 'Last State: Terminated', and the Events at the bottom show what the kubelet did. Read them before changing anything.
s1.hint: describe on the Pod shows each container's Last State with its reason and exit code.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Exit code 137 + OOMKilled = memory limit too low (needs >= 256Mi). Type the right snippet over the resources block.

checks.msg: limits.memory must be at least 256Mi.

options.why: The OOM killer enforces the LIMIT, not the request. And request > limit is rejected by the API.
256M is SI (256,000,000 bytes, about 244Mi): below the required 256Mi. Use the binary suffix Mi.
Removing the limit hides the problem: the task asks for a limit of at least 256Mi, and unlimited Pods can starve the node.

s2.recap: Raise resources.limits.memory to >= 256Mi, then recreate the Pod.
s2.explain: Exit 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL): the kernel killed the process because it exceeded its memory limit (OOMKilled). Restarting changes nothing; raise the limit above what the app needs (>= 256Mi). Keep requests <= limits, or the Pod is rejected.
s2.hint: Keep a small request, raise the LIMIT to at least what the cache needs: both under resources.

questions.title: A NotReady worker node
questions.scenario: Node 'node01' is NotReady. Walk from the cluster view down to the root cause on the node, then fix it.
questions.tip: The kubelet is NOT a Pod: it is a systemd service on the node. NotReady almost always means 'kubelet stopped talking to the API server'.
questions.stakes: A NotReady node quietly stops hosting your Pods after the eviction delay.
questions.analogy: The kubelet is the node's heartbeat: no pulse and the control plane writes it off.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show node01's Conditions and recent Events.

options.why: kubectl logs only works on Pods (and workload resources).
Needs metrics-server and a working kubelet - a NotReady node reports nothing.
Same table plus IPs and versions: no conditions, no events.

s1.explain: Start from the cluster view: 'Ready False' with 'Kubelet stopped posting node status' says the node's own agent stopped reporting. That tells you to go and look on the node.
s1.hint: describe on the Node shows its Conditions and recent Events.

context: Ready   Unknown   NodeStatusUnknown   Kubelet stopped posting node status.
s2.prompt: Step 2 - ssh to node01: check whether the kubelet service is running.

options.why: The unit is called 'kubelet'.
The kubelet is a systemd service on the node, not a Pod.
kubectl is a client CLI, not a service.

s2.explain: The control-plane components are static Pods, but the kubelet and the container runtime run as systemd services, so a dead kubelet is checked with systemctl, not with kubectl.
s2.hint: The kubelet is a systemd service: ask systemd for its state.

context: ● kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Read the last 50 kubelet log lines (no pager).

options.why: There is no kubelet Pod to read logs from.
A unit is selected with -u.
On systemd hosts (kubeadm installs) the kubelet logs to journald.

s3.explain: The status tells you it is down, the journal tells you why. journalctl -u <unit> is the tool for every systemd component: kubelet, containerd, ...
s3.hint: journalctl for one unit, the last N lines, without a pager.

context: Stopped kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent.
s4.prompt: Step 4 - The service was stopped and disabled. Start it now AND make it survive a reboot.

options.why: Starts it now, but it stays disabled: after a reboot the node is NotReady again.
Survives a reboot, but is not started right now.
Destroys the node's cluster state: a very drastic, unneeded step.

s4.explain: The service was stopped AND disabled: a plain start would be undone by the next reboot. 'enable --now' does both. Confirm with 'kubectl get nodes' from the control plane.
s4.hint: systemctl can enable a unit for boot and start it now in a single command.

questions.title: Pods cannot resolve Service names
questions.scenario: Pods report 'bad address' when resolving Service names. Test DNS, inspect CoreDNS, then fix its configuration.
questions.tip: CoreDNS Pods carry the label k8s-app=kube-dns and live in kube-system. Their config is the 'coredns' ConfigMap (the Corefile).
questions.stakes: DNS down makes every Service call fail, so it looks as if everything is broken.
questions.analogy: DNS is the phone book: the phones work, but nobody can call by name.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - From a throw-away busybox:1.28 Pod named 'dnstest', resolve kubernetes.default. The Pod must vanish afterwards and its output must be shown.

options.why: Without -it --rm you see no output and the Pod stays behind (Completed).
Assumes a Pod 'dnstest' already exists.
ping tests ICMP, and Service IPs are virtual and do not answer it. nslookup/dig test DNS itself.

s1.explain: Test from where the problem is: a Pod inside the cluster. --rm -it --restart=Never is the standard throw-away debug Pod. Use busybox:1.28: newer busybox says NXDOMAIN for 'kubernetes.default' even when DNS works. 'bad address' means the lookup failed.
s1.hint: kubectl run with --rm and an interactive TTY shows the output and deletes the Pod; busybox 1.28 has a reliable nslookup.

context: ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Read the logs of the CoreDNS Pods.

options.why: No Pod is named exactly 'coredns' (names carry a random suffix); select by label instead.
Missing '-n kube-system': it would search the current namespace.
kubeadm labels CoreDNS Pods k8s-app=kube-dns, even though they are named coredns.

s2.explain: Cluster DNS is served by the CoreDNS Pods (label k8s-app=kube-dns): their logs say whether queries fail or the upstream is unreachable. Selecting by label avoids looking up the Pod names.
s2.hint: CoreDNS Pods carry the historical label k8s-app=kube-dns in kube-system: logs can select by label.

context: [ERROR] plugin/errors: 2 HINFO: read udp 10.244.0.5:40841->10.255.255.1:53: i/o timeout
s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system': upstream queries go to a dead IP. Type the right line in place of the broken 'forward' line.

checks.msg: Use 'forward . /etc/resolv.conf'.
Do not remove the 'kubernetes' plugin: it serves the cluster domain.

forbid.msg: The dead upstream 10.255.255.1 is still configured.

options.why: Works only with Internet access and bypasses the node's DNS settings (internal domains break). The task asks for the node's resolver file.
Missing the zone: the syntax is 'forward FROM TO...', and FROM '.' means every name.
The 'proxy' plugin was removed from CoreDNS long ago; 'forward' replaced it.

s3.recap: Change 'forward . 10.255.255.1' to 'forward . /etc/resolv.conf' (the 'reload' plugin applies it).
s3.explain: CoreDNS answers cluster names itself (the 'kubernetes' plugin) and sends everything else to 'forward'. '. /etc/resolv.conf' hands those queries to the node's own resolvers; a dead IP there breaks every lookup that leaves the cluster. 'reload' applies the change within ~2 minutes, or restart the Deployment.
s3.hint: Forward upstream queries to the node's own resolvers: the file the kubelet gives CoreDNS.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Saved. Make CoreDNS pick up the fixed Corefile now, the declarative way.

options.cmd: kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system
aliases: kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment coredns

options.cmd: kubectl rollout restart deployment kube-dns -n kube-system
options.why: kube-dns is the SERVICE's name; the Deployment is called coredns: 'deployments.apps "kube-dns" not found'.
Deletes the configuration itself: new CoreDNS Pods cannot even mount it and DNS goes down for good.
A Corefile is CoreDNS syntax, not a Kubernetes manifest: kubectl cannot parse it.

s4.explain: The kubeadm Corefile has the 'reload' plugin, which picks up a changed ConfigMap after a while on its own. A rollout restart applies it at once, Pod by Pod, so DNS never fully stops; deleting Pods by hand would work too, less gracefully.
s4.hint: Restart the Deployment's Pods one by one; mind its real name.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Repeat the test of step 1: the throw-away dnstest Pod must now resolve kubernetes.default.

options.why: Logs show CoreDNS started, not that a Pod's lookup now succeeds end to end.
Runs on your host, with the host's resolvers: they know nothing about cluster names.
Without --rm -it you see no output and the Pod stays behind: the next run fails with AlreadyExists.

s5.explain: Test the way users hit it: a fresh Pod uses the cluster DNS through kube-dns. 'Address 1: 10.96.0.1 kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local' closes the incident; testing the same way as before the fix makes before/after comparable.
s5.hint: Same throw-away Pod, same lookup as at the start.

questions.title: A Deployment stuck in ImagePullBackOff
questions.scenario: Deployment 'api' (namespace default, container 'api') was just updated and its new Pod never starts. The intended image is nginx:1.27.
questions.tip: ImagePullBackOff = the kubelet cannot pull: wrong name/tag, private registry without imagePullSecrets, or no network. The exact reason is in the Events of 'describe pod'.
questions.stakes: A tag typo leaves the rollout at zero healthy replicas.
questions.analogy: Like ordering with the wrong product code: the store has no such item.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the Events that explain why the image cannot be pulled.

options.why: The container was never created, so there are no logs: kubectl only answers 'waiting to start: trying and failing to pull image'.
Adds the node and IP columns, but no events and no pull error.
A container that never started uses no resources and has no metrics.

s1.explain: ImagePullBackOff has several causes and the event tells them apart: 'not found' = wrong name or tag, 'unauthorized' = credentials, a timeout = network. The Events show the full error returned by the runtime.
s1.hint: Pull errors are events of the Pod: describe it.

context: Normal   Pulling  kubelet  spec.containers{api}: Pulling image "nginx:1.277"
Warning  Failed   kubelet  spec.containers{api}: Failed to pull image "nginx:1.277": rpc error: code = NotFound
desc = failed to pull and unpack image "docker.io/library/nginx:1.277": failed to resolve image:
Warning  Failed   kubelet  spec.containers{api}: Error: ErrImagePull
Warning  Failed   kubelet  spec.containers{api}: Error: ImagePullBackOff
s2.prompt: Step 2 - The tag is a typo. Fix the Deployment so its container 'api' uses nginx:1.27, without editing YAML.

aliases: kubectl set image deployment api api=nginx:1.27

options.why: The part before '=' is the CONTAINER name, which is 'api' here: kubectl fails with 'unable to find container named nginx'.
'set image' has no --image flag: it takes CONTAINER=IMAGE pairs.
