Patches only this one Pod: the Deployment template still says nginx:1.277, so every replacement Pod breaks again.

s2.explain: The cause is the tag, so fix the Deployment, not the Pod: 'set image' edits the Pod template, which starts a new rollout and replaces the broken Pod. 'kubectl edit deployment api' would work too.
s2.hint: set image takes CONTAINER=IMAGE on the deployment.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Wait until the new rollout has completed (or report that it failed).

options.why: Lists the stored revisions; it does not wait for or report on the current rollout.
rollout status only works on Deployments, DaemonSets and StatefulSets, and this Pod is being replaced anyway.
Triggers yet another rollout; it does not tell you whether the current one succeeded.

s3.explain: A fix is not proven until the rollout finishes: rollout status blocks until all new replicas are available and exits non-zero if the progress deadline is exceeded.
s3.hint: One rollout subcommand blocks until the rollout succeeds or fails.

questions.title: Pods Pending: Insufficient cpu
questions.scenario: The 3 Pods of Deployment 'batch' (namespace default) stay Pending. The team confirms the app needs only 500m of CPU.
questions.tip: The scheduler packs Pods by REQUESTS, not by real usage: compare the Pod's requests with the node's Allocatable minus 'Allocated resources'.

docs.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

questions.stakes: Pending Pods are lost capacity, and adding nodes does not help if requests are oversized.
questions.analogy: Requests are reserved seats: a theatre can look empty and be fully booked.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Find the scheduler's message for one of the Pending Pods.

options.why: A Pending Pod was never placed on a node: no container ran, so there are no logs.
The Deployment's events only say it scaled its ReplicaSet; the FailedScheduling event is attached to the Pod.
NODE is simply <none>: the table does not say why.

s1.explain: FailedScheduling events say, per node, why it was rejected: taints, selectors/affinity or 'Insufficient cpu/memory'. Here the answer is a resource problem, not a taint.
s1.hint: The scheduler's message is a FailedScheduling event on the Pod.

context: Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s)
had untolerated taint(s). preemption: 0/3 nodes are available: 2 No preemption victims found for
incoming pod, 1 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Show node01's Allocatable CPU and how much is already requested by other Pods.

options.why: Shows REAL usage. The scheduler ignores usage and adds up the requests ('Allocated resources' in describe).
Labels say nothing about capacity or what is already requested.
Adds IPs, OS and runtime versions: no capacity, no allocated requests.

s2.explain: The scheduler places Pods by REQUESTS, not by real usage. Compare 'Allocatable: cpu' with 'Allocated resources: cpu requests': the difference is what a new Pod may request.
s2.hint: describe on the Node shows Allocatable and the 'Allocated resources' table.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Each worker has 1400m free, each Pod requests 1500m. In 'kubectl edit deployment batch', type the resources block with a CPU request of 500m (keep the rest). Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'requests:' must stay a child of 'resources:'.
requests.cpu must be 500m (2 more spaces than 'requests:').
Keep 'memory: 256Mi' under requests.
Keep the limits (cpu "2").

forbid.msg: The 1500m request is still there.

options.why: Without the 'm' suffix, 500 means 500 CPU cores: bigger than the limit (rejected) and than any node.
The scheduler looks at requests, not limits. And a request (1500m) above its limit (500m) is rejected by the API.
With no requests block, requests default to the limits: the Pod would now request a full 2 CPUs and still not fit.

s3.recap: Lower resources.requests.cpu from 1500m to 500m in the Pod template; saving 'kubectl edit' rolls out new Pods.
s3.explain: Each Pod asks 1500m but a worker has only 1400m free, so none fits. With a request of 500m, 2 Pods per worker (1000m) fit and all 3 replicas schedule. If requests cannot change, scale down ('kubectl scale') or add nodes.
s3.hint: Lower only the CPU request; keep memory request and both limits as they were.

questions.title: A Pod Pending because of a forgotten taint
questions.scenario: Pod 'monitor' (namespace default) is Pending. The cluster has one control-plane node and one worker, node01, whose maintenance window ended yesterday.
questions.tip: Before adding a toleration, ask whether the taint is intentional. A leftover maintenance taint must be removed; a deliberate reservation calls for a toleration.
questions.stakes: The Pod stays Pending while nodes sit idle behind a forgotten taint.
questions.analogy: A 'reserved' sign on every table.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the scheduler's reason for leaving 'monitor' Pending.

options.why: The Pod was never scheduled: no container ran, so there are no logs.

options.cmd: kubectl get pod monitor -o yaml | grep nodeName
options.why: nodeName is empty for a Pending Pod; it does not say why.
The static Pod is named kube-scheduler-<node>; and the per-Pod reason is published as a Pod event anyway.

s1.explain: The FailedScheduling event names the check that rejected each node: here '2 node(s) had untolerated taint(s)'. Recent releases no longer print the taints themselves, so it sends you to the nodes' taints.
s1.hint: The scheduler's reason is an event of the Pending Pod.

context: Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler  0/2 nodes are available: 2 node(s) had untolerated
taint(s). preemption: 0/2 nodes are available: 2 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Display the taints currently set on node01.

options.cmd: kubectl describe node node01 | grep -i taints
aliases: kubectl describe node node01 | grep Taints
kubectl describe nodes node01 | grep -i taints

options.why: Labels and taints are different things: taints live in spec.taints and are not shown here.
Taints are not a resource type; they are a field of the Node object.

options.cmd: kubectl describe pod monitor | grep -i taints
options.why: A Pod has tolerations, not taints: the taints are on the node.

s2.explain: The event blames a taint, so list the taints: 'describe node' shows a 'Taints:' line (more taints continue on the following lines); the raw field is spec.taints.
s2.hint: describe the node and filter the Taints line (case-insensitive).

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The taint is a leftover: the maintenance is over. Choose the right fix and type it.

options.why: uncordon only removes the 'unschedulable' flag (node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable taint); the custom maintenance taint stays.
Opens the control plane to regular workloads instead of removing the forgotten taint on node01.
A toleration would let this one Pod in, but node01 would stay closed to every other workload: the leftover taint is the real bug.

s3.explain: A trailing '-' removes a taint. A toleration is the answer only when the taint is intentional (a dedicated or reserved node). The Pending Pod schedules by itself once the taint is gone.
s3.hint: Remove the leftover taint from the NODE: same key=value:effect with a trailing minus.

questions.title: A nodeSelector that matches no node
questions.scenario: Pod 'ssd-app' (manifest pod.yaml, namespace default) must run on an SSD node but stays Pending. The node labels are the reference: do not change them.
questions.tip: Label keys and values are case-sensitive. 'kubectl get nodes --show-labels' (or '-L key' for one column) shows what selectors can match.
questions.stakes: A label typo and the Pod is Pending forever, with no message in the app.
questions.analogy: Dialling a number nobody owns: the FailedScheduling event is the busy tone.

context: Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's
node affinity/selector, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s). preemption: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 ...
s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the nodes together with all their labels.

options.why: Shows the POD's labels; the selector is matched against NODE labels.
The message is 'didn't match node affinity/selector': this is about labels, not taints.
There is no --labels flag: it is --show-labels (or -L KEY for chosen columns).

s1.explain: The scheduler places the Pod only on a node carrying EVERY key=value of its nodeSelector, so compare the selector with the real labels: it is an exact match.
s1.hint: get nodes can print every label of every node.

context: NAME           STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION   LABELS
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Fix the selector in pod.yaml so it matches node01's label: type the right line over the wrong one. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: The selector must be 'disktype: ssd' (lowercase), 4 spaces under 'nodeSelector:'.

forbid.msg: 'SSD' (uppercase) matches no node: label values are case-sensitive.

options.why: Quoting does not change the value: "SSD" is still uppercase and matches no node.
nodeSelector is a map of key: value; 'disktype=ssd' is a plain string and the API rejects the Pod.
The key is 'disktype' (no prefix): a different key matches no node.

s2.recap: Change the nodeSelector value from 'SSD' to 'ssd' to match the node label disktype=ssd.
s2.explain: Selectors compare strings exactly: 'SSD' != 'ssd'. The task says the node labels are the reference, so you fix the Pod. If the node were wrong, 'kubectl label nodes node01 disktype=ssd' would fix that side.
s2.hint: The selector's key must equal node01's label key and value exactly.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Make the cluster run the corrected Pod (a Pod's nodeSelector cannot be changed in place).

aliases: kubectl delete pod ssd-app && kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl delete pod ssd-app && kubectl create -f pod.yaml

options.why: Rejected: 'pod updates may not change fields other than image, activeDeadlineSeconds, tolerations...'.
Changes the reference label instead of the Pod: every other workload selecting disktype=ssd would lose node01.
rollout only works on Deployments, DaemonSets and StatefulSets, and would not read pod.yaml anyway.

s3.explain: A Pod's nodeSelector cannot be changed in place, so 'replace --force' deletes and recreates the Pod from the file in one command: the standard way to change immutable Pod fields.
s3.hint: nodeSelector is immutable on a Pod: replace it, forcing the delete and re-create.

questions.title: CrashLoopBackOff after a command change
questions.scenario: Deployment 'worker' (manifest deploy.yaml, namespace default) runs a small Python web server on port 8080. Since the last change its Pods crash-loop.
questions.tip: 'kubectl logs --previous' (-p) shows the output of the container instance that just crashed. 'command' replaces the image ENTRYPOINT, 'args' replaces CMD.
questions.stakes: A Pod that exits at once is restarted forever: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom, not a cause.
questions.analogy: A car that stalls right after the key turns: restarting just repeats it.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Read the output of the container instance that just crashed.

options.why: exec needs a RUNNING container; between crashes it is waiting in back-off, so exec fails.
describe has no --previous flag; --previous belongs to 'kubectl logs'.
Usage metrics say nothing about why the process exits.

s1.explain: A crash-looping container has just been restarted, so its current log is often empty. --previous reads the instance that crashed, which holds the error message.
s1.hint: logs of the Pod's previous container instance: the one that crashed.

context: python -m http.server: error: argument port: invalid int value: 'port=8080'
s2.prompt: Step 2 - The port is a positional argument. Type the corrected 'command' line over the broken one. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Use command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8080"] - one list item per argument.

forbid.msg: 'port=8080' is still there: the argument is just the number.

options.why: A single string is ONE argv entry: the runtime looks for an executable literally named 'python -m http.server 8080' (StartError).
http.server has no --port option ('unrecognized arguments: --port'): the port is positional.
Without -m, python tries to run a FILE named 'http.server': 'can't open file ... No such file or directory'.

s2.recap: Fix the command to ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8080"]: one list item per argument.
s2.explain: command is an exec-style list: each item is ONE argument, with no shell parsing, so the port must be its own item. Use ["sh", "-c", "..."] when you need a shell.
s2.hint: In exec form every argument is its own list item; the port is a separate positional argument.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Push the corrected manifest to the existing Deployment.

options.why: The Deployment already exists: create fails with AlreadyExists.
Restarts Pods from the template stored in the cluster, which still has the broken command: the file was never applied.
A client dry-run only prints what would happen; nothing is changed.

s3.explain: The change alters the Pod template, so a new ReplicaSet is created and the crash-looping Pods are replaced. Check with 'kubectl rollout status deployment/worker'.
s3.hint: Send the corrected file to the existing Deployment.

questions.title: A Pod waiting for a missing Secret
questions.scenario: Pod 'shop' (namespace default) is stuck in CreateContainerConfigError right after deployment.
questions.tip: CreateContainerConfigError = the kubelet cannot build the container's config: usually a missing ConfigMap/Secret or key referenced by env/envFrom. Create it and the kubelet retries by itself.
questions.stakes: The app never starts and its logs are empty, so you search in the wrong place.
questions.analogy: A recipe missing an ingredient: nothing cooks, so there is no smoke to see.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Find what the kubelet is missing to create the container.

options.why: The container was never created: kubectl answers 'waiting to start: CreateContainerConfigError'.
There is no previous instance either: the container never ran.
Lists the Secrets that exist, but not which one (or which key) the Pod needs.

s1.explain: CreateContainerConfigError means the kubelet could not even build the container's config, so no container ever ran and there are no logs. 'describe' shows the exact missing Secret or key in the Events.
s1.hint: The kubelet's complaint is an event of the Pod: describe it.

context: DB_PASSWORD:  <set to the key 'DB_PASSWORD' in secret 'shop-db'>  Optional: false
Warning  Failed  kubelet  spec.containers{shop}: Error: secret "shop-db" not found
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Create the missing Secret with key DB_PASSWORD and value Sup3rS3cret.

options.why: The Pod references a SECRET (secretKeyRef): a ConfigMap with the same name does not satisfy it.
'create secret' needs a sub-type: generic, tls or docker-registry.
--from-file reads a FILE named Sup3rS3cret; a literal value needs --from-literal.

s2.explain: The Pod references the Secret by name and key, so create it with exactly those. kubectl base64-encodes the value for you. Within seconds the kubelet retries and starts the container; the Pod needs no restart.
s2.hint: A generic Secret from a literal key=value, with the name the Pod expects.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Verify that the variable DB_PASSWORD is set inside the running container.

options.why: Your LOCAL shell expands $DB_PASSWORD (empty) before kubectl runs: the container just echoes an empty line.
Proves the Secret exists, not that the container received the variable.
Applications do not print their environment; the logs prove nothing.

s3.explain: Check the container, not the manifest: printenv runs inside it. For a shell expression, wrap it: sh -c 'echo $VAR' (single quotes keep your local shell from expanding it).
s3.hint: Print one environment variable from inside the container.

questions.title: A Service with no endpoints
questions.scenario: Service 'web' (namespace default) times out although its Pods are Running and Ready.
questions.tip: No endpoints = the selector matches no Ready Pod. Compare 'describe svc' (Selector) with 'get pods --show-labels'.
questions.stakes: 'Service up, app down': one typo in the selector and every request fails.
questions.analogy: A forwarding number that points at nobody.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the Service's selector and endpoints.

options.why: Shows type, ClusterIP and ports only; the selector appears with -o wide or in describe.
There is no Pod named 'web': Pod names carry ReplicaSet and random suffixes.
The ports are not the problem: no endpoint exists at all, which points at the selector.

s1.explain: Selector, TargetPort and Endpoints side by side: an empty 'Endpoints:' line while the Pods are Running means the selector matches no Ready Pod. That is your lead.
s1.hint: describe the Service: Selector and Endpoints are side by side.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - List the Pods with ALL their labels to compare with the selector.

options.why: Confirms that nothing matches ('No resources found') but does not show the labels the Pods really have.
describe has no --show-labels flag, and it would show the Service's labels anyway.
No such flag: it is --show-labels (or -L KEY).

s2.explain: A Pod becomes an endpoint only if it carries EVERY key=value of the Service selector, so compare the labels the Pods really have with the selector.
s2.hint: get pods can print every label of every Pod.

context: NAME                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   LABELS
s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'kubectl edit svc web': type the right selector over the wrong one. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: The selector must contain 'app: web' (4 spaces, directly under 'selector:').

forbid.msg: No Pod carries app=web-frontend.
A Service selector is a plain map: no matchLabels.
Never select on pod-template-hash: it changes with every rollout.

options.why: Service selectors are a plain key: value map (unlike Deployments): matchLabels is rejected.
Selector entries are ANDed: Pods would need app=web-frontend AND tier=frontend, so still nothing matches.
pod-template-hash changes on every rollout: the Service would lose all its endpoints at the next update.

s3.recap: Set the Service selector to app: web, a label the Pods really carry.
s3.explain: Unlike a Pod's nodeSelector, a Service's selector can be edited in place: the endpoints controller picks up the matching Pods within seconds. Use the label the Pods actually carry, not the one you wish they had.
s3.hint: The selector must match the Pods' real label key and value.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Confirm that the Service now has endpoints, using the EndpointSlice API.

options.why: EndpointSlices are named <service>-<random>: none is called exactly 'web'. Select them by the service-name label.
Shows the selector again, not whether Pods matched it.
Proves the Pods match the label, not that the Service picked them up.

s4.explain: Prove the fix with the endpoints, not with the YAML. EndpointSlices (label kubernetes.io/service-name) are the current API; the legacy 'kubectl get endpoints web' still works but v1 Endpoints is deprecated.
s4.hint: EndpointSlices point at their Service through a well-known label: select by it.

questions.title: Running but never Ready
questions.scenario: Deployment 'orders' (namespace default): all 3 Pods are Running with no restarts, but READY shows 0/1 and its Service has no endpoints.
questions.tip: A failing readinessProbe never restarts a container: it only keeps the Pod out of the Service endpoints. Restarts come from a failing livenessProbe.
questions.stakes: A Running but never Ready Pod gets no traffic: the 'healthy' deployment serves nothing.
questions.analogy: The shop is open, but the 'closed' sign is still on the door.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Find out why the Pods never become Ready.

options.why: RESTARTS is 0: there is no previous instance, kubectl reports 'previous terminated container not found'.
New Pods get the same probe and fail the same way: diagnose first.
Resource usage does not explain a NotReady container.

s1.explain: Running is not Ready: Ready is decided by the readiness probe. Probe failures appear as 'Unhealthy' events with the exact URL and error.
s1.hint: Readiness failures are events of the Pod: describe one of them.

context: Warning  Unhealthy  kubelet  spec.containers{orders}: Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.7:8080/healthz":
s2.prompt: Step 2 - 'kubectl edit deployment orders': the probe targets the wrong port. Type the corrected readinessProbe block over the old one. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Keep a readinessProbe with httpGet (2 more spaces).
The httpGet port must be the number 3000 (unquoted).
The path /healthz is correct: keep it.

forbid.msg: Port 8080 is still there: nothing listens on it.

options.why: Turning it into a livenessProbe removes the readiness gate: Pods receive traffic before they are ready. The task is to fix the probe, not change its kind.
A quoted "3000" is a STRING, i.e. a named port; a port name must contain a letter, so the API rejects it.
The error is 'connection refused' on 8080: nothing listens there, whatever the path. The port is the problem.

s2.recap: Point readinessProbe.httpGet.port at 3000, the port the app listens on.
s2.explain: The error tells which probe field is wrong: 'connection refused' = wrong port (nothing listens there); HTTP 404 = wrong path; a timeout = app too slow or timeoutSeconds too short.
s2.hint: The probe's port must be the one the app really listens on; keep path and period.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Block until the Deployment 'orders' is Available again (60 s timeout).

options.why: During a rollout the old Pods still match the label: the ones being replaced never become Ready, so this fails on them (exit 1) even though the fix worked.
Deployments have no Ready condition (they have Available and Progressing): this just times out.
--for needs a form like condition=NAME, delete or jsonpath=...; a bare 'Available' is rejected: unrecognized condition.

s3.explain: A Deployment is Available once enough Pods are Ready, which is true only after the fix has rolled out. Waiting on 'pod -l' also counts the old Pods still terminating, which never become Ready and fail the command. Ready Pods join the EndpointSlice.
s3.hint: kubectl wait blocks on a named condition of the Deployment, with a timeout.

questions.title: Roll back a stuck rollout
questions.scenario: Deployment 'payments' (namespace default) was updated to a new image; the rollout never finishes and the new Pods crash. Restore the last working version.
questions.tip: rollout history lists revisions (CHANGE-CAUSE comes from the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation); 'rollout undo' goes back one revision, '--to-revision=N' to a chosen one.
questions.stakes: A rollout stuck at 50 % leaves half your users on a broken version.
questions.analogy: Rollback is the undo button: know where it is before you need it.

context: Waiting for deployment "payments" rollout to finish: 1 out of 4 new replicas have been updated...
error: deployment "payments" exceeded its progress deadline
s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the revisions recorded for the Deployment.

options.why: There is no 'rollout list' sub-command: it is 'rollout history'.
'get' has no --revisions flag; revisions are read with 'rollout history'.
Prints the current progress once; it lists no revisions.

s1.explain: Each change to the Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet = a new revision, and the old ones are kept. The list tells you which revision was the last good one.
s1.hint: The rollout command family lists recorded revisions.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Before rolling back, display the Pod template stored in revision 2.

options.why: --to-revision is a flag of 'rollout undo'; history uses --revision.
'get' always returns the CURRENT object; it has no --revision flag.
ReplicaSets are named <deployment>-<pod-template-hash>, not by revision number.

s2.explain: Check before you roll back: --revision=N prints that revision's Pod template (image, env, labels), so you restore the version you really want and not just 'the previous one'.
s2.hint: The same history subcommand can show the Pod template of one revision.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Revision 2 is the last good one. Roll the Deployment back to it.

options.why: Revision 3 is the broken 2.0.0 release that is currently being rolled out.
Restarts Pods from the CURRENT (broken) template: they keep crashing.
Freezes the rollout halfway: the broken Pods stay and nothing is rolled back.

s3.explain: Undo copies the old template into a NEW revision, so the history is never rewritten: the chosen revision comes back as the newest one. Confirm with 'kubectl rollout status deployment/payments'.
s3.hint: undo can go to a specific revision number.

questions.title: A Pod stuck in Init:0/1
questions.scenario: Pod 'shop-api' (namespace default) has an init container 'wait-db' that waits until the name 'db' resolves; the main container 'api' never starts.
questions.tip: Init containers run one by one, each to completion, before the app containers. Read them with 'kubectl logs POD -c INIT_CONTAINER'.
questions.stakes: A stuck init container blocks the whole Pod, and plain 'logs' shows nothing useful.
questions.analogy: The stagehand has not finished, so the show cannot start.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Read the logs of the init container.

options.why: Defaults to the app container 'api', which has not started: 'waiting to start: PodInitializing'.
wait-db is a CONTAINER of the Pod shop-api, not a Pod: select it with -c.
There is no --init-container flag: init containers are selected with -c like any other container.

s1.explain: Init:0/1 = zero of one init containers have finished, so the main container waits. The init container's logs say what it is waiting for.
s1.hint: logs can target a container by name, including an init container.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The name 'db' does not resolve. Check whether a Service 'db' exists in this namespace.

options.why: Cluster DNS names come from Services, not Pods (and Pod names carry suffixes).
Runs on your workstation with its own resolver, not with cluster DNS: proves nothing about the cluster.
The init container resolves 'db' in its OWN namespace (default), not in kube-system.

s2.explain: The init loop waits for the name 'db', so check what should answer it: a Service 'db' in namespace default gets db.default.svc.cluster.local, and Pods in the same namespace can use just 'db'.
s2.hint: Look for the Service by name in the current namespace.

context: Error from server (NotFound): services "db" not found
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Write the missing Service: type the selector and ports in place of the TODO (then 'kubectl apply -f db-svc.yaml'). Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: select the db Pods and expose port 5432

checks.msg: The selector must be 'app: db' (4 spaces under 'selector:').
ports is a LIST: each entry starts with '- '.
Expose port 5432.

forbid.msg: The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.
A Service selector is a plain map: no matchLabels.
The database container listens on 5432.

target: # TODO: select the db Pods and expose port 5432

options.why: A Service selector is a plain key: value map; matchLabels is only for Deployments, ReplicaSets, Jobs...
The db Pods are labelled app=db, not name=db: this selector matches nothing and the Service has no endpoints.
ports is a list: without '- ' it is a map and the API rejects the Service.

s3.recap: Create Service 'db' with selector app: db and port 5432; the init container then completes by itself.
s3.explain: As soon as the name resolves, the init container's loop ends, it exits 0 and the kubelet starts 'api' (Init:0/1 -> PodInitializing -> Running). 'kubectl expose deployment db --port=5432' would do the same imperatively.
s3.hint: A Service needs a selector matching the database Pods' label and a port to its container port.

questions.title: Logs of a multi-container Pod
questions.scenario: Pod 'web' (namespace default) has two containers: 'nginx' and a sidecar 'log-shipper' that stopped forwarding logs.
questions.tip: Without -c, kubectl logs picks the default (first) container and says so. -f follows, --tail=N limits lines, --since=10m limits time, --all-containers reads them all.
questions.stakes: 'logs' without -c reads the wrong container, and you debug a healthy sidecar.
questions.analogy: A house with two meters: read the right one.

context: Defaulted container "nginx" out of: nginx, log-shipper
s1.prompt: Step 1 - That was nginx. Show the logs of the sidecar container instead.

options.why: TYPE/NAME syntax: kubectl reads 'web' as a resource type and fails.
log-shipper is a container, not a Pod: the Pod is 'web'.
That is the default behaviour: you still get only the nginx container.

s1.explain: Without -c, 'kubectl logs' picks the default container of the Pod, here nginx, not the sidecar. -c / --container selects the one you mean.
s1.hint: With several containers, logs needs the container's name.

context: level=warn msg="output elasticsearch: connection refused, retrying in 30s"
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Stream the sidecar's logs live, starting with its last 20 lines.

options.why: -n is --namespace: kubectl looks for the Pod in a namespace called '20'.
kubectl logs has no --watch flag (that is for 'get'): follow with -f / --follow.
--lines is a journalctl option; kubectl logs uses --tail=N.

s2.explain: -f keeps the stream open (Ctrl+C to quit); --tail=20 starts with the last 20 lines instead of the whole history. Watching live shows whether the sidecar is stuck now or only logged an old error.
s2.hint: Follow the stream, starting from the last N lines.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Show the logs of the last 10 minutes from BOTH containers in one command.

options.why: There is no container named 'all': the flag is --all-containers.
--since-time expects an RFC3339 timestamp (2026-10-31T09:00:00Z); a relative duration goes in --since.
No --containers flag exists: use --all-containers.

s3.explain: One command for both containers lets you correlate events in time. Add --prefix to tag each line with [pod/web/container]. --since takes a Go duration: 30s, 10m, 1h.
s3.hint: logs can include every container of the Pod and limit to a duration.

questions.title: Pods that never finish terminating
questions.scenario: Pod 'legacy' (namespace default) has been Terminating for 25 minutes. The operator that used to manage it was uninstalled last week.
questions.tip: Terminating forever: either a finalizer nobody removes (patch it away) or a node that is gone (force delete). --force does NOT bypass finalizers.
questions.stakes: A namespace stuck Terminating blocks the release and the clean-up.
questions.analogy: A finalizer is a 'do not demolish until I sign off' sticker, and the signer has left.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Print only the finalizers of Pod 'legacy'.

options.why: Object finalizers live in metadata.finalizers (only Namespaces also have a spec.finalizers list).
Finalizers are not a resource type; they are a metadata field of the object.
logs reads container output; there is no --finalizers flag.

s1.explain: While metadata.finalizers is not empty, the API server keeps the object (deletionTimestamp set) and waits for the controller that owns each entry to clear it. The list shows who is blocking.
s1.hint: Finalizers live in metadata: print that list with jsonpath.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The controller for that finalizer no longer exists. Remove the finalizers so the deletion completes.

options.why: Force deletion skips the graceful wait, but the API server still keeps an object until its finalizers list is empty.
Pods have no spec.finalizers: the finalizers are in metadata.
Finalizers are not annotations: this removes nothing.

s2.explain: The finalizer's owner (the uninstalled operator) will never clear it, so the Pod would stay forever. Removing it by hand skips the cleanup it stood for: only do it when its controller is truly gone.
s2.hint: A merge patch setting the finalizers list to null clears it; the deletion then completes.

context: NAME      READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE   IP            NODE
(node02 is powered off and NotReady; cache-0 has no finalizers)
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Another Pod waits for a kubelet that will never answer. Remove it from the API immediately.

options.why: --now means a 1-second grace period: the API server still waits for the dead kubelet to confirm.
Without --force, kubectl turns a grace period of 0 into 1: still a graceful delete that waits for the kubelet.
--cascade is about dependent objects; the Pod still waits for its kubelet.

s3.explain: Force deletion removes the object from etcd without the kubelet's confirmation. For StatefulSet Pods make sure the node is really down: two Pods with the same identity could otherwise run.
s3.hint: Skip the grace period and force the removal from the API (the node will never confirm).

questions.title: Find the right events fast
questions.scenario: Something is failing in namespace 'shop'. Use events to find what, without scrolling through hundreds of lines.
questions.tip: Events are not sorted by default and expire after 1 hour. --sort-by=.lastTimestamp orders them; --field-selector filters on involvedObject.name, reason or type.
questions.stakes: Events vanish after about an hour: read them while the problem is fresh.
questions.analogy: Events are the cluster's diary, with a short memory.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the events of namespace 'shop', oldest first and newest last.

options.why: There is no --sort flag; --sort-by takes a JSONPath such as .lastTimestamp.
'describe' has no --sort-by flag: sorting is a 'get' feature.
No --reverse flag exists: the newest events already come last.

s1.explain: Events have no useful order by default. --sort-by=.lastTimestamp puts the newest last, where the problem usually is. --sort-by works on any 'get' list.
s1.hint: Events can be sorted by a field path: the last time each one happened.

context: LAST SEEN   TYPE      REASON      OBJECT                              MESSAGE
2m          Warning   BackOff     pod/checkout-7d9f8c6b5-k2xpl        Back-off restarting failed container
1m          Normal    Pulled      pod/cart-5c6d7b8f9-m4wq7            Container image already present
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Show only the events about Pod checkout-7d9f8c6b5-k2xpl.

options.why: -l filters on LABELS; involvedObject.name is a field, so this returns 'No resources found'.
Looks for an EVENT object with that name (event names carry a suffix): NotFound.
'pod' is not a supported field: event field selectors use involvedObject.name, involvedObject.kind, reason, type...

s2.explain: Events about one object cut the noise. 'kubectl describe pod NAME' shows them at the bottom too, but a field selector works for any kind of object.
s2.hint: A field selector on the involved object's name keeps one object's events.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Now list only Warning events, across ALL namespaces.

options.why: Without -A it only covers the current namespace.
type is a field, not a label: -l finds nothing.
--types belongs to the newer 'kubectl events' command, not to 'kubectl get events'.

s3.explain: Warning events are the failures, Normal ones are routine, and -A finds problems in any namespace at once. 'kubectl events -A --types=Warning' is the equivalent dedicated command. Events are kept only about an hour.
s3.hint: A field selector on the event type, across every namespace.

questions.title: Find the hungriest Pod
questions.scenario: The cluster is short on memory. Find the Pod using the most memory in the whole cluster and record its name in /opt/course/top-pod.txt. metrics-server is installed and working.
questions.tip: kubectl top shows REAL usage (from metrics-server); describe node shows REQUESTS. --sort-by accepts cpu or memory.
questions.stakes: One hungry Pod starves the node, and 'top' finds it in seconds if you sort.
questions.analogy: Like checking which app drains your phone battery.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the Pods of ALL namespaces sorted by memory usage.

options.why: Without -A only the current namespace is listed.
'get' sorts by a JSONPath field of the object; live usage is not stored in Pod objects.
Shows capacity and REQUESTS, not what each Pod really uses.

s1.explain: 'top' reads live metrics (metrics-server), and --sort-by=memory puts the biggest consumer first. -A covers every namespace, which the task requires.
s1.hint: kubectl top for Pods, in every namespace, sorted by memory.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Write the name of that Pod (name only) to /opt/course/top-pod.txt.

options.why: The task asks for the name only: an automated grader compares the exact string.
That is the Deployment name; the task asks for the Pod name.
Writes the whole table with headers, not the single Pod name.

s2.explain: Tasks like this are graded by reading the file: write exactly what is asked (the name only), nothing more. Double-check with 'cat'.
s2.hint: Write just the Pod name into the file with a shell redirect.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Which node is the busiest? List the nodes sorted by CPU usage.

options.why: Nodes are cluster-scoped: 'top node' has no -A/--all-namespaces flag and rejects it.
describe has no --sort-by flag and shows requests, not usage.
Lists containers per Pod, not node totals.

s3.explain: The same tool works for nodes: CPU(cores), CPU(%), MEMORY(bytes) and MEMORY(%) are relative to each node's allocatable, so you see which node is closest to its limit.
s3.hint: kubectl top for nodes, sorted by CPU.

questions.title: The API server is gone after an edit
questions.scenario: A colleague edited /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml on 'controlplane'. Since then kubectl cannot connect. Find out why without kubectl, then fix the manifest.
questions.tip: When the API server is down, kubectl is blind: go to the node and use crictl (ps -a, logs). Back up a manifest before editing it - but never inside /etc/kubernetes/manifests.
questions.stakes: One typo in the manifest and kubectl itself is dead: the fix lives in files and crictl.
questions.analogy: You sawed off the branch you were sitting on.

context: The connection to the server 172.30.1.2:6443 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?
s1.prompt: Step 1 - ssh to controlplane: list the kube-apiserver containers, including the exited ones.

options.why: kubectl talks to the API server - the very thing that is down.
kubeadm clusters run containerd since dockershim was removed (v1.24): there is no docker daemon.
Lists pulled images, not containers or their state.

s1.explain: kubectl is dead, but crictl talks to the container runtime through the CRI socket, so it still works. -a includes Exited containers: a crash-looping API server is rarely Running when you look.
s1.hint: kubectl is down: ask the container runtime, including exited containers, filtered by name.

context: CONTAINER      IMAGE          CREATED          STATE    NAME             ATTEMPT   POD ID         POD
3f2a1b9c8d7e   c3994bc69631   15 seconds ago   Exited   kube-apiserver   6         b81d4e2f0a93   kube-apiserver-controlplane
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Read what the crashed container printed before exiting.

options.why: kubectl logs is served by the API server: it cannot work while the API server is down.
In a kubeadm cluster kube-apiserver is a static Pod, not a systemd unit: there is no such journal unit.
Prints the container's JSON status and spec (exit code, mounts...), not the program's output.

s2.explain: The crashed container's last output usually names the bad flag. crictl logs works on exited containers too, until the kubelet garbage-collects them.
s2.hint: crictl prints a container's output by its ID, even after it exited.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml': type the corrected line in place of the misspelled flag.

checks.msg: The line must read '    - --advertise-address=172.30.1.2'.

forbid.msg: The misspelled flag --advertise-addres is still there.

options.why: Without the leading '--' it is a positional argument, and kube-apiserver refuses any argument that is not a flag.
'flag: value' turns the list item into a YAML map: command must be a list of strings, so the manifest no longer decodes.
The flag takes an IP address only; the port is set by --secure-port. '172.30.1.2:6443' is not a valid IP.

s3.recap: Fix the typo '--advertise-addres' -> '--advertise-address=172.30.1.2'; the kubelet recreates the static Pod on save.
s3.explain: The fix goes in the static Pod manifest: the kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests and recreates the Pod when the file changes. Give it 30-60 s, then 'kubectl get nodes' should answer again.
s3.hint: Correct the flag's spelling; keep the same value and indentation.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - The kubelet noticed the changed manifest. On controlplane, check that a NEW kube-apiserver container is Running.

options.why: The API server is a static Pod, not a systemd service: 'Unit kube-apiserver.service not found'.
That is the OLD crashed container: you read the same error again, not the new container's state.
Lists images on disk: present all along, they say nothing about a running container.

s4.explain: The kubelet recreates a static Pod whenever its manifest changes. A new container ID with STATE Running and a growing uptime (no new exits) means the flag is accepted; kubectl will follow within seconds.
s4.hint: Ask the container runtime about the API server's containers.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Back on your terminal: check that kubectl can talk to the cluster again.

options.why: --client never contacts the server: it succeeds even with the API server down.
Prints your local kubeconfig file: no request reaches the cluster.
Plain HTTP on the TLS port: the server answers 'Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server', which proves nothing about kubectl.

s5.explain: Any real request through your kubeconfig proves the whole chain: TLS, authentication, the API server and etcd behind it. Nodes listed again closes the incident.
s5.hint: Any kubectl command that must reach the API server.

questions.title: New Pods are never scheduled
questions.scenario: Every new Pod stays Pending: no node assigned and not a single event. Existing Pods keep running. Find the broken component and fix its manifest.
questions.tip: Pending with NO events at all means no scheduler looked at the Pod. Pending WITH a 'FailedScheduling' event means the scheduler ran but found no node.
questions.stakes: No scheduler: Pods stay Pending with no events at all, which is eerie.
questions.analogy: A hotel full of guests and nobody handing out room keys.

context: NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP       NODE     NOMINATED NODE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Check the control-plane Pods.

options.why: In a kubeadm cluster the scheduler is a static Pod run by the kubelet, not a systemd service.
The Pod was never scheduled: no container ever started, so there are no logs.
Control-plane static Pods live in kube-system, not in default.

s1.explain: Control-plane static Pods appear in kube-system as mirror Pods named <component>-<node>, e.g. kube-scheduler-controlplane. Pending with NO events at all means no scheduler looked at the Pod, so check it first.
s1.hint: The control-plane Pods live in kube-system: list them and look at STATUS and RESTARTS.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The API server works: read the scheduler Pod's logs with kubectl.

options.why: Static mirror Pods are suffixed with the node name: the Pod is kube-scheduler-controlplane.
Missing '-n kube-system': kubectl looks in the current namespace (default).
There is no kube-scheduler systemd unit: it runs in a container.

s2.explain: Because the API server works, kubectl logs works for static Pods too: the kubelet serves their container logs. The scheduler's log names what it cannot load.
s2.hint: logs of the scheduler's static Pod, named after the node, in kube-system.

context: E1031 09:12:44.512331       1 run.go:72] "command failed" err="stat /etc/kubernetes/schedulr.conf: no such file or directory"
s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml': type the corrected --kubeconfig line in place of the broken one.

checks.msg: The scheduler must use '--kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf'.

forbid.msg: The misspelled path schedulr.conf is still there.

options.why: admin.conf is not mounted into the scheduler container (only scheduler.conf is), and it is the cluster-admin identity, not the scheduler's.
--config expects a KubeSchedulerConfiguration file, not a kubeconfig - and the scheduler would still have no --kubeconfig.
Not mounted in the container, and '~' is not expanded: no shell runs the command list.

s3.recap: Fix --kubeconfig to /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf; Pending Pods get scheduled as soon as the scheduler is back.
s3.explain: Each control-plane component has its own kubeconfig in /etc/kubernetes (scheduler.conf, controller-manager.conf) mounted via hostPath. The kubelet restarts the static Pod on save; the Pending Pods are then scheduled without any action.
s3.hint: The scheduler's credentials file sits next to admin.conf; fix the flag's path.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - The kubelet restarts the scheduler when its manifest changes. Check its Pod, selected by label.

options.why: kubeadm runs the scheduler as a static Pod, not a Deployment: NotFound.
Without '-n kube-system' you search the current namespace: 'No resources found'.
There is no kube-scheduler service on a kubeadm node: 'Unit kube-scheduler.service could not be found'.

s4.explain: Static control-plane Pods carry the label component=<name>. Running with a fresh AGE and no new restarts means the corrected kubeconfig path works and the scheduler has taken its leader lease again.
s4.hint: Control-plane static Pods carry a 'component' label.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Check that the Pods that were Pending now have a node assigned.

options.why: The node's view: its own Pods and capacity, not whether the Pending Pods were placed.
Shows CPU and memory usage; a Pod never scheduled has no metrics and the NODE is not shown.
Looks in kube-system, where nothing was waiting: your Pending Pods are in the current namespace.

s5.explain: The scheduler works through the backlog of unscheduled Pods: each gets a NODE and a 'Scheduled' event. If one stays Pending now, its events show an ordinary reason (resources, affinity) instead of the earlier silence.
s5.hint: The wide output adds the node each Pod was assigned to.

questions.title: A Deployment that creates nothing
questions.scenario: 'kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --replicas=3' succeeded, but no ReplicaSet and no Pod ever appear. Find the component that should react and fix it.
questions.tip: Deployment -> ReplicaSet -> Pods is the controller-manager's work; Pod -> node is the scheduler's. 'No ReplicaSet' points at the controller-manager.
questions.stakes: The Deployment exists but never creates Pods: nobody reads the order tickets.
questions.analogy: An order written down, and nobody in the kitchen reads tickets.

context: No resources found in default namespace.
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Check the Pod of the component that turns Deployments into ReplicaSets (select it by label).

options.why: The scheduler only places existing Pods on nodes; here not even a ReplicaSet was created.
Only changes the Pod template; with no controller running, nothing acts on it either.
The kubelet is a systemd service, not a Pod - and it only runs Pods already bound to its node.

s1.explain: Deployments are turned into ReplicaSets and Pods by kube-controller-manager, so a Deployment that creates nothing points at it. kubeadm labels its static Pods component=<name> and tier=control-plane.
s1.hint: Deployments are reconciled by the controller manager; static Pods carry a component=<name> label.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Show the logs of the previous (crashed) run of that Pod's container.

options.why: It is a static Pod managed by the kubelet, not a Deployment: deploy/kube-controller-manager does not exist.
There is no kube-controller-manager systemd unit in a kubeadm cluster.
Shows the Deployment's spec and events - and no controller has written any event for it.

s2.explain: --previous (-p) shows the output of the last terminated container: in a CrashLoopBackOff the current one may not have printed anything yet.
s2.hint: logs of the PREVIOUS container instance of that Pod, in kube-system.

context: E1031 09:20:11.428339       1 run.go:72] "command failed" err="unable to load client CA provider: open /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crtt: no such file or directory"
s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml': type the corrected --client-ca-file line over the broken one.

checks.msg: --client-ca-file must point to the cluster CA certificate /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt.

forbid.msg: The misspelled path ca.crtt is still there.

options.why: ca.key is the CA's PRIVATE key; a client CA file must contain the CA certificate.
apiserver.crt is the API server's serving certificate, not the CA that signs client certificates.
/root is not mounted into the container: only /etc/kubernetes/pki (and a few others) are hostPath volumes.

s3.recap: Fix --client-ca-file to /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt; the controller-manager then creates the ReplicaSet and Pods.
s3.explain: Once the static Pod is back, the Deployment controller creates the ReplicaSet and the ReplicaSet controller the Pods. Verify with 'kubectl get rs,pods -l app=web'.
s3.hint: The CA certificate is in the kubeadm pki directory; fix the flag's path.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - The controller manager is running again. Check that Deployment 'web' finally has its ReplicaSet.

options.why: A Deployment's ReplicaSet is named web-<hash>: 'replicasets.apps "web" not found'.
Shows READY counts, not whether a ReplicaSet exists.
'web' was created in the current namespace, not in kube-system.

s4.explain: The Deployment controller, inside kube-controller-manager, reconciles the backlog as soon as it starts: it creates web-<hash>, and the ReplicaSet controller then creates the 3 Pods. 'kubectl create deploy' labels everything app=web.
s4.hint: kubectl create deploy labels its objects app=<name>; the ReplicaSet name has a suffix.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Wait until all 3 replicas of 'web' are available.

options.why: A Deployment has no Ready condition (it has Available and Progressing): kubectl waits until the timeout.
Lists revisions; it does not wait for the replicas.
A snapshot: you cannot tell when all 3 Pods are ready.

s5.explain: rollout status follows the Deployment until 3/3 replicas are updated and available, then exits 0: the proof that the whole chain Deployment -> ReplicaSet -> Pods works again.
s5.hint: Follow the Deployment until its replicas are available.

questions.title: The API server cannot reach etcd
questions.scenario: kubectl is refused on 6443. On 'controlplane', crictl shows etcd Running but kube-apiserver exiting again and again. Find and fix the broken link.
questions.tip: etcd: 2379 = client port (the API server connects here), 2380 = peer port (etcd members only). The API server reaches etcd over TLS with the --etcd-cafile/certfile/keyfile flags.
questions.stakes: If the API cannot reach etcd, the whole cluster stops answering.
questions.analogy: A library with its catalogue room locked.

context: CONTAINER      IMAGE          CREATED          STATE     NAME             ATTEMPT   POD ID         POD
8c1e2f4a9b3d   c3994bc69631   20 seconds ago   Exited    kube-apiserver   9         2be0c71d5a44   kube-apiserver-controlplane
5d7f0a2c6e41   2e96e5913fc0   30 days ago      Running   etcd             0         f13a96c8e2b7   etcd-controlplane
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the last 20 lines logged by the crashed API server container.

options.why: That is the etcd container, which is Running fine: the one failing is the API server.
kubectl needs the API server, which is exactly what is down.
kube-apiserver is a static Pod, not a systemd unit: journald has no such unit.

s1.explain: The API server's own log says what it cannot reach or load. Pick the CONTAINER id of the failing container; crictl logs accepts --tail like kubectl logs.
s1.hint: crictl logs by container ID can limit the output to the last lines.

context: W1031 10:02:11.481902  1 logging.go:55] [core] [Channel #3 SubChannel #4] grpc: addrConn.createTransport failed
to connect to {Addr: "127.0.0.1:2397", ServerName: "127.0.0.1:2397", }. Err: connection error: desc =
"transport: Error while dialing: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:2397: connect: connection refused"
E1031 10:02:31.482117  1 run.go:72] "command failed" err="error creating storage factory: etcd grpc
connection not ready: context deadline exceeded"
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Check on which client URLs etcd really listens (grep its static Pod manifest).

options.why: The API server is the etcd CLIENT: its manifest has --etcd-servers, not etcd's listen URLs.
kubectl cannot work while the API server is down.
admin.conf holds the API server URL used by kubectl (port 6443), nothing about etcd.

s2.explain: The API server and etcd must agree: --listen-client-urls on the etcd side must match --etcd-servers on the API server side. etcd Running while the API server keeps exiting points at a mismatch.
s2.hint: etcd's client listen address is a flag in its manifest: search for it.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml': type the corrected --etcd-servers line over the broken one.

checks.msg: --etcd-servers must be https://127.0.0.1:2379 (etcd's client URL).
Keep --etcd-cafile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt.

forbid.msg: The wrong port 2397 is still configured.

options.why: 2380 is etcd's PEER port (member-to-member traffic), not the client port.
kubeadm's etcd only serves TLS on its client URLs: plain http fails the handshake.
6443 is the API server's own port: it would try to use itself as its database.

s3.recap: Set --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379 (etcd's client port) in kube-apiserver.yaml.
s3.explain: Other classic breaks of this link: a wrong --etcd-cafile/--etcd-certfile/--etcd-keyfile path (logs show 'open ...: no such file or directory' or x509 errors). The etcd CA lives in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/, separate from the cluster CA.
s3.hint: Point the API server at the address and port etcd really listens on, over https.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - On controlplane, check that the new kube-apiserver container now stays Running.

options.why: That is the old crashed container's log: the same etcd error again.
No such service: the API server is a static Pod run by the kubelet.
etcd was running all along; the API server is the component to check.

s4.explain: A changed manifest makes the kubelet replace the container. STATE Running with no new exit means the API server reached etcd at startup: it exits when it cannot.
s4.hint: Ask the container runtime about the API server's current container.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Ask the API server for its readiness checks, one line per check (etcd among them).

options.why: etcd was Running all along: it proves nothing about the API server's link to it.
etcd's client port requires TLS and a client certificate: this fails even on a healthy cluster.
--client stays local: no request reaches the API server.

s5.explain: /readyz?verbose lists each check with [+] or [-], including '[+]etcd ok': the API server itself confirms it can read and write etcd. The load balancer and kubelet probes use the same endpoint.
s5.hint: The API server has a readiness endpoint that can list each of its checks.

questions.title: A kubelet that will not start
questions.scenario: Node 'node01' is NotReady. On node01 the kubelet service is enabled but keeps exiting with an error. Read its logs, find the bad setting in its systemd configuration and fix it.
questions.tip: kubelet settings live in 3 places: the systemd drop-in 10-kubeadm.conf (flags), /var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env, and /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (KubeletConfiguration). 'systemctl cat kubelet' shows the unit and its drop-ins.
questions.stakes: A dead kubelet means a NotReady node and its Pods rescheduled elsewhere.
questions.analogy: journalctl is the kubelet's own diary: read it first.

context: ● kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent
Active: activating (auto-restart) (Result: exit-code) since Sat 2026-10-31 10:14:02 UTC; 4s ago
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Jump to the end of the kubelet's journal, with explanations (the command systemd itself suggests).

options.why: Wrong unit: containerd is fine, it is the kubelet process that exits with status 1.
systemctl has no 'logs' verb: logs are read with journalctl.
The kubelet is a systemd service, not a Pod: there is nothing to read with kubectl.

s1.explain: -u selects the unit, -e jumps to the end, -x adds explanatory text. 'activating (auto-restart)' means: started, crashed, systemd will retry (Restart=always).
s1.hint: journalctl for one unit, jumping to the end, with explanations: the flags systemd itself suggests.

context: kubelet[4121]: E1031 10:14:02.118734    4121 run.go:72] "command failed" err="failed to load kubelet config file,
path: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yml, error: open /var/lib/kubelet/config.yml: no such file or directory"
s2.prompt: Step 2 - The --config flag points to a missing file. Print the kubelet unit together with its drop-in files to find where that flag is set.

options.why: That is the KubeletConfiguration file itself; the path to it is passed by the --config flag elsewhere.
That is the kubelet's kubeconfig (how it talks to the API server), not its flags.
'kubeadm config view' was removed long ago, and it never showed kubelet flags.

s2.explain: The log says the --config file is missing, and the flag is set somewhere in the unit or its drop-ins. 'systemctl cat' prints the unit and every drop-in with its path, so you find the file to edit: here /usr/lib/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf.
s2.hint: systemctl can print a unit file together with all its drop-ins.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'sudo vi /usr/lib/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf': type the corrected KUBELET_CONFIG_ARGS line over the broken one.
prefill: # Note: This dropin only works with kubeadm and kubelet v1.11+
# This is a file that "kubeadm init" and "kubeadm join" generates at runtime, populating the KUBELET_KUBEADM_ARGS variable dynamically
# This is a file that the user can use for overrides of the kubelet args as a last resort.

checks.msg: The line must be: Environment="KUBELET_CONFIG_ARGS=--config=/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml"

forbid.msg: The wrong path config.yml is still there.

options.why: --kubeconfig expects a kubeconfig (API server credentials), not a KubeletConfiguration - and it is already set in KUBELET_KUBECONFIG_ARGS.
kubelet.conf is the kubelet's kubeconfig, not its KubeletConfiguration file.
/etc/kubernetes/manifests is the staticPodPath, for Pod manifests only; there is no config.yaml in it.

s3.recap: In 10-kubeadm.conf point --config to /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.
s3.explain: kubeadm writes the KubeletConfiguration to /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (it also contains staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests). Node-specific flags go to /var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env.
s3.hint: The kubelet's config file lives under /var/lib/kubelet; keep the Environment= syntax.

context: Warning: The unit file, source configuration file or drop-ins of kubelet.service changed on disk.
s4.prompt: Step 4 - Make systemd re-read the changed drop-in, then restart the kubelet (one line).

options.cmd: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
aliases: sudo systemctl daemon-reload; sudo systemctl restart kubelet

options.why: Without daemon-reload systemd keeps the old, cached unit definition: the kubelet restarts with the same broken flag.
The kubelet unit has no ExecReload: systemd refuses ('Job type reload is not applicable'), and the drop-in is still not re-read.
Restarts the container runtime, which was never the problem.

s4.explain: Any change to a unit file or drop-in needs 'systemctl daemon-reload'. A change to /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml or kubeadm-flags.env only needs a restart. Then 'kubectl get nodes' shows node01 Ready.
s4.hint: systemd must re-read changed unit files before the restart.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - From the control plane, check that node01 is Ready again.

options.why: On the control plane this shows ITS kubelet, not node01's.
Pods on node01 may still show their last known state: the node's condition is what matters.

options.cmd: kubectl describe node node01 | grep -i taint
options.why: Taints alone do not show Ready; the not-ready taint also takes a moment to be removed.

s5.explain: The kubelet posts the Ready condition through its heartbeat: STATUS Ready proves it runs with a valid config, reaches the API server and has a working network plugin. Pods can be scheduled there again.
s5.hint: The node's STATUS column comes from the kubelet's heartbeat.

questions.title: The container runtime is down
questions.scenario: Node 'node01' turned NotReady after maintenance. The kubelet is running, but complains about the runtime. Diagnose and bring the node back.
questions.tip: kubelet and containerd are BOTH systemd services on every node. 'container runtime is down' = look at containerd; 'crictl info' shows whether the CRI endpoint answers.
questions.stakes: The kubelet is up but no container can start because the runtime is down.
questions.analogy: A chef with no stove.

context: $ kubectl describe node node01 | grep -A1 Ready
Ready   False   KubeletNotReady   [container runtime is down, PLEG is not healthy: pleg was last seen
s1.prompt: Step 1 - On node01, check the state of the container runtime service.

options.why: Kubernetes has not talked to Docker Engine since dockershim was removed (v1.24): kubeadm nodes use containerd.
containerd is a systemd service on the host - it RUNS the Pods, it is not one of them.
The kubelet already told you its problem: the runtime. Look at the runtime's service now.

s1.explain: The kubelet reaches containers through the CRI: PLEG relists them there, and if the runtime does not answer, the node goes NotReady. So check the runtime's service first.
s1.hint: containerd is a systemd service: ask systemd for its state.

context: Active: inactive (dead) since Sat 2026-10-31 09:40:12 UTC; 4min ago
s2.prompt: Step 2 - containerd was stopped and disabled. Start it now and at every boot.

options.why: Runs it now, but it stays disabled: after the next reboot the node is NotReady again.
The kubelet is fine; without a runtime it still cannot run any container.
Runs containerd by hand, outside systemd: no restart policy, gone at logout or reboot.

s2.explain: containerd was stopped AND disabled: 'enable --now' starts it and keeps it across reboots. The kubelet reconnects to the CRI socket by itself, so no kubelet restart is needed.
s2.hint: Enable for boot and start now, in a single systemctl command.

context: Active: active (running) since Sat 2026-10-31 09:44:51 UTC; 3s ago
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Through the CRI, print the runtime's status conditions (RuntimeReady, NetworkReady).

options.why: Proves the socket answers, but prints only versions - no RuntimeReady/NetworkReady conditions.
Shows CPU/memory of containers, not the runtime's status.
Only the systemd state: it does not query the CRI endpoint the kubelet uses.

s3.explain: crictl reads its endpoint from /etc/crictl.yaml (unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock). 'crictl info' shows status.conditions: RuntimeReady and NetworkReady must both be true; then node01 goes Ready.
s3.hint: crictl has a subcommand that dumps the runtime's status, including its conditions.

questions.title: kubectl cannot reach the cluster
questions.scenario: On 'controlplane', kubectl suddenly fails, yet every control-plane container is Running. Inspect your kubeconfig and fix it.
questions.tip: 'connection refused' + a healthy kube-apiserver = check the server: line of your kubeconfig. 'kubectl config view --minify' shows only what the current context uses.
questions.stakes: Wrong kubeconfig or address: you debug a healthy cluster for an hour.
questions.analogy: Dialling the wrong number and concluding the person is gone.

context: The connection to the server 172.30.1.2:6334 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show only the part of your kubeconfig used by the current context.

options.why: Prints only the context NAME: no server URL, no user.
Lists cluster names only, without their server URLs.
That is the kubelet's own kubeconfig, not the one kubectl uses (~/.kube/config).

s1.explain: Before blaming the cluster, check what kubectl actually uses: --minify keeps only the current context, its cluster and its user, so you see the exact server address it dials.
s1.hint: kubectl config view can reduce the output to what the current context uses.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Port 6334 looks suspicious. Show which TCP port the kube-apiserver process really listens on.

options.why: kubectl cannot connect yet - and that Service shows the in-cluster port 443, not the host port.
Confirms the container runs, but shows no listening port.
Hits the same wrong port again: refused, nothing new learned.

s2.explain: Compare what kubectl dials with what the API server really listens on: ss shows the listening TCP port and its process. kubeadm's API server listens on --secure-port=6443.
s2.hint: ss lists listening TCP sockets with their process; filter for the API server.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'vi ~/.kube/config': type the corrected server: line over the broken one.

checks.msg: The server must be https://172.30.1.2:6443.

forbid.msg: The wrong port 6334 is still there.

options.why: The API server only speaks TLS: a plain-http request is rejected ('client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server').
443 is the port of the in-cluster 'kubernetes' Service (ClusterIP); nothing listens on 443 on the node itself.
10250 is the kubelet's API port, not the API server's.

s3.recap: Set server: https://172.30.1.2:6443 in ~/.kube/config (or: kubectl config set-cluster kubernetes --server=...).
s3.explain: Same fix without an editor: 'kubectl config set-cluster kubernetes --server=https://172.30.1.2:6443'. If the context is wrong instead, 'kubectl config get-contexts' + 'kubectl config use-context NAME'.
s3.hint: Fix the port on the server line; keep the https scheme and the IP.

questions.title: The cluster certificates have expired
questions.scenario: Logged in as root on 'controlplane' after a year without upgrades, kubectl fails with x509 errors. Check, renew, restart and get your access back.
questions.tip: kubeadm client/server certificates last 1 year (the CAs 10 years). 'kubeadm certs check-expiration', then 'kubeadm certs renew all', then restart the static Pods and refresh your kubeconfig.
questions.stakes: 'x509: certificate has expired' on every command, with everything else fine.
questions.analogy: An expired passport: the country is fine, the border will not let you in.

context: Unable to connect to the server: tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid:
s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the expiry dates of every kubeadm-managed certificate.

options.why: The 'alpha certs' commands graduated to 'kubeadm certs' and the alpha form was removed years ago.
Needs a working API connection - and CSRs are requests, not the cluster's certificates.
Checks only the CA, which is valid for 10 years: the expired ones are the leaf certificates.

s1.explain: check-expiration covers the certificates in /etc/kubernetes/pki and those embedded in the kubeconfig files (admin.conf, scheduler.conf...).
s1.hint: kubeadm's certs command family has a subcommand that prints every expiry date.

context: CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY   EXTERNALLY MANAGED
CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY   EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   EXTERNALLY MANAGED
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Renew all of them in one command.

options.why: Needs a target (all, apiserver, admin.conf...): without one it only prints the help.
Only prints a random key used to upload control-plane certs for 'kubeadm join'; renews nothing.
Wipes the control plane: a disaster, not a renewal.

s2.explain: 'renew all' re-signs every leaf certificate with the existing CAs and rewrites the kubeconfig files in /etc/kubernetes. It only writes new files: the running components still hold the old ones.
s2.hint: Renew every leaf certificate at once.

context: Done renewing certificates. You must restart the kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler and etcd,
so that they can use the new certificates.
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Make the kubelet stop the control-plane Pods: move all their manifests into the empty directory /root/sp (you move them back after ~20 s).

options.why: Restarting the kubelet does not restart running containers: the old processes keep the old certificates.
kubectl is not working yet, and deleting a static Pod's mirror object does not stop the static Pod anyway.
Stops them, but the manifests are gone: you would have to regenerate them with kubeadm.

s3.explain: Static Pods are owned by the kubelet, not the API server. Removing a manifest stops the Pod; putting it back (after the kubelet noticed, ~20 s) starts it again with the new certificates.
s3.hint: Static Pods stop when their manifest leaves the watched directory: move the files out.

s5.prompt: Step 4 - ~20 s later the control-plane Pods are stopped. Move the manifests back so they restart with the renewed certificates.

options.why: Puts the directory INSIDE manifests/: the kubelet ignores subdirectories and the control plane stays down.
The manifests are still in /root/sp: the kubelet has nothing to start.
The API server is one of the stopped Pods: 'connection refused'.

s5.explain: Static Pods read their certificates only at startup: stopping and restarting them is what makes the renewed files effective. The kubelet starts each Pod again as soon as its manifest reappears.
s5.hint: The kubelet runs whatever appears in its static Pod directory.

context: error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)
s4.prompt: Step 5 - Your ~/.kube/config still embeds the old, expired admin certificate. Replace it with the renewed admin kubeconfig.

options.why: That is the node's identity (system:node:controlplane), limited by the Node authorizer - not cluster-admin.
A CA certificate is not a kubeconfig: no server, no user credentials.
Switches to the same context in the same file - still the same expired client certificate.

s4.explain: The server certificate is now valid, so the error changed: the API server rejects the expired CLIENT certificate (Unauthorized). renew all refreshed admin.conf; copy it again.
s4.hint: Your kubeconfig is a copy: replace it with the admin kubeconfig kubeadm just regenerated.

questions.title: Pods evicted from a full node
questions.scenario: Several Pods on 'node01' show status Evicted and new Pods avoid that node. Find the pressure condition, free space on the node and clean up.
questions.tip: Node conditions: MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure. Under pressure the kubelet evicts Pods and the node gets a matching node.kubernetes.io/*-pressure taint.
questions.stakes: Disk pressure evicts Pods without warning: low-priority ones leave first.
questions.analogy: A lifeboat: when it is full, the least critical passengers go first.

context: NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show node01's conditions and taints.

options.why: Shows CPU and memory usage only: nothing about disk, conditions or taints.
Adds IPs, OS and runtime columns: no conditions, no taints.
An evicted Pod's containers are gone: there are no logs to read, and the cause is on the node.

s1.explain: describe node shows Conditions, Taints, Allocated resources and Events like 'EvictionThresholdMet'.
s1.hint: describe on the Node shows its Conditions (DiskPressure) and taints.

context: MemoryPressure   False   KubeletHasSufficientMemory   kubelet has sufficient memory available
DiskPressure     True    KubeletHasDiskPressure       kubelet has disk pressure
Events:  Warning  EvictionThresholdMet  Attempting to reclaim ephemeral-storage
s2.prompt: Step 2 - ssh to node01: show the usage of every mounted filesystem in human-readable units.

options.why: Shows memory, but the condition is DiskPressure.
Lists block devices and their sizes, not how full the filesystems are.
Measures one tiny config directory; the kubelet watches /var/lib/kubelet and the containerd image store.

s2.explain: The kubelet evicts Pods when a filesystem passes its threshold, so find which one is full: nodefs (/var/lib/kubelet) or imagefs (/var/lib/containerd). Default hard thresholds include nodefs.available<10% and imagefs.available<15%.
s2.hint: df with human-readable sizes, for every mounted filesystem.

context: Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Old images fill the disk. Remove every image not used by any container, through the CRI.

options.why: Removes ALL images, including those of running Pods: they must be pulled again on the next restart.
There is no Docker on a containerd node; its images live in containerd's store.
Destroys the runtime's state under running containers: you would have to rebuild the node.

s3.explain: The kubelet also garbage-collects images itself above imageGCHighThresholdPercent (85% by default); --prune does it now. DiskPressure clears once space is back above the threshold.
s3.hint: crictl can remove every image no container uses, in one command.

context: DiskPressure     False   KubeletHasNoDiskPressure     kubelet has no disk pressure
s4.prompt: Step 4 - Back on the control plane: delete the Evicted Pod objects left in namespace default (they are in phase Failed).

options.why: Evicted is the REASON; the phase is Failed. This selector matches nothing.
Also deletes the healthy Running Pods.
-l selects labels; no Pod carries a 'status' label.

s4.explain: Evicted Pods keep their object (phase Failed, reason Evicted) so you can inspect them; their ReplicaSet already replaced them. The taint is removed by the kubelet when the condition clears.
s4.hint: Evicted Pods have phase Failed: delete by a field selector on status.phase.

questions.title: Nodes NotReady: no network plugin
questions.scenario: A freshly built kubeadm cluster (--pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16): every node is NotReady and the CoreDNS Pods stay Pending. The Flannel manifest was downloaded to /root/kube-flannel.yml.
questions.tip: 'cni plugin not initialized' = no CNI config in /etc/cni/net.d. kubeadm does not install a network plugin: you must apply one (Flannel, Calico, Cilium...).
questions.stakes: Nodes NotReady with no CNI config: the cluster is built and nothing can talk.
questions.analogy: A phone without a SIM card: the hardware is fine, the network is missing.

context: $ kubectl describe node node01 | grep Ready
Ready   False   KubeletNotReady   container runtime network not ready: NetworkReady=false
reason:NetworkPluginNotReady message:Network plugin returns error: cni plugin not initialized
s1.prompt: Step 1 - On node01, list the directory where the runtime looks for CNI network configurations.

options.why: That is the static Pod directory; CNI configuration is not there.
CNI is not a service: plugins are binaries called by the runtime, configured by files.
DNS resolver settings: unrelated to the Pod network plugin.

s1.explain: /etc/cni/net.d holds the network config (*.conflist), /opt/cni/bin the plugin binaries. Empty net.d = 'cni plugin not initialized'.
s1.hint: The runtime reads CNI config files from a fixed directory under /etc/cni.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Install the network plugin from /root/kube-flannel.yml.

options.why: net.d expects CNI JSON configs, not a Kubernetes manifest; Flannel's DaemonSet writes its own conflist there.
The static Pod directory only accepts Pods, and only on that one node: a DaemonSet cannot run from there.
The manifest's objects declare namespace kube-flannel; kubectl refuses a conflicting -n.

s2.explain: The CNI runs as a DaemonSet: one agent per node writes /etc/cni/net.d/10-flannel.conflist and sets up routes. Flannel's default network 10.244.0.0/16 matches --pod-network-cidr.
s2.hint: Apply the manifest file the scenario gives.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Check that a Flannel Pod runs on every node (show the node column).

options.why: Looks in the current namespace (default); Flannel runs in kube-flannel.
kube-flannel-ds is the DaemonSet; its Pods have random suffixes. And logs do not show where Pods run.
Here Flannel runs as a DaemonSet Pod, not as a systemd service.

s3.explain: Once each node's CNI Pod is Running, the nodes turn Ready and CoreDNS gets scheduled. Recent Flannel releases use the kube-flannel namespace (older ones used kube-system).
s3.hint: Flannel runs as a DaemonSet in its own namespace: list its Pods with the node column.

questions.title: Service IPs answer nothing
questions.scenario: From node01, the Pod IP behind Service 'web' answers, but the Service's ClusterIP times out. The EndpointSlice is correct. Find the broken component and fix its configuration.
questions.tip: Pod IP works but ClusterIP does not = kube-proxy (it programs the iptables/nftables rules for Services). kubeadm runs it as DaemonSet kube-proxy, configured by ConfigMap kube-proxy, both in kube-system.
questions.stakes: Pod IPs answer but Service IPs do not: the translator is down.
questions.analogy: kube-proxy is the switchboard operator who maps a Service number to a Pod.

context: curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3001 milliseconds
s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the kube-proxy Pods (by label) with the node they run on.

options.cmd: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
aliases: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide

options.cmd: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-proxy -o wide
options.why: component= is the label of kubeadm's static Pods; the kube-proxy DaemonSet uses k8s-app=kube-proxy.
kubeadm runs kube-proxy as a DaemonSet, not a systemd service.
There is no kube-proxy namespace: it lives in kube-system.

s1.explain: kube-proxy runs once per node and turns Services + EndpointSlices into packet rules. If it is down, ClusterIPs are dead while Pod IPs still work.
s1.hint: kube-proxy Pods carry the label k8s-app=kube-proxy in kube-system; add the node column.

context: NAME               READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE   NODE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Read the logs of node01's kube-proxy Pod.

options.why: kube-proxy is the DaemonSet's name; no Pod has that exact name (use the Pod name, or ds/kube-proxy).
No kube-proxy systemd unit exists: it runs in a container.
crictl logs takes a CONTAINER id, not a Pod name - and kubectl works fine here.

s2.explain: All the kube-proxy Pods crash the same way, and they share one ConfigMap, so it is the prime suspect. The log names the setting it cannot use.
s2.hint: logs of the kube-proxy Pod running on node01, in kube-system.

context: E1031 11:20:07.411302  1 run.go:72] "command failed" err="failed validate: KubeProxyConfiguration.Mode.ProxyMode:
Invalid value: \"iptable\": must be iptables, ipvs, nftables or blank (blank means the best-available proxy ..."
s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'kubectl -n kube-system edit cm kube-proxy': the cluster uses iptables mode. Type the corrected mode line over the broken one.

checks.msg: Set '    mode: "iptables"' inside config.conf (4-space indent).
