Keep clusterCIDR: 10.244.0.0/16.

forbid.msg: The invalid mode 'iptable' is still there.

options.why: The userspace proxy mode was removed in v1.26.
kernelspace is the Windows-only mode; on Linux nodes it fails validation.

s3.recap: Fix mode: "iptables" in ConfigMap kube-proxy (kube-system), then restart the DaemonSet.
s3.explain: Linux modes are iptables, ipvs and nftables (an empty mode means the default, iptables). clusterCIDR must match the Pod network.
s3.hint: The mode value must be the one the cluster uses, quoted, at the same indentation.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - kube-proxy reads its config only at start-up: restart all its Pods the declarative way.

options.cmd: kubectl rollout restart ds kube-proxy -n kube-system
aliases: kubectl rollout restart daemonset kube-proxy -n kube-system
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart ds kube-proxy
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart daemonset kube-proxy

options.cmd: kubectl rollout restart deploy kube-proxy -n kube-system
options.why: kube-proxy is a DaemonSet, not a Deployment: 'deployments.apps "kube-proxy" not found'.
Missing '-n kube-system': there is no kube-proxy DaemonSet in the default namespace.
kube-proxy is not a systemd service in a kubeadm cluster.

s4.explain: rollout restart stamps a restartedAt annotation on the Pod template, so every node gets a fresh kube-proxy reading the fixed ConfigMap. Then retest: curl 10.96.120.15.
s4.hint: kube-proxy is a DaemonSet: restart its Pods the declarative way.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - From a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod, call Service 'web' by name (3 s timeout).

options.why: DNS resolving the name was never broken: it says nothing about the ClusterIP path.
The slice was correct all along: it does not test kube-proxy's rules.
A Pod IP bypasses kube-proxy entirely: it worked before the fix too.

s5.explain: Calling the Service by name goes DNS -> ClusterIP -> kube-proxy's iptables rules -> a Pod. A page coming back proves the restarted kube-proxy programmed the rules again.
s5.hint: Go through the Service's virtual IP, the part kube-proxy handles.

questions.title: kubectl top has no metrics
questions.scenario: metrics-server was installed in kube-system from the upstream manifest, but 'kubectl top nodes' fails. In this lab the kubelets use self-signed serving certificates.
questions.tip: kubectl top -> APIService v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -> Service/Deployment metrics-server in kube-system -> kubelets on :10250. Follow that chain.
questions.stakes: Without metrics-server 'kubectl top' fails and the HPA cannot scale.
questions.analogy: A dashboard with the speedometer unplugged.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Check the aggregated APIService that serves the Metrics API.

options.why: APIService objects are named <version>.<group>: v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io.
Looks in the default namespace; metrics-server lives in kube-system.
Same Metrics API, same error: it tells you nothing new.

s1.explain: The API server proxies /apis/metrics.k8s.io to the Service named in the APIService. AVAILABLE tells you whether that backend is healthy.
s1.hint: The Metrics API is served through an aggregated APIService; get it by its group/version name.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - No ready backend. Read the logs of the metrics-server Deployment without looking up its Pod name.

options.why: Without a type prefix kubectl looks for a Pod named exactly metrics-server; its Pods have random suffixes.
Missing '-n kube-system'.
metrics-server is a Deployment in the cluster, not a systemd service.

s2.explain: MissingEndpoints = the Service has no ready Pod: metrics-server's readiness probe fails until it can scrape the kubelets.
s2.hint: logs can target a Deployment directly; metrics-server lives in kube-system.

context: E1031 12:01:44.902114  1 scraper.go:149] "Failed to scrape node" err="Get \"https://172.30.1.3:10250/metrics/resource\":
tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: cannot validate certificate for 172.30.1.3 because it doesn't contain any IP SANs" node="node01"
s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'kubectl -n kube-system edit deploy metrics-server': lab only - skip kubelet certificate verification. Type the snippet over the --metric-resolution line (keep that line).

checks.msg: Add '        - --kubelet-insecure-tls' to the args list (8-space indent).
Keep '--metric-resolution=15s'.

forbid.msg: --kubelet-insecure-tls=false keeps verification on.

options.why: Explicitly false: certificate verification stays on and scraping keeps failing.
--insecure-skip-tls-verify is a kubectl/kubeconfig option: metrics-server exits with 'unknown flag'.
At 6 spaces the item belongs to the containers list, not to args: the Deployment is rejected.

s3.recap: Add '--kubelet-insecure-tls' to metrics-server's args (lab only); the Deployment rolls out a new Pod.
s3.explain: Saving the edit changes the Pod template, so a new Pod rolls out; after ~1 min the APIService turns True and 'kubectl top nodes' works. In production, enable serverTLSBootstrap on the kubelets and approve their CSRs instead.
s3.hint: Keep the existing argument and add the flag that skips kubelet certificate verification.

questions.topic: Static Pod logs without the API
questions.title: Reading etcd's logs with the API down
questions.scenario: You are root on 'controlplane'. The API server is unreachable and you suspect etcd. Get etcd's logs without kubectl, two different ways.
questions.tip: No API = no kubectl logs. On the node: 'crictl ps -a --name X' + 'crictl logs ID', or the files under /var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/.
questions.stakes: With the API down, 'kubectl logs' is dead: only crictl can read the container.
questions.analogy: When the lift stops, take the stairs: crictl.

context: The connection to the server 172.30.1.2:6443 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?
s1.prompt: Step 1 - List the etcd containers, running or exited, through the CRI.

options.why: Lists Pod sandboxes, not containers: you get a POD ID, not the container id that crictl logs needs.
ctr defaults to containerd namespace 'default'; Kubernetes containers live in namespace k8s.io (ctr -n k8s.io ...).
Any kubectl call needs the API server, which is down.

s1.explain: --name filters by container name (a regular expression); -a also shows exited containers.
s1.hint: crictl lists containers, running or exited, filtered by name.

context: CONTAINER      IMAGE          CREATED          STATE    NAME   ATTEMPT   POD ID         POD
a1b2c3d4e5f6   2e96e5913fc0   25 seconds ago   Exited   etcd   6         9f8e7d6c5b4a   etcd-controlplane
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Print the last 30 lines of that container's log.

options.why: That is the POD ID (the sandbox): crictl logs needs the CONTAINER id from the first column.
In kubeadm clusters etcd is a static Pod, not a systemd unit (unlike some 'external etcd' setups).
Shows the container's status and spec as JSON, not its output.

s2.explain: Container ids may be shortened to any unique prefix. Each restart is a new container: older attempts appear in 'crictl ps -a' with their own ids until the kubelet garbage-collects them.
s2.hint: crictl logs by container ID, limited to the last lines.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Same lines without crictl: tail the log files the kubelet keeps for the etcd container (use a glob for the UID).

options.why: Containerized etcd writes to stdout/stderr, collected by the runtime under /var/log/pods - there is no /var/log/etcd.log.
Those are etcd's binary write-ahead log DATA files, not its log output.
Pod log directories are named <namespace>_<pod>_<uid>, with one subdirectory per container.

s3.explain: Layout: /var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/<restart>.log; /var/log/containers/ holds symlinks named <pod>_<ns>_<container>-<id>.log. Both survive while the API server is down.
s3.hint: The kubelet keeps container logs under /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/.

questions.title: A drain blocked by a disruption budget
questions.scenario: Cluster: controlplane, node01, node02. 'kubectl drain node01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data' kept retrying, so you stopped it. Deployment 'web' (namespace default, 2 replicas) must keep its availability guarantee.
questions.tip: drain evicts through the Eviction API, which honours PodDisruptionBudgets. ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 0 = drain retries forever: add replicas (or relax the PDB), never delete it blindly.

docs.title: Specifying a Disruption Budget for your Application

questions.stakes: minAvailable equal to the replica count blocks every drain: the upgrade window closes with nothing done.
questions.analogy: 'At least 2 cashiers open' with exactly 2 cashiers: nobody takes a break until a third one arrives.

context: error when evicting pods/"web-7d4b9c6f8-2xkqp" -n "default" (will retry after 5s): Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.
error when evicting pods/"web-7d4b9c6f8-h8vnl" -n "default" (will retry after 5s): Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.
s1.prompt: Step 1 - The eviction is refused: list the PodDisruptionBudgets of namespace default.

options.why: The blocked Pods live in default (-n "default" in the error): a budget only covers Pods of its own namespace, kube-system holds nothing relevant.
No such resource type: the server answers 'doesn't have a resource type'. The short name is pdb, the full one poddisruptionbudgets.
Shows the node's Pods and that it is cordoned, not the budget that refuses the eviction.

s1.explain: drain does not delete Pods: it calls the Eviction API, which checks every PodDisruptionBudget selecting the Pod. 'violate the pod's disruption budget' means a PDB of the Pod's namespace allows 0 disruptions right now. Without --timeout, drain retries every 5 s forever.
s1.hint: Budgets are namespaced objects with a short name; list them in default.

context: NAME      MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Keep minAvailable 2 but make room: scale Deployment web to 3 replicas.

options.why: A PodDisruptionBudget has no scale subresource: kubectl refuses it. Replicas belong to the Deployment.
The drain would pass, but the guarantee is gone: both web Pods could be evicted at once, now and at every later drain.
1 healthy Pod for minAvailable 2: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS stays 0 and you lose half the capacity.

s2.explain: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS = healthy Pods - minAvailable = 2 - 2 = 0: no voluntary eviction can pass. A third replica (on node02, node01 is cordoned) makes it 3 - 2 = 1: drain evicts one Pod, waits for its replacement to be Ready, then the next.
s2.hint: Make room above minAvailable: scale the Deployment up.

context: NAME      MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Finish the drain of node01 (it runs DaemonSet Pods and Pods with emptyDir volumes).

options.why: Deletes the Pods directly, bypassing every PodDisruptionBudget: both web Pods of node01 could go at once. Keep it for a budget that can never be met.
Makes node01 schedulable again: nothing is evicted and the maintenance cannot start.
Refuses at once: DaemonSet-managed Pods and emptyDir data need --ignore-daemonsets and --delete-emptydir-data.

s3.explain: With 1 disruption allowed, the Eviction API accepts one web Pod, refuses the second until its replacement is Ready on node02, and drain simply retries until 'node/node01 drained'. Scale web back to 2 after the maintenance if the extra replica is not wanted.
s3.hint: drain again: DaemonSet Pods and emptyDir data each need an explicit flag.

questions.title: A DaemonSet that skips the control plane
questions.scenario: DaemonSet 'node-exporter' (namespace 'monitoring') must run on EVERY node, the control plane included. The cluster has 3 nodes (controlplane, node01, node02), but the DaemonSet shows DESIRED 2.
questions.tip: DESIRED below the node count and no Pending Pod? A taint. A DaemonSet gets automatic tolerations for node problems (not-ready, pressure...), never for the control-plane taint.
questions.stakes: The monitoring agent misses the control plane: the node you most need to watch becomes the blind spot.
questions.analogy: A 'staff only' door: the cleaning crew skips that room until it is handed a staff pass.

context: NAME            DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR   AGE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - No node selector, yet one node is skipped. Display the taints of node controlplane.

options.cmd: kubectl describe node controlplane | grep -i taints
aliases: kubectl describe node controlplane | grep Taints
kubectl describe nodes controlplane | grep -i taints

options.cmd: kubectl describe ds node-exporter -n monitoring | grep -i taints
options.why: A DaemonSet has no taints: its Pod template may carry tolerations, but taints live on Nodes.
Shows node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane as a LABEL; the taint with the same key lives in spec.taints and is not listed here.
Shows that no Pod runs on controlplane, which DESIRED 2 already told you, not why.

s1.explain: DESIRED counts the nodes where the DaemonSet controller wants a Pod; a node whose taints the template does not tolerate is simply left out, so no Pending Pod and no event appear. With no node selector a taint is the usual cause: kubeadm taints control-plane nodes NoSchedule.
s1.hint: describe the control-plane node and filter its Taints line.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - 'kubectl edit ds node-exporter -n monitoring': type the snippet over the line '      containers:' (it ends with that line). Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Under template.spec (6 spaces): tolerations with key node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, operator Exists, effect NoSchedule, right before containers.

forbid.msg: The 'master' taint key is gone since v1.25.
The taint's effect is NoSchedule, not NoExecute.
The control-plane taint has no value: use operator Exists.

options.why: kubeadm stopped applying the 'master' taint in v1.25: this toleration matches nothing, DESIRED stays 2.
The taint has an EMPTY value: Equal with value "true" does not match it. Use Exists (or Equal with no value).
A toleration only matches the same effect (or every effect when it is empty): NoExecute does not tolerate a NoSchedule taint.

s2.recap: tolerations: key node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, operator Exists, effect NoSchedule, in the Pod template spec.
s2.explain: The toleration belongs in the Pod TEMPLATE spec (spec.template.spec), next to containers: the controller then counts controlplane and creates its Pod. Exists matches the taint whatever its value; the effect must be NoSchedule (or empty, for every effect).
s2.hint: Tolerate the control-plane taint by key (any value) for NoSchedule, in the Pod template; keep 'containers:'.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Check that a node-exporter Pod now runs on controlplane (show the node of each Pod).

aliases: kubectl get pods -n monitoring -l app=node-exporter -o wide

options.cmd: kubectl get ds node-exporter -n monitoring -o wide
options.why: DESIRED 3 is a good sign, but -o wide only adds containers, images and selector: never the node of each Pod.
Adds the labels, not the NODE column: you cannot see where each Pod runs.
Lists the nodes with their IPs and runtime, not the Pods running on them.

s3.explain: -o wide adds the NODE column: expect three Pods, one per node, controlplane included (and DESIRED 3 on the DaemonSet). Each DaemonSet Pod is pinned to its node by a node affinity on the node name, so it never drifts elsewhere.
s3.hint: List the DaemonSet's Pods with the node column, in its namespace.

questions.title: Endpoints, yet connection refused
questions.scenario: Service 'web' (namespace default, port 80) has endpoints, but every call from inside the cluster is refused. The Pods of Deployment 'web' are Running and Ready.
questions.tip: Endpoints present + 'Connection refused' = the targetPort is not where the app listens. No endpoints = selector or readiness. A silent time-out = suspect a NetworkPolicy.
questions.stakes: Everything looks green, Pods Ready and endpoints present, yet every request is refused because of one port number.
questions.analogy: The right building, the wrong door number: the address is valid, but nobody waits behind that door.

context: wget: can't connect to remote host (10.96.112.45): Connection refused
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the Service's selector, port, TargetPort and endpoints in one view.

options.why: PORT(S) shows 80/TCP, the Service port only: neither the targetPort nor the endpoints.
Shows the Service's own labels, not its selector, target port or endpoints.
No Pod is named 'web': Deployment Pods carry ReplicaSet and random suffixes.

s1.explain: 'Connection refused' is not a time-out: something answered with a reset. The Service does route, but to a port where nothing listens. describe shows Port, TargetPort and the endpoint addresses with their port side by side.
s1.hint: describe on the Service shows selector, port, TargetPort and endpoints together.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Show the port declared by the container of Deployment 'web'.

options.why: Adds the CONTAINERS, IMAGES and SELECTOR columns, not the container ports.
Shows Pod IPs and nodes: the IPs match the endpoints, but no port.
Repeats what describe said (endpoints on port 80): where the Service sends traffic, not where the app listens.

s2.explain: The Pod template in describe lists each container's Port. containerPort is informative (it opens nothing), but here it is what the app really binds: 8080. Traffic sent to 80 hits a closed port and the Pod's kernel answers with a reset: refused.
s2.hint: describe on the Deployment shows the container's declared port.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'kubectl edit svc web': type the corrected port lines over the current ones. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Clients call port 80: keep 'port: 80'.
HTTP needs protocol: TCP.
targetPort must be 8080, the container's port.

options.why: Changes the port clients call (web:8080) and still sends to 80: still refused, and every client using web:80 now fails too.
HTTP runs over TCP: a UDP Service port never carries the TCP connection, the call still fails.
A string targetPort is a port NAME; '8080/TCP' is not a valid name, so the API server rejects the edit.

s3.recap: targetPort: 8080, the port the container listens on; port 80 stays for the clients.
s3.explain: port is what clients call (web:80); targetPort is where the traffic goes on the Pod. Fix only targetPort: the EndpointSlice switches to :8080 within seconds, no Pod restarts. A named targetPort (the containerPort's name) avoids this mismatch when ports change.
s3.hint: Keep the Service port; the target port must be the container's real port.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Prove it from a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod (3 s timeout), the way clients call it.

options.why: The Service listens on 80; 8080 is the Pod side. Nothing serves 8080 on the ClusterIP, so the call fails although the fix is right.
busybox has no curl: the container fails to start with 'executable file not found'.
A ClusterIP is virtual: it does not answer ICMP, so ping fails even on a healthy Service.

s4.explain: Test the way clients do: the Service name on port 80. The page printed by wget proves that 80 -> 8080 works; 'kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web' now shows 8080.
s4.hint: From a throw-away busybox Pod, call the Service by name with a short timeout.

questions.title: A policy that forgot the new frontend
questions.scenario: Since this morning's frontend release, Pod 'frontend' in namespace 'shop' times out on Service 'api' (port 8080). Nothing changed on the api side. Restore access for the frontend Pods of 'shop' only.
questions.tip: Pods time out between each other? 'kubectl get netpol -A', then compare each rule's selectors with 'get pods --show-labels'. Policies only ADD allowances: one isolating policy is enough to drop traffic.
questions.stakes: A harmless label rename in a release silently cuts the frontend off its API: a full outage with every Pod Running.
questions.analogy: A guest list written under the old name: the guest changed name, the bouncer still checks the old one.

context: $ kubectl exec -n shop frontend -- wget -qO- -T 3 api:8080
s1.prompt: Step 1 - A time-out, not a refusal: list the NetworkPolicies of every namespace.

options.why: Lists the default namespace only: 'No resources found', while the policy sits in shop.
The Service and its endpoints are fine: a NetworkPolicy drops the packets after the Service has routed them.
kube-proxy only programs Service rules; NetworkPolicies are enforced by the CNI plugin, and these logs say nothing about them.

s1.explain: A refusal means something answered; a silent time-out means packets were dropped, the signature of a NetworkPolicy. -A matters: a policy lives in the namespace of the Pods it protects, which may not be the client's.
s1.hint: A silent time-out often means a NetworkPolicy: list them in every namespace.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Show what api-ingress allows.

options.why: Looks in the default namespace: NotFound. The policy is in shop.

options.cmd: kubectl get netpol api-ingress -n shop -o wide
options.why: The same columns as before (name, pod selector, age): the ingress rules are not shown.
A Pod does not list the policies selecting it: read the policy itself.

s2.explain: describe renders the policy in words: which Pods it isolates (PodSelector) and, per rule, the allowed sources and ports. A Pod selected by any Ingress policy drops all inbound traffic that no policy explicitly allows.
s2.hint: describe on the policy prints its rules in plain words.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Compare with reality: show the labels of the Pods in shop.

options.why: Answers 'No resources found': it proves the rule matches nothing, not which label the frontend carries now.
Namespace labels feed a namespaceSelector; this rule is a podSelector on Pod labels.
Adds IPs and nodes, not labels.

s3.explain: A podSelector with no namespaceSelector matches Pods of the policy's OWN namespace by label. If the release renamed the label, app=web-frontend matches nothing and only the isolation remains.
s3.hint: Show every label of the Pods in shop and compare with the policy's 'from'.

context: NAME                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   LABELS
s4.prompt: Step 4 - 'kubectl edit netpol api-ingress -n shop': let in the frontend Pods of shop and nothing else. Type the new source over the old one. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: The only source: '- podSelector' with matchLabels app: frontend, directly followed by ports.

forbid.msg: No namespaceSelector: the frontend is in the same namespace.
No Pod carries app=web-frontend any more.
An empty podSelector lets in every Pod of shop.

options.why: An empty podSelector selects every Pod of shop: the frontend gets in, but so does any other Pod of the namespace.
namespaceSelector matches NAMESPACE labels: no namespace carries app=frontend, so nothing is let in.
In the same item (no dash) both selectors are ANDed: app=frontend Pods of EVERY namespace get in, not only those of shop.

s4.recap: from: podSelector matchLabels app: frontend (same namespace, nothing else).
s4.explain: A podSelector alone stays inside the policy's namespace, so app: frontend lets in exactly the frontend Pods of shop. The CNI applies the change to new connections at once, no restart. Labelling the Pod app=web-frontend would also work, but fights the release.
s4.hint: One podSelector source matching the frontend's real label; same namespace, so no namespaceSelector.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Prove it from the real client, Pod 'frontend' (3 s timeout).

options.cmd: kubectl exec -n shop frontend -- wget -qO- -T 3 api:8080
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -n shop -- wget -qO- -T 3 api:8080
options.why: This Pod carries run=t, not app=frontend: it must still time out. A check of the denial, not of the fix.

options.cmd: kubectl exec -n shop frontend -- wget -qO- -T 3 api
options.why: Without :8080 wget uses port 80, which Service api does not expose: it fails whatever the policy says.
Without -n shop kubectl looks for Pod frontend in default: NotFound.

s5.explain: Only a Pod carrying the allowed label proves the rule, and frontend is that Pod: expect the api's reply. A throw-away Pod in shop (label run=t) should still time out: that proves api is still protected.
s5.hint: exec into the real client Pod and fetch the api Service on its port, with a short timeout.

questions.title: Debug a container that has no shell
questions.scenario: Pod 'payments' (namespace default, container 'app', a distroless image running as root) keeps restarting. Its config comes from ConfigMap 'payments-config', mounted at /etc/app. 'kubectl exec' cannot help.
questions.tip: No shell in the image? 'kubectl debug -it POD --image=busybox:1.36 --target=CONTAINER' brings the tools; /proc/1/root reaches the app's files. Ephemeral containers stay in the Pod until it is deleted.
questions.stakes: Without kubectl debug you end up rebuilding the image with a shell, while the payment service keeps crashing.
questions.analogy: A sealed engine: instead of drilling into it, you plug a diagnostic tool into its port and read what it sees.

context: error: Internal error occurred: error executing command in container: failed to exec in container:
OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process:
exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH: unknown
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Attach an interactive busybox:1.36 ephemeral container to 'payments' that sees the processes of container 'app'.

options.why: Adds an ephemeral container, but without --target it has its own process namespace: ps shows only your shell, not the app.
A distroless image has no busybox either: the same 'executable file not found'.
Creates a COPY of the Pod with fresh processes: you no longer inspect the instance that misbehaves.

s1.explain: Ephemeral containers are added to a RUNNING Pod through the API, with their own image and tools. --target=app joins the app container's process namespace, so ps shows the app and /proc/<pid>/root reaches its files. Without it the app stays invisible.
s1.hint: kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container; target the app container to share its process namespace.

context: If you don't see a command prompt, try pressing enter.
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Your busybox has its own filesystem. Print the app's /etc/app/config.yaml through its process (PID 1).

options.why: Looked up in the busybox image: 'No such file or directory'. Only the process namespace is shared, not the filesystem.
chroot then runs cat FROM the app's image, which has no cat: 'can't execute'.
There is no kubectl in the debug container, and kubectl cp needs tar in the target container, which a distroless image lacks.

s2.explain: /proc/<pid>/root is the root directory as that process sees it, mounted volumes included: the app's files without touching its image. It works because both run as root; for an app running as another user you need the same user or the SYS_PTRACE capability.
s2.hint: Every process exposes its root filesystem under /proc/<pid>/root.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Back on your terminal: 'app' restarted 3 times. Read what its crashed (previous) instance printed.

options.why: Shows the CURRENT instance, still starting: the error that killed the last one is in --previous.
That is your ephemeral container: it never restarted, so it has no previous instance.
describe has no --previous flag; it shows the last exit code and reason, not the program's output.

s3.explain: A restarted container's last output is kept as its PREVIOUS instance: --previous (-p) reads it, -c picks 'app' now that the Pod also holds a debugger container. Here it ties the crash to the config: the lookup of 'postgres.payment' fails.
s3.hint: logs of the previous instance of the app container.

context: 2026-11-06T09:14:02Z FATAL cannot connect to database: dial tcp: lookup
s4.prompt: Step 4 - The database is Service 'postgres' in namespace 'payments'. 'kubectl edit cm payments-config': type the fixed host line over the wrong one. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: db_host must be postgres.payments.svc.cluster.local (4 spaces, inside the block).

forbid.msg: The misspelled namespace 'payment' is still there.

options.why: With 2 spaces the line leaves the 'config.yaml: |' block: the next indented line breaks the YAML and kubectl edit refuses to save.
The pod subdomain is for Pod IPs (a-b-c-d.ns.pod...): a Service name there never resolves.
No namespace in the name: it would be read as Service 'postgres' of a namespace 'svc', which does not exist.

s4.explain: A Service's DNS name is <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. A ConfigMap mounted as a volume (without subPath) is refreshed in the Pod after a short delay, so the crash-looping app reads the fixed file at its next restart: no need to delete the Pod.
s4.hint: A Service in another namespace needs its full DNS name: service.namespace.svc.cluster.local.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - The ConfigMap volume refreshes and the kubelet restarts 'app' again. Read the CURRENT logs of container 'app'.

options.why: That is the run before this one: the old database error again.
The distroless image has no cat: 'executable file not found', and the file would not prove the app connected.
Shows the corrected value, not whether the application used it.

s5.explain: A mounted ConfigMap is updated in place after a short delay; the app reads it at start, so the next restart uses the right host. Its current log shows the connection, and RESTARTS stops growing.
s5.hint: Current run of the same container, not the crashed one.

questions.title: One control-plane node down
questions.scenario: HA cluster: control-plane nodes cp1, cp2, cp3 with stacked etcd, behind a load balancer. cp3 rebooted after maintenance and stays NotReady. You are root on cp1, in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd, with etcdctl.
questions.tip: etcd needs a majority: 3 members survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2, and 4 still only 1. Check with 'etcdctl endpoint health --cluster' and 'endpoint status --cluster -w table'.
questions.stakes: Shrug at 2 of 3 and skip the repair: the next node failure freezes every write in the cluster.
questions.analogy: A committee of 3 needs 2 votes: one absent member changes nothing; with two absent, no decision passes.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - kubectl still answers. Check the health of EVERY etcd member, not only the local one.

options.why: Checks only 127.0.0.1, cp1's own member: 'healthy', while the dead member on cp3 stays invisible.
member list shows the configured members, all 'started', even a dead one: membership, not health.
No CA and no client certificate: the TLS handshake fails before any member is checked.

s1.explain: --cluster takes the member list from the local member and checks every member's client URL. One unhealthy member out of three is expected here: cp1 and cp2 still answer, which is why kubectl through the load balancer keeps working.
s1.hint: etcdctl with endpoint, CA, client cert and key; endpoint health, for every member of the cluster.

context: https://192.168.10.11:2379 is healthy: successfully committed proposal: took = 9.84ms
https://192.168.10.12:2379 is healthy: successfully committed proposal: took = 11.2ms
https://192.168.10.13:2379 is unhealthy: failed to commit proposal: context deadline exceeded
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Is there still a leader? Show every member's status (leader, raft term) as a table.

options.why: Without --cluster only the local member is shown: you learn whether cp1 leads, not who does.
Members and URLs only: no leader, no raft term, so it cannot tell whether quorum holds.
Health again, as a table: there is no IS LEADER column.

s2.explain: A leader on cp1 or cp2 proves quorum: 3 members need 2 (a majority) to elect a leader and commit writes, so 2 of 3 keeps the cluster working. Lose one more and the last member has no majority: no leader, writes and the API server stop.
s2.hint: Same connection flags; endpoint status for every member, printed as a table.

context: cp3$ systemctl is-enabled kubelet; systemctl is-active kubelet
s3.prompt: Step 3 - On cp3 the kubelet, which starts etcd and the API server as static Pods, did not come back. Start it now AND at every boot.

options.why: kubeadm's etcd is a static Pod started by the kubelet, not a systemd unit: 'Unit etcd.service not found'.
Works today, but the unit stays disabled: the next reboot takes cp3 and its etcd member down again.
Removes the Node object, not the problem: the etcd member stays registered and down, and cp3 would have to be joined again.

s3.explain: Once running, the kubelet reads /etc/kubernetes/manifests and restarts etcd and the API server. The etcd member keeps its data directory and catches up from the leader: no 'member add', the member never left the cluster.
s3.hint: systemctl can enable a unit for boot and start it now in one command.

s4.prompt: Step 4 - Back on cp1: check that an etcd Pod runs again on every control-plane node (show the node column).

options.cmd: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=etcd -o wide
aliases: kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l component=etcd -o wide
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o wide

options.why: Looks in default: 'No resources found'. Control-plane static Pods live in kube-system.

options.cmd: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=etcd -o wide
options.why: kubeadm labels its static Pods component=etcd and tier=control-plane: app=etcd matches nothing.
component=etcd is a Pod label, not a node label: no node matches.

s4.explain: Expect etcd-cp1, etcd-cp2 and etcd-cp3 Running, one per node, and cp3 Ready again. A Running Pod is not yet a caught-up member: rerun 'endpoint health --cluster' and wait for 3 healthy.
s4.hint: etcd static Pods carry component=etcd in kube-system; add the node column.

s5.prompt: Step 5 - Finally, check that cp3 is Ready again as a control-plane node.

options.why: Run on cp1 it checks cp1's kubelet; even on cp3, 'active' does not mean the node is Ready.
Shows the API server Pods, not the nodes' Ready condition.
Lists the API servers serving the 'kubernetes' Service, not the node status.

s5.explain: cp3 Ready means its kubelet heartbeats again: with etcd back as the third member the cluster can again lose one control plane without losing quorum.
s5.hint: One listing shows each node's Ready status.
